notes.text: Alfonso (Alonso) de Aragón (1470–1520), natural son of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Aldonza Ruiz de Ivorra. Provided to the see of Zaragoza by Sixtus IV on 14 August 1478, aged about eight, initially as administrator; ordained priest and bishop only on 7–8 November 1501; archbishop of Valencia 1512; d. 24 February 1520. In May 1486 he was about sixteen, which explains the comparison with royal-born *adolescentes* at §s001-05. Source: Fernández Serrano, *Cuadernos de Historia Jerónimo Zurita* 19–20.

On the author’s order there is disagreement: Catalan scholarship on Scotism (in the journal *Enrahonar*) calls him ‘fra Guillem Gorris, de la Província d’Aragó’, whereas the *Catholic Encyclopedia* article ‘Scotism and Scotists’ states that he was *not* a Franciscan. The incipit (§s002-t) styles him only ‘professor of arts and sacred theology’ and ‘Aragonese’ (‘Aragonensis… artium et sacre theologie professor’).
The vicar general of the archdiocese of Zaragoza. As Alfonso held the see as a minor administrator, government was exercised through vicars general; the individual meant here is not yet identified.
Gorris writes from Toulouse (cf. §s001-06 ‘Tholosanis vigiliis’), i.e. away from his native Aragon.

Print reads *sumulatim* (possibly with a faint nasal stroke). Taken as *summulatim*, ‘in the form of summaries’, a rare adverb from *summula*; *simulatim* is less likely in context. Translation follows *summulatim*. B prints *sūmulatim* (= *summulatim*), confirming the reading.

The image of drawing water from a deep, dark well into a shallow one is Gorris’s programme for the whole book: Scotus’s doctrine made accessible by abridgement. Cf. the ‘rivulus … a fonte’ image at §s002-09.
Lat. *pontifex*, in fifteenth-century usage simply ‘bishop’; rendered ‘prelate’ to avoid the papal connotation of ‘pontiff’.
Lat. *quam vellem sic legas, vt eam tenuem et inopem nec scriptione magnopere dignam iudices*: a modesty topos; the construction is loose and the translation interprets it.

Printed *mortaliū*. Grammar expects *omnes mortales* (subject of *indicant*); possibly a compositor’s error, or an ellipse (*omnes mortalium [linguae]*). Kept as printed; translated as if *mortales*. B has the same *mortaliū iudicant*, so the anomaly is not a Toulouse misprint; B’s *iudicant* (‘judge’) is the better verb (A *indicant*, ‘declare’; both make sense).
So printed. *insectatio* normally means ‘pursuit, hostile pursuit’; here apparently ‘zealous pursuit (of studies)’. A misprint for *inspectio* / *inspectatio* (‘scrutiny’) cannot be excluded.
Printed *castigauēt* with r-abbreviation; expanded *castigauerit*.
Question mark supplied by the editor; the print has a colon after *potest*.
Printed *vnūq3*. Read *vnumque* (‘and one [single] light’); *vnumquemque* is palaeographically possible but gives poorer sense.

So printed. Apparently a noun formed from *antistare* (‘to excel’), ‘pre-eminence’, parallel to *principatum*. Not in classical lexica; kept. B reads *antistitum* (‘of prelates’): ‘[among] prelates you hold [such pre-eminence] in virtues’. B’s reading is easier and may be right; A is kept as copy-text, but the translation is compatible with either.
A striking coinage, *trans hominem*, ‘beyond the human’; rendered ‘more than human’.

The book was printed at Toulouse by Henricus (Heinrich) Mayer; the Biblioteca Nacional de Portugal record of this copy (INC. 535, purl.pt/32008) dates it ‘posterior a 10 Maio 1486’, i.e. after the date of this letter; [256] leaves, 4°. Collated here with B = the Speyer reprint ([Peter Drach, c. 1492]; GW 10961; Munich BSB 4 Inc.s.a. 910 a), which omits the dating clause *Datum Tholose … lxxxvi°* altogether. A manuscript copy of c. 1490 (Edinburgh, NLS, from the Carmelites of Baccarat) has not yet been consulted.
10 May 1486: the letter’s date and the terminus post quem of the printing. *May* = *Maii*, printed thus.
*sensus* here in the sense of judgement/understanding (cf. *sensus communis*), not sense-perception.

‘Scotus of / for the Poor’: the *pauperes* are students who cannot afford, or have no time for, the many volumes required (cf. §s002-02 *ob plurimorum librorum reuolutionem*). The title places the work in the tradition of compendia ‘for the poor’ such as the *Biblia pauperum* and the *Thesaurus pauperum*.

Peter Lombard, *Sententiae in IV libris distinctae*. The text Gorris abridges is Scotus’s *Ordinatio* (*Opus Oxoniense*): his lemmata in the Prologue reproduce its wording verbatim, e.g. *Dicta tamen responsio ad secundam rationem* (§s003-08 = *Ord.* prol. n. 80), *Alia datur responsio quod ex solis maioribus* (§s003-09 = n. 85), *Ad primum distinguo de obiecto naturali* (§s003-10 = n. 90). Which printed or manuscript form of the *Ordinatio* he used remains to be established (note that his argument-numbering is one lower than the Vatican edition’s).
A space was left by the printer for the initial, supplied in this copy by hand as a red *Q* (likewise the red *C* at §s003-01).
Lit. ‘to be curdled, congealed’, i.e. condensed; rendered ‘to condense’.
Elliptical (no verb); sense apparently ‘since the path [through them] is no short one’. Translation conjectural.
‘Those who travel’: plausibly wandering scholars or mendicants who cannot carry a library; Gorris returns to them at §s002-02.
Divided in the print across a line-break (*ob | res*); not *obres*.

Printed *Citacoꝝ*. Unidentified. Possibly for *psittacorum*/*sitacorum* (‘of parrots’), hence the hesitant translation; *cicadarum* is palaeographically less likely. The bee-image of gathering flowers into one place is a classical commonplace for compilation (Seneca, *Ep.* 84; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, praef.). B prints the same unintelligible form, so the crux goes back to the copy-text and is not resolved by collation.
*p* with a superscript stroke: read *pre-* (*preeligendos*, ‘to be picked out’); *per-* (*perlegendos*) is not excluded. B: *preeligendos* in full, confirming the reading.
*alveus*: hollow, channel, or beehive; rendered ‘hive’ to keep the bee simile.
John Duns Scotus (c. 1265/66–1308), the *Doctor Subtilis*.
*alterum … alterum*: taken as referring respectively to the conclusions of arguments and the abridgements of opinions.
First word of p. 4, printed thus: = *hortor*, without the aspirate.
Isaiah 53:7 (Vulg.): *quasi agnus coram tondente se obmutescet et non aperiet os suum*; cf. Acts 8:32.
The type appears to read *fouoris*: either a misprint or a damaged *a*. Read *fauoris*. B: *fauoris*, confirming the reading.

The sense (‘though least, yet unworthy’) is awkward; perhaps for *et* or *tanquam*. Translated freely (‘and unworthy withal’). B reads the same phrase (misprinted *mimus* for *minimus*), so the wording is authorial; the awkwardness is Gorris’s own.
*magister sacrae paginae*: the standard title of a master (doctor) of theology.
Literally ‘bodies’; whether Gorris means the hearers’ bodies (prosperity, honour) or ‘bodies’ of learning is unclear. Translated literally.

The formula *omnium fidelium mater et magistra* for the Roman Church is standard (cf. Fourth Lateran Council, const. 5). [Checked: Liber Extra (Friedberg text via SCTA) X 5.33.23 *Antiqua* = Lateran IV c. 5: ‘Romanam ecclesiam, quae … utpote mater universorum Christi fidelium et magistra’. Gorris’s exact wording *cunctorum/omnium fidelium mater est et magistra* is closer to Lateran IV c. 2 (X 1.1.2 *Damnamus*, ‘quam Romana tenet ecclesia, quae disponente Domino cunctorum fidelium mater est et magistra’), also in X 1.3.5 and 3.31.18. Standard curial formula.]

Gorris is quoting the Digest. Cf. Gaius, *Dig.* 1.2.1: *quanto magis interpretationem promittentibus inconveniens erit omissis initiis atque origine non repetita … protinus materiam interpretationis tractare? namque nisi fallor istae praefationes et libentius nos ad lectionem propositae materiae producunt et cum ibi venerimus, evidentiorem praestant intellectum*; and Pomponius, *Dig.* 1.2.2 pr.: *Necessarium itaque nobis videtur ipsius iuris originem atque processum demonstrare. Et quidem …*. The ‘greatest lawgiver’ is presumably Justinian, in whose name the Digest speaks (or Gaius himself).
*epigramma* in the sense of ‘title, inscription’.
*scotizare*, ‘to scotize’: to follow, or think along with, Scotus. Kept as a neologism in quotation marks; cf. *scotizarent* §s002-10.
Scotus’s customary epithet; capitalised in the translation (‘the Subtle Doctor’).
‘Articles’: the subdivisions of Scotus’s questions in the edition(s) Gorris used.

A fourfold summary of the *Sentences* (Trinity; creation; Incarnation; sacraments and resurrection) attributed to Scotus (*prout a Scoto traditur*). The exact source has not yet been identified. [Checked: not found in Scotus, *Ord.* I (Wadding/Vivès text via SCTA), nor in Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* (Quaracchi via SCTA); a different rhymed division is in the commentaries’ *Divisio quattuor librorum*. Source still unidentified.]
The *Filioque*: procession of the Holy Spirit from Father and Son (Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 11).
Beginning of the commentary proper (p. 6, verso). Headed *Prologus*; hand-supplied red initial *C* at the start of the question. B adds no separate heading here.

= Scotus, *Ordinatio*, Prologus, pars 1, q. unica, n. 1 (Vatican ed., vol. I): *Quaeritur utrum homini pro statu isto sit necessarium aliquam doctrinam specialem supernaturaliter inspirari, ad quam videlicet non posset attingere lumine naturali intellectus.* Gorris reads *supernaturalem* for *supernaturaliter* and *possit* for *posset*.

*pro statu isto*: Scotus’s technical expression for the condition of the wayfarer in this life (as opposed to the state of innocence or of glory). Rendered ‘in the present state’, as is standard in Scotist English.

So A. B reads *Videtur quod non*, and the *Ordinatio* (prol. n. 1) *Et quod non, arguo sic*: the argument concludes that no supernatural doctrine is necessary. A’s *sic* is kept as copy-text; the translation follows B and the *Ordinatio* (see the English note on ‘It seems not’).
*ens inquantum ens*, the first (adequate) natural object of the intellect for Scotus; rendered ‘being *qua* being’.
Scholastic *posse in* + acc.: ‘to have power over, extend to’ an object; rendered ‘can extend to’.

Aristotle, *De anima* II. Scotus (*Ord.* prol. n. 1) proves the major by the example of the first object of sight, which points to *De anima* II.7 (418a26 ff.). Exact locus intended by Gorris to be confirmed.

Avicenna, *Liber de philosophia prima* I, c. 5: *ens et res … prima impressione imprimuntur in anima*; cited by Scotus at the same point (*Ord.* prol. n. 1). Abbreviated in the print as *metha.*; expanded *methaphisice*.

anchor.lemma: non est qui possit scire vias eius

notes.text: Baruch 3:31 (Vulg.); cited by Scotus *ad oppositum*, *Ord.* prol. n. 4. *eius* refers to wisdom, hence ‘her ways’.

anchor.lemma: in alium non profundum puteolum luculenter transferendam

notes.text: B omits *et in alium … transferendam* (the second half of the well image), leaving only *ab obscuro et centro terre proximo puteo exhauriendam decreui*.
B: *tibi reuerendissimo pontifici* (om. *et illustrissimo*).
B omits *atque regalem*: *tuam archiepiscopalem dignitatem*.
B: *iniuriam*.
B: *sciri potest*.
B: *admonitum me fuisse*, supplying the subject of the infinitive.
The translation follows B (*Videtur quod non*) and the *Ordinatio* (*Et quod non*) against A’s *Videtur quod sic*; see Latin note on *Videtur quod sic*.
B: *Sed potentia nostra intellectiua*, with the *Ordinatio* (n. 1: *sed intellectus noster*).

‘Two pages further on’: *Ord.* prol. n. 42, *Contra istam quaestionem arguo, et probo quod quaecumque necessaria …*. Gorris’s ‘first opinion’ is Henry of Ghent’s position as reported and attacked by Scotus at nn. 40–48; cf. Henry, *Summa quaestionum ordinariarum* a. 1 q. 4 (attribution as given by the Vatican editors; not yet checked in Henry).

Henry of Ghent (d. 1293), *doctor solemnis*. ‘Sorbonist’ is a late-medieval tag (he was associated with the Sorbonne milieu and a benefactor of it is sometimes claimed); Gorris’s etymology ‘from his college … from his homeland’ is his own. [Checked: no further evidence sought beyond standard reference works; the Sorbonne connection is not documented in Henry’s Summa or Quodlibeta. Remains open.]

anchor.lemma: incipit. hec ratio est contra philosophos

notes.text: B: *quedam incipit*, ‘a certain [argument] begins’, and prints *in scoto* for A’s *in Scoto*. Gorris refers to the opening of Scotus’s rebuttal, *Ord.* prol. n. 43 ff.

*Ord.* prol. n. 49 (*Quarto sic: omne agens per cognitionem …*, Vatican wording differs slightly). Gorris assigns it to Thomas, *Summa theologiae* I q. 1 a. 1 corp.: *homo ordinatur ad Deum sicut ad quendam finem qui comprehensionem rationis excedit*; the Vatican apparatus gives the same reference.
B: *Quinto arguitur sic. Omne agens*, agreeing with the *Ordinatio* (n. 51); A’s *nullum* is a slip.

anchor.lemma: in §. hec ratio videtur concludere contra eum

notes.text: *Ord.* prol. n. 52: *Haec ratio videtur concludere contra eum …*. The ‘him’ attacked is the author of the argument (Henry/Ware), whose own principles would forbid such knowledge.

William of Ware OFM (fl. c. 1290–1305), Scotus’s supposed master, *In I Sent.*, prol. q. 2 (unedited; numbered differently in the manuscripts). Gorris names Ware constantly as Scotus’s silent interlocutor, an important testimony to how fifteenth-century Scotists read the *Ordinatio*. [Checked: Henry’s argument is *Summa* a. 3 q. 4 (‘Utrum contingat hominem scire omnia ex puris naturalibus’), ed. Badius (Paris 1520) via SCTA: ‘ab agente per instrumentum non potest procedere actio ad quam instrumentum se extendere non potest … lumine naturali … limitatum est’. Ware, *In I Sent.* prol. q. 2, is unedited and could not be checked; status stays open for that half.]
*Ord.* prol. n. 79: *Ad rationem tertiam quaere responsionem Thomae in Summa I q. 1*. Gorris calls it ‘the second’ because he counts the arguments one lower than the Vatican edition.

Gorris’s ‘prima parte q. 54 a. 2’ must mean the *Prima Secundae*: Thomas, *ST* I-II q. 54 a. 2 (‘Utrum habitus distinguantur secundum obiecta’), co.: habit ‘et est forma quaedam, et est habitus’, so habits are distinguished like forms ‘secundum diversa principia activa’; ad 2: the astronomer and the natural philosopher prove the earth round by different *media*, ‘sicut diversa principia activa’ (Leonine text, Corpus Thomisticum). This is exactly the exposition in *Ord.* prol. p. 1 q. un. (Wadding/Vivès text via SCTA), ‘Dicta autem responsio ad secundum exponitur sic: habitus et est habitus, et est forma …’, and Gorris’s ‘soluendo argumentum 2um’ fits. The first reply (‘quere responsum Thome’) is *ST* I q. 1 a. 1 ad 2 (‘diversa ratio cognoscibilis diversitatem scientiarum inducit … terra est rotunda’), likewise verified. *ST* I q. 54 a. 2 (on angels) is not meant. The English keeps Gorris’s ‘First Part’.

Godfrey of Fontaines, *Quodlibet* XIV? Godfrey’s quodlibets number fifteen; the locus is not yet identified. B prints the reference without *seu c. 9*. [Checked: Godfrey, *Quodl.* XIV in Hoffmans’s edition (Philosophes Belges V, 1932–35, archive.org) has only 5 qq.; q. 4 is ‘Utrum praeter iustitiam sit alia virtus appetitiva generalis’ (p. 357), unrelated. Searches of Quodl. XI–XIV for the habitus/forma/*principia activa* argument and the ‘terra rotunda’ example found nothing. Godfrey VIII–X not searched in full. Still open; ‘c. 9’ may reflect a different division.]

A prints *ppositiuo* (*p* with stroke). The form is meaningless as it stands. B reads *ex ppositio in .i. parte sum.*, i.e. *ex proposito in prima parte summe*, ‘expressly in the first part of the *Summa*’, which the translation adopts. Alternatively *Praepositiuo*, i.e. Praepositinus of Cremona’s *Summa*; but the ‘first part of the *Summa*’ strongly suggests Thomas again (*ST* I q. 1). Cf. *Ord.* prol. n. 84.
*Ord.* prol. n. 85, verbatim (*Alia datur responsio quod ex solis maioribus …*). B: *ex maioribus solum*.

anchor.lemma: Ad primum distinguo de obiecto naturali

notes.text: *Ord.* prol. n. 90, Scotus’s reply to the first principal argument. B omits *ex fratre* in the following sentence.

Augustine, *De Trinitate* XV.27.50 (the last chapter, as Gorris says): *Quae igitur causa est cur acie fixa ipsam videre non possis nisi utique infirmitas, et quis eam tibi fecit nisi utique iniquitas?* Gorris quotes freely (*possumus*, *non nisi*). Scotus does not cite this text here; it is Gorris’s own addition. Checked against the Latin Library text of *De Trin.* XV.

Summary of *Ord.* prol. nn. 57–62, Scotus’s distinction of natural and supernatural by comparison of the receptive power to the act received and to the agent; ‘God begets’, ‘God is three and one’ are Scotus’s examples.
Cf. *Ord.* prol. n. 90 ff. (reply to the first argument): the intellect can know God under the general concept of being, but not under the proper concept of deity.
*respondet affirmatiue titulo*: ‘answers the [question’s] title affirmatively’, i.e. Scotus holds that supernatural doctrine is necessary.
Translating the conjecture *ex proposito* (from B’s *ex ppositio*); see the Latin note on *propositiuo*.
*intellectus agens et fantasma*, the two natural concauses of intellection in Scotus; whatever exceeds their causality is ‘supernatural’ to the intellect.
A difficult sentence: *Dum contra eum dicit doctor subtilis* seems to identify the person against whom Scotus turns the argument (cf. *Ord.* prol. n. 52). The bracket makes the reference explicit.
= *Ord.* prol. p. 2 q. un., n. 95: *Utrum cognitio supernaturalis necessaria viatori sit sufficienter tradita in sacra Scriptura*.

Augustine, *De civitate Dei* XI.3: *huic [scripturae] fidem habemus de his rebus quas ignorare non expedit nec per nos nosse idonei sumus*; cited at *Ord.* prol. n. 98. Gorris reads *His*; B *Hic*. The verb *nosse* has dropped out in A.
*Ord.* prol. n. 99 names Augustine *and* Damascene *De haeresibus* (B: *aug. et damas.*); Gorris’s A drops Damascene. The examples (Manichaeans via *De utilitate credendi*; Jas 5:16) are Scotus’s.
Jas 5:16; the heresy is that confession may be made to, and absolution given by, a layman (*Ord.* prol. n. 99: *dicendo illud posse a quocumque non sacerdote …*).

Scotus (*Ord.* prol. n. 101) cites Augustine, *De civ. Dei* XII.10: *vera esse praeterita ex his quae futura praenuntiavit, cum tanta veritate implentur, ostendit*; B agrees (*xii … c. x*). A’s ‘X, at the end’ garbles this reference; the translation keeps A’s wording.
Augustine, *De civ. Dei* XVIII.41–43 (concord of the canonical writers, the Septuagint); *Ord.* prol. n. 102 cites XVIII.42 (B: *c. xlij*).

Richard of St Victor, *De Trinitate* I c. 2, which has both *a summae sanctitatis viris* and *Domine, si error est, a te decepti sumus* (n105); ‘c. 3°’ in A is a slip, and Gorris’s own later ‘primo de trini. c. 2’ is right. Checked through Bonaventure, *Qq. de myst. Trin.* q. 1 a. 2 (Quaracchi V), which quotes both sentences as ‘Richardus primo libro de Trinitate capitulo secundo’; Ribaillier’s edition (1958) was not consulted directly. Scotus cites the same chapter at *Ord.* prol. nn. 105, 113.
So A; B and the *Ordinatio* (n. 107, after Augustine, *De civ.* XVIII.38): *diuina inspiratione*. The translation follows *inspiratione*.
A’s *Dieronimum* is a misprint (D for H); B *Hieronimum*. Augustine, *Ep.* 82.1.3 to Jerome; in Gratian, *Decretum* D. 9 c. 5 (*Ego solis*). Cited at *Ord.* prol. n. 107.
Augustine, *Ep.* 82.3: *didici hunc timorem honoremque deferre*. A’s *dedisti … diferre* is corrupt; B *Didici … deferre*. Translation follows Augustine and B. Checked against augustinus.it.
Augustine: *quantalibet sanctitate doctrinaque praepolleant*. A corrupt; B *quanta sanctitate quantaue doctrina*. Translation follows Augustine.
Augustine, *De civ. Dei* XVIII.38 on the Book of Enoch (Jude 14) and the lost books cited in Kings; *Ord.* prol. n. 107.
The quotation *Hoc fac et viues* is Luke 10:28, not Matthew 7; B reads *Lu. x*. Scotus (*Ord.* prol. n. 108) cites Matt 7:12 (*Hoc facias alii …*, the Golden Rule). A conflates the two.
B: *nihil est vanius* without *quo*. The phrase replaces Scotus’s *in quibus nihil est numinis* (*Ord.* prol. n. 109).

Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* I.5, 1095b19–22 (Sardanapallus as the type of the life of pleasure). Scotus’s text at n. 109 speaks rather of the Saracens’ ‘gluttony and coition’ and cites Avicenna, *Metaph.* IX; Gorris transfers the charge to the pagans.
B: *expectant*, ‘await’, which the translation follows.

Augustine, *De utilitate credendi* 17.35 (*Dubitabimus nos eius Ecclesiae condere gremio …*), cited at *Ord.* prol. n. 111. ‘8°’ is not a book number (the work has one book); perhaps a chapter number in Gorris’s source. [Checked: Aug., *De utilitate credendi* 17.35 (PL 42, text at augustinus.it): ‘dubitabimus nos eius Ecclesiae condere gremio …’. Verified; ‘8°’ still unexplained.]

anchor.lemma: si est error a te decepti sumus

notes.text: Richard of St Victor, *De Trinitate* I.2: *Domine, si error est, a te decepti sumus …*; *Ord.* prol. n. 113.
Josephus, *Antiquitates* XVIII.3.3 (the *Testimonium Flavianum*); *Ord.* prol. n. 118. B: *c. xxxiii*.
Augustine, *De civ. Dei* XVIII.23 (the Erythraean Sibyl’s acrostic ΙΧΘΥΣ); *Ord.* prol. n. 118.
B and the *Ordinatio* (n. 119): *querentibus toto corde*.

*Ord.* prol. n. 112 (under Scotus’s seventh way, as Gorris says): *illa incepit plusquam sexcentis annis post legem Christi, et in brevi, Domino volente, finietur, quia multum debilitata est anno Christi millesimo trecentesimo*.

A *Abynot⁹*, B *abynorus*. Evidently Hayton (Hethum) of Corycus, the Armenian prince-historian, author of the *Flos historiarum terre Orientis* (1307). He was a kinsman (nephew) of King Hethum I, not ‘brother of the king’, and the work was presented to Pope Clement V, not to Philip IV of France, although it circulated with French royal patronage. The form of the name is unexplained.
Scotus (*Ord.* prol. n. 112): *prophetia dicitur apud eos esse*, ‘among them [the Saracens]’. Gorris’s lemma reads *apud nos*.

The *Liber Sancti Jacobi* (*Codex Calixtinus*), ascribed to Pope Calixtus II; Book IV, the Pseudo-Turpin, c. 4 *De ydolo Mahummet*: the idol *Salam Cadis* at Cádiz holding a great key that will fall in the year a future king of the Franks is born. Checked against the Pseudo-Turpin text (ed. Smyser; skaldic.org text).
A *Salez cadis*, B *saulem cadis*; Pseudo-Turpin *Salam Cadis*.
A prints *met* (inverted *u*?); B *ruet*, adopted. The clause is elliptic: in the Pseudo-Turpin the key falls *anno quo rex futurus in Gallia natus fuerit*; Gorris leaves the time-clause unfinished.

Pseudo-Turpin: *Cadis dicitur locus … Salam in lingua arabica Deus dicitur*. Gorris’s sentence seems to have misplaced *deus*, which belongs with *salem* (‘*salem* in Arabic means God’); *mons* for ‘place’ is his own. *deus* is therefore probably intrusive here.

A: 1500; B: *millesimum sexcentesimum* (1600). B’s change looks like an updating of a failed prophecy-date, but 1600 could also be the original. The source of the astrological prophecy is not identified.
Paraphrase of Rom 11:25–26 (*caecitas ex parte contigit in Israel … et sic omnis Israel salvus fieret*), merged with Isa 10:22 / Rom 9:27 (*reliquiae salvae fient*).
B: *hebreorum*.
A reads *diuina miseratione* (‘by divine mercy’); the translation follows B and the *Ordinatio*/Augustine, *inspiratione*.

anchor.lemma: in his first letter to Jerome

notes.text: A’s *Dieronimum* corrected to Jerome (B *Hieronimum*). It is Augustine’s *Ep.* 82, not his first letter to Jerome; Gorris presumably means ‘first’ as quoted in the *Decretum*.
Translating Augustine’s *didici* (B) for A’s corrupt *dedisti* (‘you have given’).

anchor.lemma: This do, and thou shalt live

notes.text: Luke 10:28 (B *Lu. x*); A wrongly cites ‘Matthew 7’, and the reference has been omitted from the translation. Biblical quotations are given in the Douay-Rheims wording where possible.
Following B *expectant*; A *spectant* (‘look to’) would also do.

anchor.lemma: the brother of the King of Armenia

notes.text: Gorris’s description; historically Hayton was the king’s nephew. See Latin note on *Abynotus*.
The Latin breaks off (*que dum ruet vel ruit*); the ellipsis marks the incomplete clause rather than an omission by the translator.
Literally ‘but *deus cadis* is a mountain’; *deus* seems intrusive (see Latin note) and is not translated.
So A; B has 1600.

anchor.lemma: The remnant of Israel shall be converted in the end

notes.text: Gorris’s free version of Romans 11, translated literally.
B prefixes the title *Vtrum theologia sit de deo vt de subiecto*, which A lacks. *Ord.* prol. p. 3 qq. 1–3, nn. 124 ff.

anchor.lemma: forma inquit simplex subiectum esse non potest

notes.text: Boethius, *De Trinitate* c. 2: *forma vero quae est sine materia non poterit esse subiectum*; cited at *Ord.* prol. n. 129.

Corrupt in both witnesses: A *sexto de trinitate*, B *aug. viii. de tri.*. The quotation is Augustine, *De civ. Dei* VIII.1 (*theologian … quo verbo Graeco significari intellegimus de divinitate rationem sive sermonem*), as at *Ord.* prol. n. 132 and as Gorris himself cites it correctly at §s005-05.
B: *respicit*.

Giles of Rome, *Quodlibet* III q. 2 (ed. Louvain 1646): God as subject *sub ratione restauratoris / reparatoris*; cf. *Ord.* prol. n. 164 and n. 168. Exact question to be checked. [Checked: Giles’s *Quodlibeta* (Louvain 1646) are not available online in searchable form (SCTA holds only Quodl. I q. 6). Still open.]
A is corrupt; B reads *Vel posset poni … vt fr. Guilhel. var.*, which matches Scotus’s sequence of alternatives (*vel posset poni …*). The translation follows B.

Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 19 qq. 1–2 (‘De quo est theologia ut de subiecto’; ‘… ut de materia’), ed. Badius 1520 via SCTA: God is the subject ‘sub ea ratione … sub qua omnia cognoscendo in ipsa ad ipsum potest fieri attributio’, i.e. under a ratio to which everything is related by *attributio*. These are Gorris’s ‘duabus primis questionibus’. Henry there also rejects the view that God is subject ‘solum inquantum redemptor aut reparator’, the Giles view of n134. *Ord.* prol. n. 159 ff.

The view that Christ (*Christus integer*, head and members) is the subject of theology is commonly attributed to Robert Kilwardby and Robert Grosseteste; Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* prooem. q. 1, names the *credibile* as subject but allows Christ as *subiectum integrale*. Gorris’s attribution to Bonaventure is therefore partly right. *Ord.* prol. n. 172. [Checked: Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* prooem. q. 1 (Quaracchi I, via SCTA), conclusion: ‘Deus est subiectum theologiae radicale, Christus est subiectum integrale, res et signa sunt subiectum universale sive etiam credibile’. Gorris’s attribution is partly right, as stated.]

Henry of Ghent, *Quodlibet* III q. 6? Gorris’s identification of the source of *Ad tertiam quaestionem sic posset probabiliter dici* (*Ord.* prol. n. 196) is not yet verified. [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* III q. 6 in Badius 1518 (via SCTA) is on the vegetative and sensitive soul in Christ, which does not fit; no question of Quodl. III treats theology’s object. The reference is wrong as printed and the right locus was not found.]
Augustine, *De civ. Dei* VIII.1. Correct here, cf. note on *sexto de trinitate*.

*Ord.* prol. nn. 141 ff. (theology in itself / in us; necessary and contingent theology; the primary subject virtually containing all truths of the habit). Gorris here quotes Scotus nearly verbatim, hence the quotation marks in the translation.
Aristotle, *Metaph.* VI.1, 1026a21: *honorabilissimam scientiam oportet esse circa honorabilissimum genus*; *Ord.* prol. n. 157.

*Ord.* prol. n. 158: fourfold knowledge of man (proper; common; *per accidens*; relative). Gorris sorts Henry, Ware and Giles under these heads, which is his own (or his school’s) schematisation of nn. 159–168.
*Ord.* prol. n. 168: the first object of our theology is *ens infinitum*, the most perfect concept of God available to us *pro statu isto*.
B: *incarnatus a virgine*.

A *ex propria motione earum*; B *ex proprie motione earum*, confirming *motione*. The blessed may have natural knowledge of creatures moved by the creatures themselves, besides seeing them in the divine essence (*Ord.* prol. n. 200 ff.).
A prints *būs* (abbreviation); B has *beatus*, which confirms the expansion.
B: *grammatica siue logica*.

anchor.lemma: [Augustine, The City of God] VIII, c. 1

notes.text: The translation silently corrects A’s ‘*De Trinitate* VI’ to Augustine, *De civitate Dei* VIII.1, the real source of the definition.

anchor.lemma: Or [a science] could be posited under some attributal aspect

notes.text: Translated from B (*vel posset poni*), since A’s *Et huic nihil potest poni* gives no sense here.
*reparator*: God as restorer of fallen nature, i.e. as Redeemer.
Gorris’s compressed classification (*communis … accidentalis … respectiua*) is expanded in brackets so as to align it with the fourfold division just given.

anchor.lemma: from their own motion [upon his intellect]

notes.text: *ex propria motione earum*: the creatures themselves moving the intellect as objects.
B repeats the first words (dittography) at the start of the question.

anchor.lemma: Fortasse non erunt cogitationes nostre volubiles

notes.text: Augustine, *De Trinitate* XV.16.26: *Fortassis etiam non erunt volubiles nostrae cogitationes ab aliis in alia euntes atque redeuntes*; cited in Scotus’s Prologue, part 4. Checked against the Latin Library text.
B: *doctor subtilis superficialiter*.

Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 13 qq. 6–7 (‘Utrum eam addiscens acquirat aliquam notitiam eius super notitiam fidei’; ‘Utrum cum illa ulteriori notitia stet notitia fidei’), ed. Badius 1520 via SCTA: the theologian’s understanding of the *credibilia* grows like light ‘ab ortu diei usque ad meridiem’ (q. 7), which is the image Gorris describes (morning light, noonday light, and a ‘middle’ light advancing between them). Scotus rejects it. Gorris says the rejection is ‘in the *reportationes*’ (*reportatoriis*, confirmed by B), i.e. Scotus’s *Reportatio* (*Report. Paris.* prol.), not the *Ordinatio*: a sign that he had a *Reportatio* to hand. (The Reportatio passage itself was not checked.)
So A (and substantially B): an inverted reference, presumably *li. 1 q. 3* (William of Ware, *In I Sent.* prol. q. 3), as the translation assumes.
B: *improbata*.
A *sare* is a misprint; B *prout scire definitur*, adopted in the translation. Aristotle, *Posterior Analytics* I.2, 71b9–12 (definition of *scire*).
*Ord.* prol. n. 208: the four conditions of science in the strict sense (certain; of necessary truth; caused by evident prior necessary truth; applied by syllogistic discourse).
Aristotle, *EN* VI.3, 1139b18–24 (science of the necessary), paraphrased in the medieval *auctoritates* tradition.
B: *vi. metaph. et i. poste.*; the principle *singularium non est scientia* (cf. *Metaph.* VI.2, 1026b; VII.15).
Aristotle, *APo* I.3, 72b23–25, in its medieval *auctoritas* form.
A *theologie* is a misreading of *Thome* (*Thō*); B *opinio thome*. Thomas, *ST* I q. 1 a. 2: sacred doctrine is subalternated to the science of God and the blessed. The translation reads ‘Thomas’.
A is elliptic; B has the full text *sunt de eisdem conclusionibus. sic igitur theologia nostra non est subalternata …*, which the translation supplies in brackets.
Aristotle, *APo* I.13, 78b32 ff. (harmonics subalternated to arithmetic); *Ord.* prol. p. 4.
Latin *discursus* is kept in technical passages: the passage of the intellect from premisses to conclusion; Scotus distinguishes temporal discursus from discursus ‘in the order of nature’.
Lat. *reportatoria*: the reports of Scotus’s lectures (*Reportatio*), as opposed to his revised *Ordinatio*.
Translating the inverted reference *3. q. 1. li.* as Book I, q. 3; see Latin note.
Following B *scire* for A’s *sare*.
A reads *theologie* (‘of theology’); the translation follows B *Thome*.
Supplied from B, where A is elliptic (*sic.*).
Augustine’s *fortassis* in the quoted text (see §s006-02).

A *.31.* is a misprint (no Romans 31); B (b-0016, col. 2) *Ro. xiij.*, and so Scotus, *Ord.* prol. n. 222: *Contra: Rom. 13: Finis legis est dilectio*. The wording is a conflation (Rom 13:10 *plenitudo legis est dilectio*; 1 Tim 1:5 *finis praecepti est caritas*), already in Scotus. B checked.

Boethius, *De Trinitate* c. 2 (speculative science divided into *naturalis, mathematica, theologica*); the argument is Scotus’s *Ord.* prol. n. 219, nearly verbatim (*Boethius De Trinitate assignat tres partes speculativae, quarum una est theologia*).

Godfrey of Fontaines on the source of practical ‘extension’. Scotus names no one; the identification and the reference are Gorris’s. B agrees (*gotfre. de fontibus. qlibe. x. q. ij.*). Not checked against Godfrey’s *Quodlibeta* (ed. Philosophes Belges). [Checked: Godfrey’s *Quodl.* IX–X (Hoffmans, Philosophes Belges IV) are not on archive.org (only V–VII, VIII and XI–XIV are); the reference could not be checked. Still open.]

*Doctor solemnis* = Henry of Ghent. The view that a habit is practical from its end is Henry’s; *Quodl.* VIII q. 1 is Gorris’s reference (B: *qlibet. viij. q. i.*). Not verified in Henry’s *Quodlibeta*. [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* VIII q. 1 (‘Utrum in deo sint ideae practicae’), ed. Badius 1518 via SCTA, distinguishes speculative and practical consideration of *operabilia* by their end: ‘finis speculatiuae est verum, finis vero practicae opus’ (after *Metaph.* II). Fits Scotus’s ‘illud a quo actus et habitus dicuntur practici est finis’.]

B: *fratris Johis roditoris*. The name is unexplained. One candidate is John of Reading OFM (d. 1346), a Scotist whose prologue discusses whether theology is practical, but he is later than Scotus and cannot be the target of the *Ordinatio*. Another is John Rodington OFM (d. 1348), equally late. Gorris may be naming a later holder of the position Scotus rejects, as Scotist commentators often did. Unresolved.

Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 8 q. 3 (‘Utrum sit theorica an practica’), ed. Badius 1520 via SCTA, ad 3: the end of theology is the love and enjoyment of God, but theology is not therefore practical, ‘est enim duplex bonum voluntatis…’ (one that the will brings about in an act extending to something outside it, one that it receives); theology is ‘pure speculatiua’. A and B both print ‘articulo .9. q. 2.’, but in Badius a. 9 q. 2 is ‘Utrum Deus sit auctor sacrae scripturae’, so Gorris’s numerals are a slip (or follow a different division) for a. 8 q. 3. The English keeps the printed reference.

Gorris lists five Henrician Quodlibets for this question (V q. 4, VIII q. 1, IV q. 11, XIII q. 2, I q. 9), and VI q. 2 and XII q. 22 below (§ 8). He clearly worked from a full Henry, or from a Scotist apparatus that cited one. B agrees in all the numerals checked (b-0016/17). The individual references have not been verified. [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: V q. 4 (‘Vtrum deus necessario producat quicquid exterius immediate producit’) argues ‘diuina scientia pure speculatiua est & non practica’; VIII q. 1 (practical ideas in God; ‘finis … practicae opus’); IV q. 11 (whether God can be loved above all with natural love) distinguishes knowledge of God ‘in particulari’ and as ‘finis beatificans’, which is the end ‘in vniuersali et in particulari’; XIII q. 2 (whether God can be loved more than known): the will ‘per dilectionem magis vnitur fini quam intellectus per cognitionem’, the minor of Scotus’s third argument. All four verified. I q. 9 (‘Vtrum creatura ipsa sit suum esse’) has no evident bearing on the point; that one item stays doubtful. VI q. 2 and XII q. 22: see n187.]

anchor.lemma: Guillermi varronis in anglia. et Garronis in gallia

notes.text: William of Ware OFM, *In I Sent.* prol. q. 4 (theology not practical because its object is not contingent; and q. 4 again in § 6 for theology as *contemplativa*). Gorris’s gloss explains the two forms of the name current in the schools, *Varro* (English) and *Garro* (French/continental). B: *garronis*. B checked.

Almost certainly Hervaeus Natalis OP (Hervé Nédellec, d. 1323), a Breton (*Britonis origine*), Dominican (*predicatoris ordine*), and author of the *Defensio doctrinae fratris Thomae* (hence *defensoris theologie officio*?). *Henrici* is then an error, shared by B, for *Heruei*. His *Quodlibet* I q. 3 does not fit chronologically as a target of the *Ordinatio* prologue unless it reflects Paris disputations of c. 1307. The identification is very probable; the reference has not been verified.
*Doctor devotus* = Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* prooem. q. 3 (theology is *gratia ut boni fiamus*, an *habitus affectivus*). Scotus, *Ord.* prol. p. 5, quotes the ‘fourth way’ without naming him.
Giles of Rome OESA, *In I Sent.* prol. (theology as *scientia affectiva*). Gorris gives no question number. The ascription is standard in the Scotist apparatus.

Godfrey of Fontaines, *Quodl.* XIII q. 1 (theology has two habits, one practical and one speculative). The reference is plausible but has not been checked. [Checked: Godfrey, *Quodl.* XIII q. 1 ‘Utrum scientia theologiae sit scientia speculativa’ (Hoffmans, Philosophes Belges V, p. 169 ff., archive.org): theology is to be called ‘aliquo modo utrumque simpliciter, scilicet speculativa et practica’. Verified.]

anchor.lemma: sancti Thome prima parte summe. q. 1. articulo. 4.

notes.text: Thomas Aquinas, *ST* I q. 1 a. 4: sacred doctrine is both speculative and practical, but more speculative. Scotus thought this not worth refuting, because it makes one simple habit both at once. B: *Secunda est Thome* (omitting *sancti*), with the same reference.

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* VI q. 2 and XII q. 22, for the medicine analogy. Not checked against Henry. [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: VI q. 2 (whether the production of the persons is presupposed to that of creatures): the artisan has ‘vnam simplicis notitiae in arte vniuersali … pura speculatione, & aliam notitiae dispositiuae ad opus, qua in arte particulari’; XII q. 22 (‘vtrum intelligere practicum possit absolui ab intentione operis’): practical understanding is only that ‘quod determinat modum operandi in particulari … per habitum practicum acquisitum ex experientia’. Both are Scotus’s *quidam* who says ‘habitus universalis est speculativus, sed quando ex ea acquiritur habitus particularis, tunc fit practicus’ (Ord. prol. p. 5, Wadding/Vivès text via SCTA).]

anchor.lemma: praxis est actus alterius potentie quam intellectus

notes.text: *Ord.* prol. n. 228, verbatim: *praxis … est actus alterius potentiae quam intellectus, naturaliter posterior intellectione, natus elici conformiter rationi rectae ut sit rectus*. Gorris’s ‘three particles’ follow nn. 229–233. The corollary that only an act of the will is *praxis* is n. 230.
Aristotle, *EN* VI.2, 1139a22–26, as used in *Ord.* prol. n. 233 (*electio recta necessario requirit rationem rectam*).

The illustration with florins (gold coins of Florence, then in general circulation) is Gorris’s own and is not in Scotus. It renders the psychology of n. 234 (the commanded act is *praxis* only *quasi per accidens*) in schoolroom terms.

Aristotle, *De anima* III.10, 433a14–15, in its scholastic *auctoritas* form (*Auctoritates Aristotelis*: *intellectus speculativus extensione fit practicus*). Scotus builds the whole question on it (‘practical knowledge receives such extension’). Cf. *Ord.* prol. n. 235.
B: *in prima extensione*, without *determinatione*. B checked (b-0018).
Aristotle, *EN* VI.2, 1139b4–5 (*ὀρεκτικὸς νοῦς ἡ προαίρεσις ἢ ὄρεξις διανοητική*). A and B read *electio* as subject (‘choice is either appetitive intellect or intellective appetite’).

So A and B (*sctũs doctor*, b-0018). Elsewhere Gorris’s *doctor* without qualification is Scotus. *Sanctus doctor* probably means Thomas, canonised in 1323; cf. *ST* I-II q. 13 a. 1, where choice is substantially an act of the will. It is not obviously a misprint for *subtilis*, since both witnesses agree.

anchor.lemma: duplex est finis scilicet quo et quod

notes.text: The distinction between *finis quo* and *finis quod* (or *cuius gratia*) reconciles the Aristotelian authorities on whether practical and speculative are distinguished by end or by object. This is Gorris’s harmonisation; Scotus himself (*Ord.* prol. p. 5, the article on whence a habit is practical) argues that the end does not constitute it practical. [Checked: Scotus, *Ord.* prol. p. 5 qq. 1–2 (Wadding/Vivès text via SCTA) rejects ‘habitus dicitur practicus a fine’; the *quo/quod* distinction does not occur there. As stated.]

The five conclusions summarise Scotus’s solution in *Ord.* prol. p. 5 qq. 1–2 on necessary and contingent theology, in created and divine intellects, with *ostensio* and *ratificatio*: necessaries are practical by the object’s conformity prior to volition, contingents only through the determining will. The paragraph numbers in the Vatican edition (c. nn. 314–332) have not been checked; the Logic Museum text available covers only nn. 217–235. [Checked: the content agrees with *Ord.* prol. p. 5 qq. 1–2 in the Wadding/Vivès text (SCTA); the Vatican numbers could not be checked (Vatican volumes lending-restricted on archive.org). Open only for the paragraph numbers.]
B: *In hunc articulum*.

A *velut* (‘as if’) gives a weak sense. B reads *vel vt videar* (‘or so as to be seen’), which completes the contrast (for the love of God *or* for show), and the translation follows it. B checked (b-0019).
Aristotle, *APo* I.4, 73a34–b5: the first and second modes of *per se* predication. The rule cited is used in Scotus’s reply that faith is not a speculative habit.

So A and B (*ꝑ astrologiã me/taphisicam*, b-0019). Boethius’s three speculative parts are physics, mathematics and theology, so *astrologia* (a part of mathematics) makes no sense here. The intended reading must be *per theologiam metaphysicam*, i.e. Boethius’s ‘theology’ is philosophical theology, metaphysics, which is Scotus’s answer to n. 219. If the error is mechanical, B’s agreement is another error shared with A.
Corrected from A’s impossible *31*, with B and Scotus; see Latin note.
*Doctor solemnis*, the standard title of Henry of Ghent.
Left in Gorris’s form; the identification is unresolved (see Latin note).
Probably Hervaeus Natalis OP; see Latin note.
*Doctor devotus*: Bonaventure.
Gorris’s own example; see Latin note.
*sanctus doctor*: probably Thomas Aquinas (see Latin note).
*ostensio* and *ratificatio*: the object’s displaying of what is to be done, and the will’s confirming determination of it.

anchor.lemma: or so as to be seen by the people

notes.text: Following B *vel ut videar* for A *velut videar*.
So both prints. The sense required is surely ‘by theology Boethius means metaphysics’; see Latin note.
B: *ad cognitionem finalem*.

B: *accipit talem extensionem*, which gives the sense of Scotus's article ('from what practical knowledge receives such extension'); A's *incipit* ('begins such extension') hardly construes. The translation follows B (see note n1026).
Follows B *accipit*; A prints *incipit* (see note n1025).
B: *et etiam alibi*.
B omits *tertio*.
B: *et sumit rationem ex* (omitting *opinione*), followed by *qlib. xiij. q. ij.*
B: *vbi concludit*.
B: *Alia est opinio discordans*.
B: *Secundum in probatione non iudicat dignum*, an evident corruption; A gives the sense. B also omits *simul* before *sit practicus*.
B omits this reference to Henry's *Quodlibet* VI, q. 2. It reads only *idem quolibet. xij. q. xxij.*
B: *vi. ethi.* only, without the chapter reference.

Editorial heading. A has no heading: the question opens with a large red *C* (*Irca*), and the running headline *Di.i.* starts on p. 17. This is where the Prologue ends and Gorris’s commentary on Book I begins.
Augustine, *De diversis quaestionibus 83*, q. 30 (*fruendum est … bonis invisibilibus*). Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 1 n. 1, has *quaestione 30*, so A’s *36* is a misprint or misreading. B not checked here.

Augustine, *De doctrina christiana* I.5.5: *Res igitur quibus fruendum est, Pater et Filius et Spiritus Sanctus, eademque Trinitas, una quaedam summa res*. This is the *ad oppositum* of *Ord.* I d. 1 p. 1 q. 1.

Avicenna, *Metaph.* IX c. 4 (the emanation of the intelligences; each intelligence finds rest in what is above it). Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 1 n. 9: *videtur esse opinio Avicennae quod fruitio ordinata potest esse circa aliud a fine ultimo*. Gorris supplies the chapter.

Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* d. 1 a. 3 q. 2 (‘Utrum solo Deo sive bono increato fruendum sit’), fund. 3 (Quaracchi I, via SCTA): ‘appetitus non sufficienter quietatur nisi per aliquid quod animam implet … sed est capax Dei secundum appetitum’, with Augustine’s ‘Animam totius Trinitatis capacem nihil minus quam Trinitas potest implere’. This is the argument from the image *capax Dei*. A’s ‘articulo .2°. q. 3.’ and B’s ‘ar. xx. (?) q. iij.’ are both wrong: in Quaracchi a. 2 has only one question (whether *frui* is an act of the will).

anchor.lemma: beati Thome prima parte summe. q. 12. articulo .1.

notes.text: Thomas, *ST* I q. 12 a. 1 (the created intellect can see God’s essence; otherwise natural desire would be vain). The argument that the soul, created immediately by God, can be beatified only by him is cited by Scotus among the *alii* against Avicenna (*Ord.* I d. 1 nn. 10–12).
B: *nec in solo deo*, an easy minim error. A is right.
B: *assistendum per voluntatem*, parallel to the preceding *per intellectum*.

On proportion, not likeness, between power and object, so that a finite capacity can be ordered to an infinite object, cf. *Ord.* I d. 1 n. 17 ff.: *inter potentiam et obiectum non est relatio similitudinis sed proportionis*.

The fourfold division of the virtues by function (regulating, restraining, intensifying, both) is attributed to Ambrose, but it is not in Ambrose in this form. It resembles the scholastic doctrine of the cardinal virtues (cf. Thomas, *ST* I-II q. 61 a. 2), which is ultimately built on Ambrose, *De officiis* I. The attribution has not been verified.
Aristotle, *EN* V.2–4, 1130b30 ff. (distributive and corrective/commutative justice). Equating ‘punitive’ justice with commutative justice is Gorris’s (or his source’s) simplification.
Aristotle, *EN* III.11, 1119a6–10: insensibility (the man who delights in nothing) is *far from being human*.

anchor.lemma: que si non est virtus est cum virtute

notes.text: Aristotle, *EN* VIII.1, 1155a3–4: friendship *is a virtue or implies virtue*. B: *et si non est virtus est tamen virtut(e)* (the ending is abbreviated), without *cum*.

Augustine’s classic formula (*De div. qu. 83* q. 30: *omnis perversitas … est uti fruendis et frui utendis*), discussed by Scotus in *Ord.* I d. 1 (q. 3, n. 70). The question which of the two is worse, and its answer by the doctrine of the mean, belong to Gorris.
A prints *intellerit*; B prints *intellexerit* in full, which confirms the emendation. The subject is presumably Augustine (the *auctoritas* of the opening argument).
Scotus and Augustine have q. 30; see Latin note.
Lat. *assistendum*. The sense requires ‘adhere/assent to’, probably a corruption of *assentiendum*: cf. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 1 n. 66, on the intellect’s act *quo assentitur alicui vero propter se*.
*proportio vitalis immutationis*: a proportion of receptive capacity in a living power, not a likeness of nature.

anchor.lemma: to use what is to be enjoyed, or to enjoy what is to be used

notes.text: *uti fruendis vel frui utendis*: Augustine’s technical pair *uti/frui*, kept as ‘use/enjoy’ throughout.
Supplying the subject. The verb is *intellexerit*, as in B (A misprints *intellerit*).
B: *appetitus noster quiuis licet* (the added word looks like *quiuis*, but the reading is not quite clear).
B: *Quedam sunt ad actum intendendum*, matching *ad actum remittendum* just before.
B: *magis amati* ('more loved'), evidently a slip for A's *amatiui* ('more given to loving').
So A and B (*Videtur quod sic*). Logically the argument is for a plurality of *rationes fruibilitatis*, i.e. ‘no’; Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 1 n. 23: *Et quod sit in eo talis distinctio, probatio*.

anchor.lemma: sicut ens et verum sunt in omni genere

notes.text: B: *sicut ens et vnum sunt in omni genere*. The source is Aristotle, *EN* I.6, 1096a23–29: the good is said in as many ways as being, in all the categories.
B: *ibi erit alia et alia ratio fruibilitatis*, which is better.
B: *In principio articuli secundi*, which gives the better sense ('at the beginning of the second article'). A is construable, so the translation renders A (see note n245).

*Ord.* I d. 1 n. 30: *Ista quaestio posset habere quadruplicem difficultatem secundum quadruplicem distinctionem in divinis* (essence/person, person/person, essence/attributes, attribute/attribute). Gorris’s four ‘articles’ are a different division: wayfarer; blessed *de potentia Dei absoluta*; blessed *de potentia creaturae*; *de facto*.
*Ord.* I d. 1 n. 34, verbatim: *De secundo articulo dicitur quod non est possibile loquendo de potentia absoluta Dei quod aliquis comprehensor fruatur essentia divina non fruendo persona*.

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* II q. 7 (the number is printed with the *z*-shaped 2) and, for the reply, *Quodl.* I q. 1. Scotus names no one. These attributions are Gorris’s and have not been verified. [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* II q. 7 (Badius 1518 via SCTA) asks whether the blessed see the three persons with one intuition: ‘persona in deo non potest intelligi nisi dupliciter: vt subsistit in essentia … aut vt vna respicit alteram’. The view that one cannot enjoy the essence without the persons fits. *Quodl.* I q. 1 (‘Utrum in deo sit ponere bonitatem personalem’) is on the relation of essential and personal goodness, but the phrase ‘uniformiter respiciunt essentiam et personam’ was not found there. II q. 7 verified; I q. 1 is plausible.]

anchor.lemma: Ad secundum dicendum quod illa que vniformiter respiciunt

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 1 n. 57.

anchor.lemma: Ad quartum dicit quod de facto est vna fruitio

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 1 n. 54: *de facto erit una visio et una fruitio essentiae in tribus personis*, citing Augustine, *De Trin.* I.10.

anchor.lemma: non est in potestate eius vt actus positus

notes.text: Gorris singles out (*hoc nota diligenter*) Scotus’s principle that the will controls whether an act is posited, but not the modal condition (necessity or freedom) of the act once posited. This is relevant to the later debate on the necessity of beatific enjoyment (*Ord.* I d. 1 p. 2 q. 2). B: *cum non est in potestate eius* for A's *tamen non est …*.

The view that God and the things known in God are known by one act, with new knowledge of secondary objects arising through new relations, recalls Scotus’s own doctrine of the secondary objects of the beatific act (cf. *Ord.* I d. 1 and *Quodl.* q. 14). Gorris’s *quidam* is not identified.

Augustine, *De Trinitate* VII.1.2: *omnis essentia quae relative dicitur est etiam aliquid excepto relativo*. Gorris restricts the rule to first-order relations: a relation founded on a relation (likeness on proportion) leaves something relative when removed.

B: *Vtrum anima se intelligat* (without *semper*).

anchor.lemma: quasi per idem sicut in tertia maxime quia

notes.text: B: *quasi per idem. quia* (without *sicut in tertia maxime*).

Gorris counts eleven questions in d. 3 (the *Ordinatio* has four in p. 1, three in p. 2, four in p. 3). His q. 1 combines Scotus's p. 1 qq. 1–2 (*utrum Deus sit naturaliter cognoscibilis*; *utrum Deus sit primum cognitum*), as the phrase *in prima sunt due* says.

anchor.lemma: sicut distinguit Tho. prima parte summe. q. 12. arti. 12

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 1 q. 1–2 nn. 10–12 rejects three preliminary distinctions (negative/affirmative knowledge; *quia est* / *si est*; *si est* as the truth of a proposition). Gorris assigns the first and third to Thomas: *ST* I q. 12 a. 12 (natural knowledge of God through creatures) and *ST* I q. 3 a. 4 ad 2 (*esse* as act of being versus as the composition of a proposition). The second attribution is exact.

anchor.lemma: doctoris solennis in summa articulo. 22. q. 2. et 3

notes.text: Henry of Ghent, the *Doctor solemnis*. Scotus discusses his view in *Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 16–25. Henry's natural knowledge of God is treated in *Summa* aa. 22–24. The Vatican apparatus cites a. 24 q. 6 for the core passage, so Gorris's *a. 22 qq. 2–3* may refer to the cognate *utrum Deus sit primum cognitum*. [Checked: Henry, *Summa* a. 22 (Badius 1520 via SCTA), q. 2: God is known naturally ‘inquantum cognoscitur ens simpliciter vel bonum simpliciter’; q. 3: known ‘aut indistincte & in vniuersali … [aut] attributis’. This is exactly the view Scotus discusses, so Gorris’s *a. 22 qq. 2–3* is right. Verified.]
*Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 26–55: univocity of the concept of being. Gorris's gloss *substantie et accidenti* takes in n. 26's *univocum Deo et creaturae* and the extension in nn. 129ff.

*ST* I q. 12 a. 4: the proper object of the human intellect is the quiddity of material things. Scotus reports this view in d. 3 n. 186ff. (q. 3). B reads *q. xij arti.* followed by a numeral that is damaged at the line break.

anchor.lemma: Prima quod possumus habere aliquem conceptum

notes.text: The five *dicta* of *Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 25 (*Primo dico*), 26 (univocity), 56 (*Tertio dico… non in particulari et proprio*), 58 (*Quarto… ad multos conceptus proprios Deo*), 61 (*Quinto… per species creaturarum*). Gorris's fourth conclusion turns Scotus's *proprios* into *non proprii sed communes*. That is a misreading, or perhaps a deliberate simplification, since Scotus's *proprii* are those common to all perfections *simpliciter* as they are in God (*ens infinitum*).

Not in Scotus's text here; *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 56 has only *non cognoscitur in particulari et proprio*. The saying recalls Thomas, *De ente* c. 5 (*differentiae essentiales rerum nobis ignotae sunt*). The ascription to the punishment of sin is Augustinian in flavour. B has the same text.

anchor.lemma: Inuisibilia dei per ea que facta sunt

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 70: *primitas originis*, *perfectionis*, *adaequationis*. Arist. *Metaph.* IX 8, 1050a4 (prior in generation, posterior in substance). Arist. *Anal. post.* I 4, 73b25ff. (*primo inest*).
*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 95: *visio aquilae de sole est simpliciter perfectior quam visio mea de candela*. Gorris adds the explanation of the 'proportional' sense.
The division of actual, habitual and virtual knowledge corresponds to *Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 71 and 92 (*Quantum ad notitiam habitualem vel virtualem…*).

*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 77: *Avicenna I Metaphysicae cap. 3: metaphysica est ultima in ordine doctrinae*. Gorris's *in ordine confuse concipiendi vel ens* compresses this, and the phrase *vel ens* is obscure. Scotus's point is that what is last in learning is first in the order of nature for distinct knowledge. A and B agree.

anchor.lemma: Quarta conclusio quod primum cognitum perfectione simpliciter est deus

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 97, with the same appeal to *Eth. Nic.* X 7–8.

Scotus’s reply to the second principal argument of the first question (Aristotle, *Metaph.* II 1, 993b9–11: our intellect is to the most evident things as the owl’s eye to sunlight). After setting aside Averroes’ reading (*de difficili*), Scotus says ‘oculus noctuae non habet cognitionem nisi intuitivam et naturalem … sic intellectui nostro est impossibile naturaliter et intuitive cognoscere Deum’ (*Ord.* I d. 3 p. 1 qq. 1–2, Wadding/Vivès text via SCTA). This is the only reply to a principal argument there that turns on intuitive knowledge. The earlier note’s ‘Jn 1:18’ was not found in d. 3. The identification is corrected, and Vatican paragraph numbers were not checked.
Read John 14:7. A's *4* is probably a misprint for *14*.
*doctor solennis*: Henry of Ghent's scholastic title.
The Latin *vel ens* is elliptical. See the corresponding note on the Latin.

anchor.lemma: vtrum deus sit obiectum naturale adequatum

notes.text: = *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 1 q. 3, n. 108 (*utrum Deus sit primum obiectum naturale adaequatum respectu intellectus viatoris*).

A is stained at the end of the line. Only *quodlibeto. 1* is legible, and the rest is supplied from B. B reads *Hen. quodlib. xv. q. iiij. et quodli. xiij. q. ix*. A's first reference, *15 q. 9*, therefore differs from B's *xv q. iiij*. Henry's view that God is the first object known (implicitly) is in *Summa* a. 24 and the late quodlibets. [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: *Quodl.* XV q. 9 (whether the angel’s self-intellection is more essential to it than its intellection of God) answers ‘tam secundum rationem causae formalis quam … finalis deus est principale obiectum cuiuslibet intellectus’, which is the opinion Scotus attacks. *Quodl.* XV q. 4 is on food converted into Christ’s body and has no bearing. So A’s *15 q. 9* is right and B’s *xv q. iiij* wrong. XIII q. 9 is on the first object of the will (*bonum sub ratione convenientis*); it is a parallel only. Verified for XV q. 9.]

anchor.lemma: primum obiectum primitate adequationis est ens inquantum ens

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 137: *dico quod primum obiectum intellectus nostri est ens, quia in ipso concurrit duplex primitas, scilicet communitatis et virtualitatis*. Gorris's *virtutis* stands for Scotus's *virtualitatis*.

*Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 131–136: being is not included quidditatively in the ultimate differences or in the *passiones entis*. Gorris's *primis differentiis… entis* seems to mean the differences that divide being (the *differentiae ultimae* of the first concepts).

anchor.lemma: Nihil est quod subterfugiat rationem entis

notes.text: The phrase is a commonplace that goes back to Avicenna, *Metaph.* I c. 5–6 (being is predicated of everything). Its wording here does not appear in Scotus's text of this question. [Checked: Avicenna’s *Philosophia prima* was not consulted in a Latin edition, and the exact wording was not found. Still open.] [Checked: Avicenna, *Opera* (Venice 1508; archive.org auiceneperhypate00avic and bub_gb_JJThV3vtDJIC) was located, but its OCR is too corrupt to search, and the *Philosophia prima* was not read page by page. Still open.]

Francis of Meyronnes († c. 1328). His *Conflatus*, Prologue q. 6 (‘Utrum ens quidditative dicatur de divina essentia ultimate praecisa’), concludes: ‘Ad quaestionem igitur dico quod ens non dicitur in quid de divina essentia’. He also says ‘probatum est evidenter quod ens non dicitur quidditative, sed denominative de divina essentia’. He then distinguishes two kinds of denominative predication: ‘Una quae accipitur a posteriori et ab accidente … sicut a iustitia dicitur iustus. Alia est quae accipitur ab essentialiter posteriori, et ista potest esse univoca’. This is exactly Gorris’s ‘denominativa licet non denominativa accidentalis’. B confirms *Franci.* This is the first named Scotist after Scotus in Gorris’s text. [Checked: Franciscus de Mayronis, *Preclarissima ac multum subtilia egregiaque scripta* (Venice 1520; archive.org bub_gb_QJ4loltkxYEC), fols. 5v–6r, read from the page images because the OCR is unusable. Abbreviations expanded. Verified.]

anchor.lemma: propositiones de per se non conuertuntur

Igitur si ista est per se secundo modo 'ens est unum', haec 'unum est ens' non est per se primo modo*. Gorris, like B, writes *per se secundo modo* in the second place, where Scotus has *primo modo*.
Arist. *Metaph.* II 1, 993b24–26 (fire, the hottest, is the cause of heat in other things).
Francis of Meyronnes OFM, *doctor illuminatus et acutus*, author of the *Conflatus*. See the note on the Latin.

anchor.lemma: Veritas est rectitudo sola propria perceptibilis mente

notes.text: Anselm, *De veritate* c. 11 (*veritas est rectitudo mente sola perceptibilis*), quoted by Scotus at *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 170. A's *propria* is not in Anselm and should probably be deleted, or read as *sola mente*.

anchor.lemma: ens et res prima impressione in anima imprimuntur

notes.text: Avicenna, *Metaph.* I c. 5 (*res et ens… prima impressione imprimuntur in anima*), cited at *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 22.

Arist. *De anima* II 7, 418a29: the visible is colour, and colour is what lies on the surface of the visible *per se*.

anchor.lemma: non autem quod adequatur potentie in aliquo statu

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 186: *primum obiectum potentiae assignatur illud quod adaequatum est potentiae ex ratione potentiae, non autem quod adaequatur potentiae in aliquo statu*. Gorris reproduces the sentence and the candle example verbatim.

Scotus's solution: being is the adequate object *de ratione potentiae*. The wayfarer's *de facto* limitation (*pro statu isto*) follows from sin or from the divine will (*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 187). Gorris reduces this to the claim that God is known *sub ratione entis* but not *ut tale ens*.
Following Anselm's wording rather than A's *sola propria … mente*.

B: *illud quod ponitur visui*.

= *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 1 q. 4 (Vatican III, nn. 202–280), Scotus's question on divine illumination. The wording of the question matches n. 202 verbatim (*an aliqua veritas certa et sincera possit naturaliter cognosci ab intellectu viatoris, absque lucis increatae speciali illustratione*).

anchor.lemma: Intuemur imutabilem veritatem ex qua perfecte cum possumus diffiniamus

notes.text: Aug. *De Trin.* IX 6.9 (*intuemur inviolabilem veritatem, ex qua perfecte, quantum possumus, definiamus…*). Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 202, has *inviolabilem*. *imutabilem* is a slip of memory or an exemplar variant, and *cum* stands for *quantum*.  B: *perfecte cum possumus diffamamus* (sic), a misprint.
Rom. 1:20 (*invisibilia enim ipsius… per ea quae facta sunt intellecta conspiciuntur*), paraphrased. It is the *ad oppositum* of the Vatican text: *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 203 app.

Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 1 q. 2 (*utrum homo possit aliquid scire sine divina illustratione*), set out by Scotus at *Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 204–217. Gorris's one-line summary (being can be known *sub ratione entis*, not *sub ratione veritatis*) is Henry's distinction between knowing the *verum* and knowing the *veritas* of a thing.  B: *ponitur Hen. in sum. arti. i. qui ponit* (without *opinio*).

Henry, *Quodl.* V q. 14, so also in B (*q. xiiij*). The link Gorris makes to Scotus's second article (*Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 229ff., against the Academics) has not been traced in the Vatican apparatus. [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* V q. 14 (Badius 1518 via SCTA) is on whether the angel knows other things by its essence, by species, or otherwise. Henry argues that cognition does not need an intelligible species impressed on the intellect (‘hoc non potest esse species intelligibilis impressa intellectui’). This fits the *responsio ad tertium* Scotus reports, but it is not a denial of ‘all intelligibility of truth’. Gorris’s description is loose (he may be compressing *speciem intelligibilem*). Reference located; the characterisation is doubtful.]

A is stained at the top right of p. 34. Supplied from B (fol. 32ra: *Igitur dico ad questionem quod propter verba etc.*), which agrees with *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 261: *Ad quaestionem igitur dico quod propter verba Augustini…*

anchor.lemma: E⟨x dictis⟩ patet ad omnes auctoritates Aug. in oppositum

notes.text: Stain in A. Supplied from B (*Ex dictis patet ad omnes auctoritates Aug. in oppositum*). The words are the last sentence of *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 279.

anchor.lemma: sextus vero ⟨ar⟩ticulus de communi non reperitur in libris

notes.text: An important witness to the state of the text. At n. 218 Scotus announces six articles, the sixth to show *quomodo rationes istae quatenus sunt Augustini concludunt*. In the Vatican edition the sixth article (n. 280) breaks off after its opening sentence (*De sexto articulo videndum est… Ubi sciendum est.*). Gorris's remark that it 'is not found in the books' therefore matches the surviving tradition exactly: Scotus left it unwritten. ⟨ar⟩ and ⟨c e⟩ (in *si⟨c e⟩um*) are supplied from B (*Sextus vero articulus de omni non reperitur in libris. et sic eum non posui*). B's *de omni* (probably for *omnino*) differs from A's *de communi*. I take A's phrase as 'in the common books' (i.e. the copies in circulation), but the construction is odd.

anchor.lemma: ly in potest capi obiectiue et hoc quadrupliciter

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 261, verbatim apart from word order. The four modes are expounded in nn. 262 (first), 263 (second), 264–266 (third) and 277 (fourth, *in obiecto remoto*). Gorris's comment on the 'fourth' mode, however, gives the doctrine of n. 267f. (secondary objects have only *esse secundum quid*, so they move only by virtue of the divine intellect). That doctrine belongs to the third mode in Scotus.

Scotus cites *De Trinitate* XIV c. 15 (*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 263; Aug. *De Trin.* XIV 15.21: *ubi ergo sunt istae regulae scriptae nisi in libro lucis illius quae veritas dicitur?*). A's *9.* (B *ix* or similar) is an error, perhaps carried over from the IX cited in the opening argument. The English corrects it.

Scotus's doctrine of the divine ideas as *obiecta secundaria* of the divine intellect, produced in *esse intelligibile* or *esse deminutum* (*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 262; cf. d. 35 q. un.). It is Scotus's reinterpretation of Augustinian illumination, without any special influence.
A has an abbreviation (*ʒ⁹* with a *z*-form). It is read as *secundum*, giving the sense 'and this [is] the second mode'. It could also be *scilicet*.  B prints the same abbreviation.

Aug. *De Trin.* IV 15.20. Gorris's 'ch. 35' is not an error of his own. It reproduces Scotus's medieval chapter numbering (*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 270: *IV De Trinitate cap. 35*). The quotation follows Scotus closely, but Gorris has *nondum potuisse venire* where Scotus and Augustine have *nondum posse*.
Aug. *De Trin.* XII 14.23, cited by Scotus as *XII De Trinitate cap. 14* (*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 273). A's *c. 4* has lost a digit.
Aug. *De div. qu. 83*, q. 46.2 (*De ideis*): *non nisi purae animae*. Cited by Scotus at *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 273.

anchor.lemma: iniustus videt in regulis eternis quid iustum sit faciendum

notes.text: Aug. *De Trin.* XIV 15.21, via *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 274 (*XIV De Trinitate cap. 15*). Gorris then reduces Scotus's *non tantum ut relucent in phantasmate* to *non tamen*.

anchor.lemma: Aug. locutus est inquirendo non autem determinando

notes.text: This reply is not in *Ord.* I d. 3 q. 4 as edited, and I have not found it in Scotus's text. It looks like a scholastic commonplace for setting aside an awkward Augustinian dictum. The source (a later Scotist, or Gorris himself) is still to be identified. [Checked: the phrase was not found in the Wadding/Vivès text of *Ord.* I d. 3 (SCTA). Still open.]

anchor.lemma: obiectum proximum nobis respectu veritatum sunt obiecta secundaria

notes.text: Gorris's summary: the proximate object of our knowing the eternal truths is the *obiecta secundaria* (the divine ideas, in their *esse intelligibile*). This differs from Scotus's own cautious statement at nn. 262 and 268, which allows only that we 'may be said' to see in them. The tension between this note and the solution in ¶4 (knowledge *per ista sensibilia*) is Gorris's, not Scotus's.  B: *obiectum primum nobis*.

B omits everything from *quodlibeto. 9. q. 1. et. 2.* to the second *opinio Henrici* (homoeoteleuton) and reads *ponitur opinio Henrici quolibet. iij. q. ix.* … It therefore assigns to the second article the references that A gives to the third. [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* IX q. 1 (Badius 1518 via SCTA), ‘Vtrum omnis relatio inter deum & creaturam sit quia ipsa creatura refertur ad deum’, is the locus. anchor.lemma: in ratitudine rei. sed in aliquiditate tantum

Verified for III q. 9 and V q. 2; the other two references look wrong.]

The identification is obscure. The *Quodl.* V q. 14 reference fits Henry, not Richard of Middleton (who left only three *Quodlibeta*). Possibly *Ricardi* is a compositor's error, or *maxime* belongs with Henry ('above all *Quodl.* V q. 14'). B to be checked.  B: *Richardi maxime quoli. iij. q. xiiij.* (*iij* for A's *5°*; the numeral is clear in B).

*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 346: *Idem ponit alius doctor, negando speciem intelligibilem*. Godfrey of Fontaines, *Quodl.* IX q. 19 and XIII q. 3, is the standard identification (cf. n. 361, where Scotus's own addition names *Godefridus*).

A notable fifteenth-century gloss. Gorris aligns the deniers of the intelligible species (Henry, Godfrey) with the *nominales*, i.e. Ockham and his followers (*Rep.* II q. 12–13), who explain memory by habits. It reflects the *via antiqua / via moderna* polemics of the late fifteenth century. The point is repeated in ¶3 (*vt dicunt nominales*).

anchor.lemma: lapis non est in anima sed species lapidis

notes.text: Arist. *De anima* III 8, 431b29–432a1, cited by Scotus at *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 344.

anchor.lemma: quatuor sunt species in anima altera ex altera nata

notes.text: Aug. *De Trin.* XI 9.16: four species, *altera ex altera*, from the body to the sense, to memory, to the gaze of thought (*acies cogitantis*). Gorris's sequence (sense, phantasy, memory, act of understanding) adapts Augustine to the scholastic faculty psychology. The argument is not in *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 3 q. 1. Its source in the Scotist tradition is still to be identified. [Checked: Aug. *De Trin.* XI 9.16 (augustinus.it): ‘quattuor species reperiuntur quasi gradatim natae altera ex altera’ (in the body, in the sense, in memory, *in acie cogitantis*). Verified.]

The *cognitio matutina/vespertina* of the angels: Aug. *De Gen. ad litt.* IV 22–32. The arguments from angelic knowledge, from Christ's soul, from separated souls and from Paul's rapture (2 Cor. 12:2–4) are not in this question of the *Ordinatio*. They appear to be Gorris's or his school's additions. [Checked: Aug. *De Gen. ad litt.* IV (augustinus.it) develops the *vespera*/*mane* of angelic knowledge from c. 22 n. 39 (‘post vesperam fiat mane, cum post cognitionem suae propriae naturae … refert se ad laudandam lucem’) through c. 35. The *vespertina cognitio* is named at c. 30 n. 47. Verified for IV 22–35.]

anchor.lemma: illos non potuit habere in vnico actu

notes.text: Arist. *Eth. Nic.* II 1, 1103a14–b25 (virtues and habits arise from repeated acts); cf. I 7, 1098a18 (*una hirundo non facit ver*).

The doctrine of species and intellect as partial co-causes of intellection is Scotus's, in the next question of the *Ordinatio* (*Ord.* I d. 3 p. 3 q. 2, esp. nn. 496–500, *duae causae partiales*). Gorris anticipates it here.

anchor.lemma: ratio agendi est quidditas speciei. sed ecceitas est conditio ipsius

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 380: *Singularitas est condicio agentis, non ratio agendi, sed ratio agendi est ipsa forma*. Gorris substitutes *ecceitas* for Scotus's *singularitas*, importing the vocabulary of *Ord.* II d. 3.  B misprints *ratio angeli* for *ratio agendi*.
*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 370 (*Ad quaestionem ergo dico quod necesse est ponere in intellectu ut habet rationem memoriae, speciem intelligibilem…*).

anchor.lemma: The nominalists are of this mind

notes.text: Lit. ‘of this intention are the *nominales*’.

anchor.lemma: Istud ponit doctor alius. iste alius est

notes.text: B: *Idem ponit doctor quidam. Iste quidam est*. B's *Idem* agrees with Scotus (*Ord.* I d. 3 n. 346: *Idem ponit alius doctor*).

There is no separate question on the conservation of the intelligible species in the Vatican *Ordinatio* I d. 3. There the point is made only in the closing paragraph of p. 3 q. 1 (n. 400: *nisi ponatur eam posse conservare speciem intelligibilem praeter actum*). Gorris's text, with its own arguments and *ad oppositum*, therefore reflects either a question present in his exemplar of the *Ordinatio* (the early printed tradition counts more questions in d. 3, cf. his 'eleven' at s016) or material drawn from elsewhere in Scotus, e.g. *Ord.* IV d. 45 q. 2, on memory in the separated soul. The question needs to be identified in the incunable editions of the *Ordinatio* (Venice 1477/1481). [Checked: the Wadding/Vivès text (SCTA) of *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 3 also has only four questions, so the extra question isn’t there either. The conservation of the species is argued only at the close of p. 3 q. 1 (‘nisi ponatur eam posse conservare speciem intelligibilem praeter actum’). The incunables were not consulted. Still open.]
Stain at the top right of p. 38. Supplied; the reading is certain from the remaining *stoteles*.

Cf. Arist. *De anima* III 4, 429a27–28 (the soul as *locus specierum*, praised in the ancients, cited by Scotus at *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 342) and Averroes, *In De an.* III comm. 6. *Arca/archa specierum* as a name for memory is Augustinian–Avicennian in flavour (Avicenna, *De anima* IV 1: memory as *thesaurus* of intentions). I have not found the exact phrase in Averroes. In ¶3 Gorris ascribes the same dictum to Aristotle. [Checked: no searchable Latin Averroes *In De anima* or Avicenna *De anima* was consulted, and the phrase *arca specierum* was not found. Still open.] [Checked: Averroes, *De anima* with commentary (Venice 1516; archive.org hin-wel-all-00001468-001) and Avicenna, *Opera* (Venice 1508) were located. In both the Gothic OCR is unusable (no *arca/archa* hit), and III comm. 6 was not read from the page images. Still open.]

Avicenna, *Liber de anima* V 6: the human intellect does not retain intelligible forms when it is not actually understanding; it must turn again to the agent Intelligence to receive them. Scotus discusses the view at *Ord.* IV d. 45 q. 2. A *dicentis quod debet poni species* seems to need a negative (*non debet*), or else refers to the species abstracted from sensibles, which, on the interpretation reported next, does remain.

anchor.lemma: Intellectus inquantum intellectus potest esse sapiens de se

notes.text: Cf. Arist. *De anima* III 4, 429b5–9: once the intellect has become each thing, as the knower actually is, it can then act of itself (*potest operari per se ipsum*). The interpretation of Aristotle's text in terms of retained species is standard in the Scotist school.

Arist. *De anima* III 8, 432a8–9 (*necesse est quemcumque intelligere phantasmata speculari*). Gorris's gloss, *vel speculatum fuisse* ('or to have contemplated them'), limits Aristotle's requirement of a phantasm to the original acquisition of the species.
An application of the Aristotelian distinction between actual and potential infinity (*Phys.* III 6): the memory holds a finite number of species at any time, which can be increased without limit.

anchor.lemma: dicentis quod debet poni species. Sed aliqui exponunt Auicennam quod

notes.text: B omits these words and reads *ponitur opinio Auicenne qui sic intellexit quod duplex est species*. B thus gives the two-species account as Avicenna's own view, not as an interpretation of him.
B: *Nam est textus de anima* (without *3°.*).

No question with this title stands in the Vatican *Ordinatio* I d. 3. The material corresponds to Scotus's treatment of the *notitia genita* and of the category of intellection: *Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 600–604, the replies in the question on the image (actus secundi *sunt producti*; intellection as a form *in continua dependentia ad praesentiam suae causae*), and *Quodl.* q. 13. As with q. 7, Gorris's exemplar seems to have had a question here that the critical edition does not. [Checked: Wadding/Vivès d. 3 p. 3 has no such question either. *Quodl.* q. 13 (Vivès XXV, archive.org operaomnia25duns) does treat operation as an absolute quality (‘nullo modo erit actio de genere Actionis’). The source of Gorris’s question is still open.]

anchor.lemma: forme non est tantum generatio sed compositi

notes.text: Arist. *Metaph.* VII 8, 1033b16–19: neither the form nor the essence is generated; the composite is.

Aug. *De Trin.* IX 12.18: *ab utroque enim notitia paritur, a cognoscente et cognito*.  B: *Aug. de trini. ix. c. ix. et xi.* (the next line, at the top of B36L, begins *ca. ij.*, which is unclear). A's *c. 12* is correct.
Porphyry's definition of accident (*Isagoge*, c. 5): *accidens est quod adest et abest praeter subiecti corruptionem*.

The anonymous 'someone' who says 'more clearly' that intellection is an action not in the category of action but of quality. This is Scotus's own considered position (*Quodl.* q. 13 a. 2, and *Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 601–603). Gorris therefore seems to be contrasting the formulation of his source here with the clearer one found elsewhere in Scotus. It may also be Francis of Meyronnes or another Scotist.  B: *Sed dicit quidem et clarius*. B's *quidem* leaves the verb without its subject; A's *quidam* is right. [Checked: Scotus, *Quodl.* q. 13 (Vivès XXV, archive.org operaomnia25duns, c. pp. 575–581) holds that intellection is a *qualitas absoluta* and ‘nullo modo erit actio de genere Actionis’. The marginal cross-reference there reads ‘Operatio est qualitas, de quo late 1, d. 3. q. 6’ (Wadding numbering). The Scotus locus is verified. Whether Gorris’s *quidam* means Scotus himself is still interpretation.]

The distinction of immanent and transient action is in Arist. *Metaph.* IX 8, 1050a23–b2 (seeing and contemplating remain in the agent), not in *Ethics* VI, though *Eth.* VI 4, 1140a1–5 distinguishes making from doing. The citation is probably loose.
The next question (s024 = *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 3 q. 2) treats the causes of intellection at length.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 3 q. 2 (ed. Vat. III, nn. 401–553): *utrum pars intellectiva proprie sumpta vel aliquid eius sit causa totalis gignens notitiam actualem vel ratio gignendi*. Gorris's paraphrase (*i. si intellectus est causa totalis…*) is his own. His count of the questions of d. 3 (q. 9 here = Vat. p. 3 q. 2) confirms that his exemplar had two questions (his qq. 7–8) between Vat. p. 3 q. 1 and q. 2.

anchor.lemma: memoria fecunda est parens noticie genite

notes.text: Scotus's first principal argument (n. 401), from Aug. *De Trin.* IX and XIV 6–7 (memory as parent of the word). The *ad oppositum* in Scotus (n. 405) is Avicenna, *Metaph.* IX; Gorris replaces it with Aug. *De Trin.* IX (12.18, knowledge begotten by knower and known), which he quotes in ¶4.

The first opinion (n. 407), the whole activity attributed to the soul, imputed by Henry to Augustine. Gorris's references are Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* IV q. 7 and V q. 5 (*pro ista opinione arguitur*, n. 409). The Vatican apparatus cites Henry, *Quodl.* V q. 14 and XIII q. 8 among others. I have not checked Gorris's question numbers against the Henry edition (Leuven Opera omnia). [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: *Quodl.* IV q. 7 (self-knowledge without species) plausibly bears on the soul’s activity. V q. 5 (whether God causes the damnation of the wicked) does not fit, and may be a slip. The Vatican’s XIII q. 8 (‘Vtrum intellectus agens pertineat ad imaginem’) and V q. 14 fit better. Partly confirmed.]

The second opinion (n. 422: *Alia est opinio, quae totaliter est in alio extremo*), the whole activity attributed to the object or phantasm: Godfrey of Fontaines. The Vatican editors cite *Quodl.* VI q. 15, VIII q. 2, IX q. 19 and XIII q. 3. Gorris's 'VI q. 7' may be a slip for q. 15; his other three references agree. [Checked: Godfrey, *Quodl.* VI q. 7 (SCTA), ‘Utrum voluntas potest se movere’, argues against self-motion in general and discusses the intellect–phantasm case, so Gorris’s ‘VI q. 7’ is defensible and need not be a slip. VI q. 15 (whether the agent intellect belongs to the superior reason) has ‘per abstractionem speciei … mediante phantasmate’.
