VIII q. 2 (Hoffmans, Philosophes Belges IV, archive.org: whether a subject can be the immediate effective principle of its own accident) and XIII q. 3 (Philosophes Belges V: whether a created substance can by itself be the immediate principle of an operation) fit. IX q. 19 was not available online. Verified, except IX q. 19.]

The third opinion (n. 450): passive with respect to the first, simple and confused knowledge, active in discursive and distinct knowledge. Henry, *Quodl.* V q. 14. The fourth (n. 451, the 'retracting' position, *de passione respectu primae notitiae…*) Gorris assigns to *Quodl.* III q. 6. On the Vatican reading, n. 451 says *Iste idem doctor istam positionem… retractat*, and both opinions are Henry's. [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: *Quodl.* V q. 14 fits. The intellect is *quasi actiue … quasi passiue*, and the agent intellect abstracts and moves the possible intellect to simple apprehension. III q. 6 (whether the vegetative and sensitive souls in Christ were educed from matter) does not fit, so Gorris’s ‘III q. 6’ for the retracting position is doubtful. Verified for V q. 14.]

anchor.lemma: Thome prima parte summe. q. 85. articulo. 2

notes.text: The fifth opinion (n. 456), quoted almost verbatim by Gorris: Thomas Aquinas, *ST* I q. 85 a. 2 (the species as *id quo*), with q. 79 a. 2. The Vatican editors identify it rather as the common Thomist view (also Godfrey). Gorris's attribution to Thomas is traditional.
A *ibi informatus* agrees with the *Ordinatio* (n. 456: *tamquam materiale ibi, informatus illa specie*). B reads *non informatus*, which contradicts the opinion reported and is an error of B.

The sixth opinion (n. 460: *quae redit in idem*): the actual knowledge begotten is itself the species. Gorris names Giles of Rome, *Quodl.* III qq. 12–14. Elsewhere the view is associated with Godfrey and Henry's critics. Not checked. [Checked: the lemma *Sexta opinio, quae redit in idem* stands in the Wadding/Vivès text of p. 3 q. 2 (SCTA). Giles’s *Quodlibeta* III qq. 12–14 are not available online. Still open.]

The harmonization (*concordantur*) of the third and fourth opinions, n. 529. Its author, Scotus's *ille medius* (n. 531), is in fact an anonymous reconciler; the Vatican editors point to texts of Henry for the doctrine of the double *occursus* (*Quodl.* IV q. 8). Gorris attributes the source of the harmonization to Henry. [Checked: the harmonization (‘Iste tamen duae opiniones, scilicet tertia et quarta … concordantur ad invicem’) is in the Wadding/Vivès text of p. 3 q. 2 (SCTA). Henry’s *Quodl.* IV q. 8 (Badius 1518 via SCTA) is on whether the blessed forms a *verbum*. I could not find the *occursus* doctrine there or anywhere in the Quodlibeta (*occursu* occurs only in XV q. 2). The reference is doubtful.]

anchor.lemma: Hoc confirmatur secundum opinionem illius doctoris

notes.text: The lemma is in the Wadding/Vivès text of *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 3 q. 2 (SCTA), in Scotus’s argument against the harmonization of the third and fourth opinions: ‘sicut ultimus gradus habitus generatur ex ultimo actu, ita primus ex primo … Hoc confirmatur secundum opinionem illius Doctoris qui exponitur, quia ponit istam inchoationem esse essentiam habitus totam. Quod ulterius dicitur de occursu illo…’. So it is not an extra passage; the earlier note was wrong to say so. Vatican paragraph numbers were not checked. Gorris’s Henry reference, *Quodl.* V q. 19 (Badius 1518 via SCTA), opens the questions on infused habits (‘vtrum habitus infusus possit augeri’). The subject (degrees of a habit) is related, but the thesis that the *inchoatio* is the whole essence of the habit was not found in the short SCTA text.

B: *quolib. iiij. q. xix.* A: *quodlibeto. 5.* Henry's *Quodl.* IV has fewer than 19 questions on most counts, while *Quodl.* V has 40, so A's reading is preferable. The reference has not been verified.
Stain at the top right of p. 40. Supplied from B (*Ceterum respondendo rationibus thome in illo loco*). B omits *post*. The reply to Thomas's arguments for the fifth opinion is *Ord.* nn. 537–545.
Stain at the top right of p. 40. Supplied from B (*intellect⁹*).

*Ord.* n. 541: *quam tamen auctoritatem in tantum pertractant aliqui, ut dicant intellectum possibilem esse in pura potentia… sicut materia*. Gorris (and B: *quã ncãriã*) read *necessariam* for *in tantum*. This is probably a misreading of an abbreviation in the common exemplar. The authority is Arist. *De an.* III 4, 429a24 (*nihil est actu eorum quae sunt ante intelligere*). Thomas, *ST* I q. 87 a. 1 and q. 79 a. 2, is correctly identified.

= *Ord.* nn. 486–488, closely paraphrased (*intellectio actualis est aliquid in nobis non perpetuum sed habens esse post non esse*; neither object nor soul the total cause). Scotus's positive account of partial causes follows at nn. 494–500.

anchor.lemma: nominales volunt concludere quod non requiritur species

notes.text: Notable: Gorris turns the Augustinian dictum against the *nominales*, who deny the intelligible species (William of Ockham, *Rep.* II qq. 12–13; Gregory of Rimini, *In II Sent.* d. 7 q. 2). The argument from *Eth.* II, that there are only three things in the soul, is Ockham's (*Rep.* II q. 12–13, *Quodl.* IV q. 1 is the locus for parsimony). This is a second explicit polemic against the *via moderna* (cf. s020 *huius intentionis sunt nominales*). [Checked: no searchable text of Ockham’s *Reportatio* II (OTh V) or Rimini’s *In II Sent.* was consulted. Still open.] [Checked: Ockham’s *Reportatio* II qq. 12–13 (OTh V, 1981) is not freely online and was not opened, so the *nominales* attribution is still unchecked. Gorris’s reply to the *Eth.* II argument has an exact parallel in Aquinas, *ST* I-II q. 94 a. 1 ad 1 (bkv.unifr.ch): ‘philosophus intendit ibi investigare genus virtutis … illa tantum ponit quae sunt principia humanorum actuum’. Still open as to Ockham.]

anchor.lemma: tria sunt in anima. affectus potentia et habitus

notes.text: Arist. *Eth. Nic.* II 4, 1105b19–21: *quae fiunt in anima tria sunt: passiones, potentiae, habitus*. Gorris's reply, that Aristotle is listing principles of *action* (in the ethical sense), is apt: the passage introduces the genus of virtue.

anchor.lemma: philosophus intelligit de potentiis anime quibus sumus formaliter et in actu secundo

notes.text: *Ord.* n. 537, quoted nearly verbatim (*Philosophus locutus est communiter de potentiis animae, in quantum sunt quibus sumus formaliter in actu secundo…*).

anchor.lemma: Aristoteles non dixit quod intellectus in intelligendo non agit. ergo non agit

notes.text: The sentence as printed (also in B) contains a double negation that spoils the logic. The fallacy denounced is surely 'Aristotle did not say that the intellect acts in understanding; therefore it does not act'. The second *non* is either an error or should be read *dixit… agit*. The point corresponds to *Ord.* nn. 541–542.
Scotus, *Quodl.* q. 15, on the active role of the intellect (*utrum intellectus agens sit causa activa…*). Scotus there defends the activity of the possible intellect in producing intellection.

Another anonymous 'quidam' (cf. s023 n429): a Scotist who distinguishes the passive reception of the species from the active exit into the act. This is close to Antonius Andreas and Francis of Meyronnes. Not identified.  B reads *quidem dicit sic et bene* here too (cf. n429). [Checked: no searchable text of Antonius Andreas or Meyronnes was found. Still open.]
The principle that immanent action remains in the agent is *Metaph.* IX 8, 1050a30–b2. *Phys.* III 3, 202a13–b22 in fact places motion in the mobile. The citation of *Phys.* III is loose.

Cf. Arist. *Phys.* II 2, 194b13 (*homo hominem generat et sol*). The principle *agens est praestantius patiente* is Aug. *De Gen. ad litt.* XII 16.33, discussed at *Ord.* n. 507 (*non est immediate vera*). For *viventia non viventibus meliora*, cf. Aug. *De Trin.* XI 5.8 and *De lib. arb.* II 3.7; Scotus quotes the dictum at n. 409.  B: *sol facit hominem*, without *in*.

anchor.lemma: memoria fecunda includit potentiam intellectiuam cum obiecto

notes.text: = *Ord.* n. 547 sense: memory as *parens* includes the object present in the intelligible species (cf. d. 2 on *memoria perfecta*).
B: *Et sic habetur quod obiectum*, supplying the verb that A's elliptical phrase implies; the English sense is unaffected.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 3 q. 3 (Vat. nn. 554–568): *utrum principalior causa notitiae genitae sit obiectum in se vel in specie praesens, vel ipsa pars intellectiva animae*. A *principalis cause* is a syntactic slip (nominative needed) shared with B.

*Ord.* n. 554 (the first principal argument). Cf. Arist. *De an.* III 10, 433b11–18 (the object of appetite moves without being moved) and *Metaph.* XII 7, 1072a26.  B omits the minor *Sed obiectum mouet non motum* (homoeoteleuton on *motum*).

anchor.lemma: patet de sole et homine. 2°. phisicorum

notes.text: Arist. *Phys.* II 2, 194b13. Gorris's *ad oppositum* (the universal cause concurs principally) is not Scotus's (*Ord.* nn. 557–558: the more actual form is more active; *ens secundum quid*). Instead it anticipates Scotus's first reason in the reply (n. 559).

anchor.lemma: quando cause se habent sic quod quedam est illimitata

notes.text: *Ord.* n. 559, paraphrased: *quando causarum ordinatarum altera est indeterminata ad multos effectus, et alia determinata… illa quae est illimitata videtur esse principalior et perfectior*. Gorris omits the second reason (n. 560: the intellect acting, the object co-acts, *est enim in potestate nostra intelligere*).

*Ord.* n. 561, nearly verbatim (*posset poni habere totam causalitatem respectu visionis, aut principaliorem quam pars intellectiva, et hoc propter excellentiam talis obiecti et defectum partis intellectivae*).

anchor.lemma: lux creata vel intellectus agens quod pro eodem accipio

notes.text: The identification of the Augustinian 'created light' with the Aristotelian agent intellect is not in *Ord.* p. 3 q. 3. Note the first person (*accipio*, *dico*): Gorris is speaking in his own voice here, or reporting a source that speaks in the first person. Cf. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 3 n. 268 (illumination) and *Quodl.* q. 15. [Checked: no external source for the first-person passage was found. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: duplicem potentiam. quarum vna est omnia facere. alia omnia fieri

notes.text: Arist. *De an.* III 5, 430a14–15 (*est intellectus quidam quo omnia fieri, alius quo omnia facere*).

The fourfold co-causality of the agent intellect (species with the phantasm; act with the species; disposition to the habit; habit with the species) is a school formula. I have not found it as such in the *Ordinatio*. Cf. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 3 nn. 359–364 (species caused by agent intellect and phantasm as partial causes), *Ord.* II d. 3 p. 2 q. 1, and *Quodl.* q. 15. It may come from a later Scotist (Meyronnes? Petrus Tartaretus?). [Checked: the formula was not found in the Wadding/Vivès *Ordinatio* I d. 3 (SCTA), and no later Scotist texts were consulted. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: spiritus illam de cellula in cellulam deferentes

notes.text: The doctrine of the inner senses (common sense, imagination, estimative, memory) located in the cerebral ventricles (*cellulae*), with the animal spirits as carriers, is Avicennian–Galenic medical psychology. Cf. Avicenna, *De anima* I 5 and IV 1, and Albert, *De homine*. It is unusual in a Scotus commentary and probably reflects Gorris's own teaching, or that of the Toulouse school.

So A (and B). The sense requires *mouet non motus* ('moves without being moved'), answering the initial argument. *mouetur* is probably an error of the common exemplar. The translation follows the sense.

anchor.lemma: causa principalis in operando licet non in mouendo

notes.text: Cf. *Ord.* n. 564: *in utraque actione obiectum est secundarium movens, licet non sit motum…*. Gorris simplifies Scotus's reply.
B: *causa noticie in se genite*.

anchor.lemma: intellectus autem non mouet nisi motus

notes.text: B: *Intellectus non mouet respectu motus*, apparently a misreading of *nisi motus*; A gives the required sense.
B: *intellectionis*, omitting *modo nobis naturaliter conuenientium*.
B: *naturaliter cognita habent virtutem*, supplying the verb.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 3 q. 4 (Vat. nn. 569–604): *utrum in mente sit distincte imago Trinitatis*. Gorris's first argument (the image is proper to the Word) is not among Scotus's three principal arguments (nn. 569–572). Cf. rather Aug. *De Trin.* VI 2.3 and VII 1.2, and Peter Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 3 c. 2 / d. 27. Gorris's *ad oppositum* (Gen. 1:26) likewise replaces Scotus's (Aug. XIV 8, n. 573), which he uses instead in the reply (¶2).

anchor.lemma: Ibi querenda est ymago vbi nihil est melius in natura nostra

notes.text: Aug. *De Trin.* XIV 8.11, as quoted at *Ord.* n. 573: *Quaerenda est imago et invenienda ubi nostra natura nihil habet melius*.

*Ord.* nn. 581–582: the doubt about a 'quaternity' in the image, and the doubt about the order of origin. Gorris's references to Henry (*Quodl.* VI qq. 1–2), on the Father's fecundity for spiration remaining (*relicta*) after generation and on the Father begetting *inquantum intelligens*, identify opinions implicit in n. 588 and in Scotus's *Ord.* I d. 2 / d. 7. I have not checked the question numbers.  B reads *tria dubia*; A's *duo* agrees with Scotus. [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: *Quodl.* VI q. 1 (‘Utrum sint tres in divinis personae, nec plures nec pauciores’: two emanations by intellect and will) and VI q. 2 (whether the production of the persons is presupposed to that of creatures) bear on the Father’s fecundity and the order of the emanations. They fit Gorris’s reference in general. Verified.]
A divides the word *de-relictam* across the page break (p. 42/43). The marker is placed inside the word. B has not been checked here.

Scotus divides n. 574 into three articles (what an image is; with respect to what in the Trinity; in what it consists in us). Gorris adds a fourth: whether the powers are really distinct from one another and from the essence. This is the issue of Scotus, *Ord.* II d. 16 q. un., which Gorris cites in ¶8.

anchor.lemma: secundum viam Thome prima parte. q. 93. articulo. 6

notes.text: Thomas Aquinas, *ST* I q. 93 a. 6: image is found in rational creatures by representation of species, vestige by representation of a trace (*per modum vestigii*). Gorris's formula, image *sub ratione individui* and vestige *sub ratione speciei*, does not reproduce Thomas exactly (Thomas: image *secundum similitudinem speciei*). The passage is absent from Scotus's article (n. 575), which opens directly with 'repraesentativum totius'. [Checked: Thomas, *ST* I q. 93 a. 6 co. (Corpus Thomisticum): the image ‘repraesentat secundum similitudinem speciei’, and the vestige ‘ad speciei similitudinem non pertingit’ (e.g. the *vestigia* left by moving animals). Verified. Gorris’s formula still differs from Thomas’s, as noted above. Also confirmed: *ST* I q. 85 a. 2 co. (the opinion that the species *is* what is understood) for the fifth opinion at s024, and *ST* I q. 87 a. 1.]
Aug. *De div. quaest. 83*, q. 74, as quoted at *Ord.* n. 575 (*quantumcumque duo ova sint similia, unum non est imago alterius*). The whole paragraph follows n. 575.

anchor.lemma: trinitas constituit conceptum in intellectu nostro

notes.text: *Ord.* n. 576, closely paraphrased. Gorris adds the 'numerable whole' with the persons as 'quasi-parts', and the clause *nec respectu illius in quo sunt vnum*.

anchor.lemma: anima habet in se aliquam perfectionem

notes.text: *Ord.* n. 580 (*Anima habet in se aliquam perfectionem secundum quam est actus primus respectu notitiae genitae…*). The image consists in first and second acts together.

anchor.lemma: vna substantialitas ratione illarum trium realitatum

notes.text: *Realitates* is a characteristically Scotist term for the formally distinct perfections of one subject. Cf. *Ord.* II d. 16 (the powers as formally, not really, distinct from the essence, *contentae unitive*).  B: *vna substantialis ratione*.

The real distinction of the powers from the essence is *ST* I q. 77 a. 1. Their flowing from the essence as proper (inseparable) accidents is q. 77 a. 6. Article 8 concerns the powers remaining in the separated soul, so Gorris's 'a. 8' is inexact (a. 1/6 intended).
One of the rare passages in which Gorris argues in the first person, here against Thomas, with Augustine's text in hand.

Aug. *De Trin.* X 11.18: *Haec igitur tria, memoria, intellegentia, voluntas, quoniam non sunt tres vitae sed una vita, nec tres mentes sed una mens, consequenter utique nec tres substantiae sunt sed una substantia*. The quotation is accurate.  B reads *c. vij*, which is wrong; A's *xi* is right.

The question on the distinction of the soul's powers from its essence, and on the image, is Scotus, *Ord.* (and *Rep.*) II d. 16 q. un. (*utrum imago Trinitatis distincte sit in potentiis animae*). 'd. 15' is probably a slip for d. 16, or reflects a different distinction-numbering in Gorris's exemplar.

anchor.lemma: proprium verbi quod sit ymago patris

notes.text: Cf. Aug. *De Trin.* VI 2.3 and Thomas, *ST* I q. 35 a. 2 (*Imago* as a proper name of the Son). Man is *ad imaginem*, the image of the whole Trinity.

Later marginalia in brown ink (probably 16th century) at the heads of pp. 42–44 (*Trinitatis ymago*, *filius … deus genuit alium deum* and similar) and beside the articles on p. 43 (*respectu cuius in trinitate*, *in quo in nobis … prima*). They are only partly legible at the resolution of the digitization and are not transcribed.
B: *representat sub*, without A's otiose *quia*.
B: *totum materiale*. A's *numerabile* fits the argument (the persons as quasi-parts of a numerable whole) and is kept.
B: *representat in se noticiam genitam*. A's *recipit* matches the Scotist account of intelligence as the power that formally receives the begotten knowledge.
B: *anime sunt ymago*.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 4 p. 1 q. un. (ed. Vat. IV, nn. 1–6), *utrum haec sit vera 'Deus genuit alium Deum'*. In the Vatican edition this part survives only as a short note, sending the reader to the Cambridge question and the Paris *Reportatio* for the arguments (*Argumenta pro et contra quaere Parisius*, n. 2). Gorris's arguments therefore come from the Lombard (*Sent.* I d. 4 c. 1–2) or from the *Reportatio*.

anchor.lemma: nulla prorsus res est que se ipsam gignat vt sit

notes.text: Aug. *De Trin.* I 1.1 (*nulla enim omnino res est quae se ipsam gignat ut sit*), quoted by the Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 4 c. 1.

anchor.lemma: audi israel deus deus tuus vnus est

notes.text: Deut. 6:4 (Vulg. *Audi Israhel Dominus Deus noster Dominus unus est*). Gorris's form, *deus deus tuus*, reflects a liturgical or patristic paraphrase.

anchor.lemma: cuilibet enti correspondet adequate aliquod ens vel aliquid ens

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 4 n. 3: *Cuicumque entitati correspondens est aliquod ens vel aliquis, sicut suo 'quo'; deitas est de se 'haec'…*. Gorris's *aliquid ens* corresponds to Scotus's *aliquis* (masc.).

A *alia non ydemptitas*, B *alia non identitas*; just before, A *respondet determinate*, B *reputat determinate* (B is probably corrupt for *correspondet*). The sense is that in what is of itself singular (*de se haec*) there falls no further non-identity, i.e. no ‘otherness’ in the same form. Cf. *Ord.* n. 3 (*deitas est de se haec*).
*Brunellus* (Brownie), the stock donkey of scholastic logic, used in examples of non-human individuals (e.g. Peter of Spain, Burley).

Cf. *Ord.* I d. 4 nn. 4–5 (*'alium' connotat extrema esse eadem in forma determinabili*) and Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 4 c. 2 and d. 9 c. 1. The analysis of *alius* as conveying distinction of supposits plus numbering of the common form is standard (Thomas, *ST* I q. 31 a. 2).
Cf. *Ord.* I d. 4 n. 6 (*Aliud dubium, eundem Deum et alium Deum*). The disjunction *aut alium deum aut alium non deum* is a classic sophism; cf. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 4 c. 2.

anchor.lemma: fallacia figure dictionis commutando quale quid in hoc aliquid

notes.text: Arist. *Soph. El.* 22, 178b37–179a10: the fallacy of figure of speech by changing a *quale quid* (a common nature) into a *hoc aliquid* (a this). Scotus applies it to *Deus genuit Deum* at *Rep.* I d. 4. The *reciprocatio* is the reflexive pronoun *se*.  B: *fallacia dictionis*, omitting *figure*.

anchor.lemma: c. Audi israel. deus deus tuus vnus est

notes.text: B: *Audi israel deus*, omitting the rest of the quotation (in s027-01 B also has a single *deus*).
= *Ord.* I d. 4 p. 2 q. un. (ed. Vat. IV, nn. 7–14), *de veritate huius 'Deus est Pater et Filius et Spiritus Sanctus'*. Gorris's D4 has only these two questions, as the Vatican edition does.

Ord. n. 8 cites Augustine for *Pater et Filius et Spiritus Sanctus sunt unus Deus* (cf. *De Trin.* VIII prooem. 1, *unus Deus*). The book number is not verified in the Vatican apparatus. [Checked: Aug. *De Trin.* VIII 1.1 (prooemium; augustinus.it): ‘nec tamen tres dii aut tres boni aut tres omnipotentes, sed unus Deus, bonus, omnipotens, ipsa Trinitas’. So Gorris’s book VIII is right. Verified.]

anchor.lemma: nam deus naturam significat diuinam vt natam predicari de suppositis

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 4 n. 9: *terminus quod primo significat, hoc primo ponit in oratione* (‘Deus’ signifies the deity as *haec*, with co-reference to a supposit).

A *ē idē ydēptice*, B *est idē identitate*; later A *deitas ydemptica*, B *deitas identitate*. The contrast between formal predication (*Filius est Deus*) and identical predication (*Filius est deitas*) is Scotus's own (*Ord.* I d. 4 n. 10; cf. d. 8 on *praedicatio identica*).

anchor.lemma: quatenus deus extat pro hoc deo in quantum est ens per se deitate

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 4 nn. 11–13: *Deus* stands for *hic Deus*, for the deity as *per se ens*, not for a supposit determined by a personal property. *extat* is Gorris's *stat*.  B: *quatenus deus stat pro deo*.

*Ord.* I d. 4 n. 12: *color 'hic', singularis exsistens, non determinat sibi rationem suppositi…*. The example *color disgregat [visum]* comes from Arist. *Top.* III 5 (119a30) and *Metaph.* X 7 (1057b8).
*Ord.* I d. 4 n. 14: the proposed contradictory is not one if the distribution is over the persons. Gorris does not name the fallacy.
B: *est vera*.
B: *vt natam predicari de supposito*, repeating the formula of the previous sentence.
B: *quasi inconuersa*.
= *Ord.* I d. 5 p. 1 q. un. (ed. Vat. IV, nn. 1–45), *utrum essentia divina generet vel generetur*.

Richard of St Victor, *De Trin.* VI c. 22 (ed. Vat. n. 2), not book VIII. B agrees with A (*viij. de trini.*), so the error is in the common text. Richard's polemic (*in morem Goliae*) is aimed at the Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 5 c. 1.

anchor.lemma: extra de summa tri. et fide catholica

notes.text: *X* 1.1.2 (*Damnamus*), Lateran IV (1215), condemning Joachim of Fiore's *libellus* against the Lombard (ed. Vat. nn. 8–12).

anchor.lemma: Et est Adam li. 1. di. 33. q. 4.

notes.text: **A reader's key to sources, in Gorris's own voice.** He says that the argument *res generans etc.* (*Ord.* n. 13) ‘is Adam’, i.e. probably Adam Wodeham, I d. 33 q. 4. B agrees (*Et est adam li. i. di. xxxiij. q. iiij.*). The Vatican edition traces the argument to Henry and Godfrey and does not name Adam. The reference is not identified: either Wodeham's Oxford *Lectura* or the abbreviation by Henry Totting of Oyta (Paris 1512), whose numbering may differ. If it is Wodeham, Gorris is reading Scotus alongside a fourteenth-century source. [Checked: Wodeham’s Oxford and Paris lectures on *Sent.* I d. 33 are not available online in searchable form. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: hic doctor est Henricus in summa

notes.text: Gorris identifies the anonymous *quidam doctor* of *Ord.* n. 35 (*repetit opiniones aliorum, primam…*) as Henry of Ghent, *Summa* (a. 54? cf. a. 58 q. 2 on *essentia est pater Filii*). The Vatican apparatus names Henry, *Summa* a. 54 q. 5 [sic?], as the source of the opinions of Alexander and Praepositinus recited there. [Checked in Badius 1520 via SCTA: *Summa* a. 54 is on the mode of emanation (q. 3: whether anything emanates from the unemanating person; q. 5: whether the two emanating persons proceed from him equally and immediately). The formula *essentia generat essentiam* is discussed at a. 54 q. 3, and a. 58 q. 2 asks whether *generare* is the same as *dicere*. Gorris’s ‘in summa’ is plausible, but the precise article for the *quidam doctor* is not settled. Still open.]
*X* 1.1.2. The account of Joachim's two errors (the charge of *quaternitas* against the Lombard; a merely collective, *similitudinaria* unity) follows *Ord.* nn. 8–11.

anchor.lemma: Volo pater vt sint vnum in nobis sicut et nos vnum sumus

notes.text: John 17:21–22, conflated (*ut omnes unum sint… ut sint unum sicut et nos unum sumus*). It is quoted in *Damnamus* and at *Ord.* n. 9.

anchor.lemma: Sed veniendo ad opinionem magistri et Scoti et finaliter fidelium

notes.text: Gorris names Scotus in the third person here (*magistri et Scoti*), while elsewhere *doctor* is Scotus. This marks the text as Gorris's compilation and not a mere abbreviation.

**Misattribution, shared by B** (*in epistola ad volusianum*). *Evangelio non crederem nisi me catholicae Ecclesiae commoveret auctoritas* is Aug. *Contra epistolam Fundamenti* c. 5 n. 6, correctly cited by Scotus at *Ord.* n. 26. Gorris has substituted the letter to Volusianus (*Ep.* 137).

anchor.lemma: quandocunque est aliquod subiectum vltimate abstractum

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 5 n. 18 (*quandocumque subiectum est abstractum ultimata abstractione, de eo nihil praedicatur nisi quod est de ratione eius*), with nn. 19–24.  B reads *Quantumcunque*, an error for A's *quandocunque*.
*Actiones sunt suppositorum*: proverbial, from Arist. *Metaph.* I 1 (981a16–17, *actiones… omnes circa singulare sunt*), as in the *Auctoritates Aristotelis*.

*conseruans* is unexpected after *generans*, but B has it too (*nec generans nec conseruans*). Perhaps a slip in the common archetype for *generata* or *spirans*, or a deliberate extension to an *actio ad extra*.

anchor.lemma: nec est materia nec quasi materia

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 5 p. 2 nn. 93–97 (*tenendo cum doctoribus antiquis… nullus ausus fuit ponere materiam*), anticipated here from the next question.

anchor.lemma: in substantia est tantum vna abstractio

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 5 nn. 19–22: one abstraction in substances, two in absolute accidents, three in relations; the *ultima abstractio* is of the quiddity.

anchor.lemma: homo et risibile non quoad omnia conuertuntur

notes.text: Cf. *Ord.* I d. 5 nn. 23 and 34 (subject and attribute). The point that aptitude is predicated of *risibile* but not of *homo* is Gorris's gloss.

anchor.lemma: Ad Ricardum dicitur quod eius auctoritas hic non tenetur

notes.text: *Ord.* n. 26: *nego Richardum tenendo Magistrum*, on the authority of the Church (*Damnamus*).

anchor.lemma: ergo secundum opinionem Joachim essencia generat et generatur

notes.text: B omits the sentence (*…nec generat nec generatur. Secundus error…*). Also in this paragraph: A *indiuisibilis*, B *indiuiduabilis*.
= *Ord.* I d. 5 p. 2 q. un. (ed. Vat. IV, nn. 46ff.), *utrum Filius generetur de substantia Patris*. Gorris reduces a very long question to its doctrinal skeleton.

The citation *V c. 33* cannot be right: *De Trin.* V has 17 chapters. The dictum (*tres personas ex eadem essentia non dicimus*) is at *De Trin.* VII 6.11. B not checked. [Checked: Aug. *De Trin.* VII 6.11 (augustinus.it): ‘tres autem personas ex eadem essentia non dicimus, quasi aliud ibi sit quod essentia est, aliud quod persona’. Verified for VII 6.11; Gorris’s ‘V c. 33’ is wrong.]
A omits the book number. Ord. n. 49 gives *XV De Trinitate cap. 19* (on Col. 1:13, *Filius caritatis suae* = *Filius substantiae suae*).

anchor.lemma: opinio Henrici quodlibeto. 8. q. 9. et in summa arti. 54. q. 3.

notes.text: **Gorris names the anonymous opinion of *Ord.* n. 52** (the essence as quasi-matter, *de qua* the Son is begotten) as Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* VIII q. 9 and *Summa* a. 54 q. 3. Both match the Vatican apparatus, which cites Henry's *Summa* a. 54 qq. 3 and 6 and *Quodl.* VI q. 1 / VIII q. 9.

*Ord.* n. 59, *Huic opinioni additur ab aliis quod essentia divina dicitur generari subiective*. Gorris assigns this to Godfrey of Fontaines. The Vatican apparatus, however, refers to Henry, *Summa* a. 54 q. 3 ad 3, and *Quodl.* VI q. 1; Godfrey should be checked (*Quodl.* VII q. 2?). [Checked: the doctrine that the divine essence is begotten *subiective* is Henry’s. *Summa* a. 59 q. 2 (Badius 1520 via SCTA) has ‘non enim generatur filius obiectiue nisi quia de diuina essentia generatur subiectiue’, prepared at a. 59 q. 1 and applied at q. 3. Godfrey’s *Quodl.* I–VII (SCTA), VIII (Hoffmans) and XI–XIV (Philosophes Belges) gave no parallel for *generari subiective*. So the Vatican’s Henry identification holds, and Gorris’s ‘Godofredus’ is unsupported (though IX–X could not be searched). The locus is corrected to Henry, *Summa* a. 59 qq. 1–3.]
Henry, *Quodl.* VI q. 1 (*utrum essentia divina sit de qua Filius generatur*): correct for the *gignere per impressionem* doctrine discussed at *Ord.* nn. 72–75.

anchor.lemma: nullo modo filium dei cognoscetis si hunc de substantia patris esse negatis

notes.text: Aug. *Contra Maximinum* II 14.3 (PL 42, 772), quoted at *Ord.* n. 87: *Nullo modo verum Dei Filium cogitatis, si eum de substantia Patris esse negatis*. Gorris has *cognoscetis* and *li. 3°*. Scotus's numbering of the books differs.

*p* with a stroke reads *pro*. The sense requires *contra opinionem Henrici*, since what follows is Scotus's rejection of Henry (*Ord.* n. 93: *tenendo cum doctoribus antiquis… nullus ausus fuit…*). Perhaps the compendium was misread for *post*, or *pro* = ‘regarding’.  B has the same compendium (*p opi. hen.*), so the problem is common to both editions.

anchor.lemma: nam generatio in creaturis duo dicit

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 5 nn. 94–97: *Generatio in creatura duo dicit, mutationem et productionem… Productio enim est formaliter ipsius producti, et accidit sibi quod fiat cum mutatione*. Paraphrased closely.
A reads *effectū suū se*. *per* is supplied for the sense (cf. *Ord.* n. 96, *se sola*); perhaps read *se solo*.  B reads *effectū suū p se*, which confirms ⟨per⟩.
The four conclusions condense *Ord.* nn. 98–105: the *de* of *de substantia* conveys neither mere origination nor mere consubstantiality, but both together. The *creatura* counter-example is n. 103.

anchor.lemma: et tamen pater non est de substantia patris

notes.text: The argument requires *filii* (the Father is consubstantial with the Son but not *de substantia Filii*). A's *patris* is a printer's or author's slip; the translation emends.  B reads *pater nō est de substātia filij*, which confirms the emendation.

anchor.lemma: perfectio igitur ydemptitatis excludit omnem compositionem

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 5 n. 118 (and d. 8 n. 209?): relation and essence do not compose, because of the infinity of the essence, which makes them perfectly identical. On *identitas perfecta* see also *Ord.* I d. 2 nn. 403–406. [Checked: the Vatican paragraph numbers could not be consulted. The Wadding/Vivès text was not searched for the exact wording. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: non vt forma materie sed vt quidditas supposito

notes.text: *Ord.* I d. 5 n. 118: *essentia… communicatur ut quiditas supposito, non ut forma materiae*. This is a celebrated Scotist formula.

anchor.lemma: cum voluntas sit prima regula contingentium

notes.text: On the will as the first rule (*prima ratio*) of contingency: *Ord.* I d. 39 qq. 1–5 n. 35 and d. 8 p. 2. The question of whether the essence, prescinding from the will, is an efficient principle *ad extra* is not in d. 5 of the Vatican text. Gorris may be anticipating d. 7 n. 33 or d. 10. [Checked: the phrase *prima regula contingentium* was not found anywhere in the Wadding/Vivès *Ordinatio* (SCTA). Still open.]

A's *absoluti* stands for *absolute* ('of the essence taken absolutely'), as opposed to *cum persona originante*. B reads *de essentia absolute*, which confirms this; the English already follows that sense. Cf. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 5 c. 2, and *Ord.* n. 100.
B: *additur ab alijs*, which agrees with *Ord.* n. 59 (*ab aliis*).
B: *et cum ponit verbum*.
B: *productio perfecta*.

B: *illa relatio est perfecte eadem illi*. B's reading matches Scotus's point that the relation is perfectly identical with the essence because of its infinity. A's *ratio* still gives a sense (the notion of the relation), so the English follows A.

anchor.lemma: reddit ibidem quod aliud sit ibi substantia aliud persona

notes.text: B: *subdit ibidem quod aliud sit ibi persona aliud substantia*.
= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 6 q. un. (ed. Vat. IV), *utrum Deus Pater genuit Deum Filium voluntate*; cf. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 6 (*utrum Pater genuerit Filium voluntate vel necessitate*).

Hilary's *De Trinitate* has twelve books, so *XV* cannot be right. The dictum about the Father communicating all things to the Son *caritate et natura* is not yet located. It is perhaps from *De synodis* or *De Trin.* IX. [Checked: Scotus’s first argument for the question in the Wadding/Vivès text of *Ord.* I d. 6 q. un. (SCTA) is from Richard of St Victor, *De Trin.* VI c. 17 (‘ingenitum velle habere de se sibi conformem…’), not from Hilary. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 6 c. 1 (Quaracchi via SCTA) quotes Hilary’s *De synodis* (‘neque consilio neque voluntate Pater genuit Filium, anathematizat’) on the other side. No Hilary text with *caritate et natura* was found. Still open. Gorris’s authority may be a garbled Richard.] [Checked: Hilary, *De Trin.* (PL 10, local, books I–XII) was searched for *caritas/dilectio* with *natura*. The closest passage is IX 61: ‘Nescit autem Deus aliud aliquando quam dilectio esse, neque aliud quam pater esse. Et qui diligit, non invidet: et qui pater est, non etiam non pater totus est’, with the heading ‘ut Pater, nil non dat quod habet’. This is probably what is meant: the Father gives all by love and by being Father. *XV* would then be a misreading of *IX*, which is not certain.]

The condemnation of Eunomius (*Filium Dei non natura sed voluntate*) is in Augustine, *De Trin.* XV 20.38, not book III. A's *3°* is presumably a misreading of *15°* (*xv*). [Checked: Aug. *De Trin.* XV 20.38 (augustinus.it): ‘Quocirca ridenda est dialectica Eunomii … Filium Dei esse natura’. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 6 c. 1 (Quaracchi via SCTA) quotes the same passage as ‘in libro XV De Trinitate’. Verified.]
So A, for *Eunomii* (Eunomius of Cyzicus).

John of Rodington OFM (d. 1348), Oxford master and provincial minister, who wrote a commentary on the *Sentences*. Gorris traces the nominal/adverbial distinction of *voluntate* to Rodington, I d. 6 q. un. a. 3. This is a rare citation of Rodington in a fifteenth-century Scotist compendium. The reference is to be checked.  B reads *Johēz roditoris* (genitive of a form *Roditor*), which supports the identification with Rodington. [Checked: Rodington’s *Sentences* commentary is unedited, and no text was found online. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: Hic est Thomas prima parte summe. q. 34. articulo. 1.

notes.text: Aquinas, *ST* I q. 34 a. 1 (whether *Verbum* is a personal name in God) distinguishes *intelligere* and *dicere*. The pairing with Henry, *Quodl.* VI q. 2, for the anonymous *quidam doctor* of *Ord.* I d. 6 is Gorris's own and is to be checked against the Vatican apparatus. [Checked: Thomas, *ST* I q. 34 a. 1 co. and ad 3 (Corpus Thomisticum): ‘Anselmus vero improprie accepit dicere pro intelligere. Quae tamen differunt’. Verified for Thomas. Henry’s *Summa* a. 58 q. 2 (‘generare … idem quod dicere’, Badius 1520 via SCTA) is the closer Henry parallel.]

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* II q. 5. It is not checked whether this is the *quidam doctor* on the *intentio copulans parentem cum prole* (Augustine, *De Trin.* XI 7.12; cf. IX 12.18). [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* II q. 5 (Badius 1518 via SCTA) is on whether Christ’s body remains when the sacramental species cease. It does not fit, and *intentio copulans* does not occur anywhere in Henry’s Quodlibeta. The reference looks wrong.]
So printed, for *Hi*.

The doctrine of *signa originis* (instants of nature within the divine life) and of the Father willing in the first instant what he begets in the second follows the solution of *Ord.* I d. 6. [Checked: no external source is involved; this is Scotus’s own doctrine and was not checked further. Still open.]

The *Dialogus quaestionum LXV Orosii et Augustini* (Pseudo-Augustine), q. 7, as cited by Lombard and Scotus. The exact wording *voluntas patris preire scientiam non potest* is to be checked. [Checked: Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 6 c. 1 (Quaracchi via SCTA): ‘De hoc Orosius ad Augustinum ita ait: … praeire voluntas sapientiam non potest’. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 6 q. un. (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA): ‘est Augustini ad Orosium: Preire scientiam voluntas non potest’. Gorris’s *scientiam* matches Scotus’s wording rather than Lombard’s *sapientiam*. Verified.]
John Damascene, *De fide orthodoxa* I c. 8 (Burgundio's translation): generation is a work of nature, creation a work of will.

A reads *de 4°. scilicet de exigentia*, but the fourth necessity listed is *indigentie*. The translation reads ‘indigence’, as the reason given (*si indigens*) requires.  B also reads *exigentia*, so the slip is shared by both printings.

The four conclusions just given concern the intellect. *voluntatis* (first occurrence) is presumably a slip for *intellectus*, and the translation so takes it.  B reads *respectu voluntatis potentie*, so it offers no support for *intellectus*.

anchor.lemma: verbum nunquam est nisi a dicente

notes.text: The idea is Augustinian (*De Trin.* VII 1.2 and XV 14.23). The exact source of the wording is not found.  B reads *Verbum nunquam est sine adiciente* (*sine adiciēte*), apparently a corruption of A's reading. [Checked: Aug. *De Trin.* VII 2.3 (augustinus.it): ‘Verbum non ad se dicitur, sed tantum relative ad eum cuius Verbum est’. This is the closest Augustinian wording. The exact dictum was not found. Still open.]

Godfrey of Fontaines, *Quodl.* V q. 4. The reference is to be checked. [Checked: Godfrey, *Quodl.* V q. 4 (SCTA): ‘Utrum verbum in divinis sit solum personale soli Filio conveniens vel sit aliquod verbum essentiale in divinis’. This fits the context (*dicere*/*verbum* in d. 6). Verified.]
The Scotist *memoria fecunda* (intellect plus essence as present object) is the principle of the production of the Word: *Ord.* I d. 2 p. 2 qq. 1–4 nn. 221ff.; *Ord.* I d. 6.
Augustine, *De Trin.* XI 7.12 (the will *copulatrix* of parent and offspring), on the trinity of memory, understanding and will.
See note on the Latin reference. *caritas* is here the divine charity that is the essence; this is how the reply at §s031-11 takes it.
A *exigentia*; corrected from the list just given.
A *voluntatis*, corrected; see the Latin note.
*signum originis*: a ‘sign’ or instant in the order of origin (not of time), in which one thing is prior by nature to another.
B: *dicit quidam doctor aliter*.
B: *Quarto vtrum* (om. *dicetur*).

B: *qui non nominat rationem formalem* (*q nō noīat*). A's *variat* is clear in the print. B's reading gives an easier sense (the adverb does not name a formal ratio), but A's makes sense too, and A is kept.
B: *ergo intellectio elicit verbum*.
= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 7 q. 1 (ed. Vat. IV), *utrum potentia generandi in Patre sit aliquid absolutum vel relatio*. Cf. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 7.

anchor.lemma: eo enim est pater quo est filius

notes.text: Augustine, *De Trin.* V 5.6: ‘Pater non dicitur Pater nisi ex eo quod est ei Filius’. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 7 q. 1 (Wadding/Vivès), opens with ‘Augustinus 5. de Trinit. cap. 6. “eo Pater est, quo est ei Filius”’. The book is V, not XV; A and B (*xv.*) both err. [Checked: Augustine *De Trin.* V (augustinus.it, local) and Scotus *Ord.* I d. 7 q. 1 (Wadding/Vivès, local). Corrected and verified.]
A reads *ergo eo* at the line-end and then *est pater quo generat* at the top of p. 53. B has *ergo eo pater quo generat* (B checked).
John Damascene, *De fide orthodoxa* I c. 8 (B *li. i. c. viij.*).
So A and B (*pedis qstionis*, B checked). Apparently ‘at the foot’ (start) of the question, i.e. at the head of the body of the question after the arguments. No correction is suggested.

The view that the *potentia generandi* signifies the essence directly is Aquinas, *ST* I q. 41 a. 5 (*utrum potentia generandi significet relationem vel essentiam*). A has *q. 40*, B *q. iiij.*; both are wrong. [Checked: Thomas, *ST* I q. 41 a. 5 co. (Corpus Thomisticum): ‘quidam dixerunt quod potentia generandi significat relationem … Sed hoc esse non potest … natura divina in patre, est potentia generandi in ipso’. Verified for q. 41 a. 5.]

B: *quolib. iij. q. iij.* (B checked). Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* III; the right question is to be checked. Both agree on *Summa* a. 57 q. 7. [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: Henry, *Quodl.* III q. 3 asks ‘vtrum ratio generandi in patre sit diuina essentia, vel proprietas eius vt pirnitas, vel vtrumque’, which is exactly the point. III q. 5 is on Christ’s soul. So B’s *q. iij.* is right and A’s *q. 5* wrong. The *Summa* a. 57 text on SCTA has only qq. 1–4, so q. 7 could not be checked. Verified for *Quodl.* III q. 3.]
Aristotle, *Metaph.* V.12, 1019b21–33 (*possibile* in the logical sense, i.e. non-contradiction of terms).  B reads *ij. metha.*.

The division of being by act and potency is *Metaph.* V.7, 1017a35–b9, and IX.1. *Metaph.* IV is presumably a slip.  B reads *ij. metha.* here too (B checked), so neither printing gives the right book. [Checked: Bekker references not re-checked against a Greek or Latin text. Still open.] [Checked: *Metaph.* V 7, 1017a35–b2 (Greek, Perseus/Ross), ‘ἔτι τὸ εἶναι σημαίνει καὶ τὸ ὂν τὸ μὲν δυνάμει ῥητὸν τὸ δʼ ἐντελεχείᾳ’, and IX 1, 1045b32–34, ‘τὸ δὲ κατὰ δύναμιν καὶ ἐντελέχειαν’. Both loci verified. A’s *4.* and B’s *ij.* are both wrong.]

anchor.lemma: Tunc doctor soluit questionem. et tenet duas conclusiones

notes.text: Scotus's answer: the *potentia generandi*, taken for what it denominates *per se* (its proximate foundation), is something absolute, namely the divine essence as *memoria fecunda* in the Father. The relation is co-signified. Cf. *Ord.* I d. 7 q. 1. [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 7 q. 1 in the Wadding/Vivès text (SCTA) is ‘Utrum potentia generandi in Patre sit aliquid absolutum vel proprietas Patris’. Verified as the locus.]

Why the Son, who has the same fruitful memory, does not beget, and why there cannot be several Sons: the power is exhausted by its adequate term. Cf. *Ord.* I d. 7 q. 2 (*utrum in divinis possint esse plures filii*), which Gorris folds into q. 1.  B reads *habet terminum adequatum* and omits *vel prehabet*. [Checked: the Wadding/Vivès text (SCTA) also has only one question in d. 7, so the folding into q. 1 is not peculiar to Gorris. Still open as to the precise passage.]

*Ord.* I d. 7 q. 1: divine generation as univocal production, in which the offspring is like the begetter in nature.  B reads *vniuocata*. [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 7 q. 1 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA) argues from univocal generation (‘impossibile est agens communicare terminum formalem productionis, nisi agat forma aeque perfecta si agit univoce’). The objection that divine generation is *aequivoca* is answered there. Verified.]
So A (abbreviated *ꝙrit. q.*) and B (*vt querit questio*, B checked).

anchor.lemma: at the foot of the question

notes.text: Lat. *pedis questionis*; see the Latin note.
*potentia logica*: possibility as mere non-repugnance of the terms, as opposed to real (active or passive) power.
*repugnantia terminorum*: a ‘Son begetting’ would require a term (a second Son) whose existence is impossible.
B: *fundamento primo*.
= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 1 (ed. Vat. IV), *utrum Deus sit summe simplex*. Cf. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 8 cc. 3–8.
Aristotle, *Phys.* I.3, 186a34–b4: *quod vere est* (Parmenides' *ens*) is not an accident of anything (*nulli accidit*), in the medieval *auctoritas* form.

Augustine, *De Trin.* VI 6.8: God is *vere summeque simplex*. B reads *Aug. vi. de tri. deus summe simplex est*, without the chapter number (B checked).  B also lacks the chapter number (*Aug. vi. de tri. deus summe simplex est*).

The equality of the Holy Spirit *propter summam simplicitatem* is in Augustine, *De Trin.* VI 5.7 (augustinus.it): ‘aequalis est igitur etiam Spiritus Sanctus, et si aequalis in omnibus aequalis, propter summam simplicitatem quae in illa substantia est’. B, like A, has *v.* (B checked), so book V is wrong in both printings. The earlier ‘VI 7.9’ has been corrected.

anchor.lemma: simplex est quod non est resolubile

notes.text: On the simply simple concept (*conceptus simpliciter simplex*) as the term of resolution, see Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 1 qq. 1–2 nn. 71–73, and *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 1. [Checked: *resolubile* and *simpliciter simplex* were not found in the Wadding/Vivès d. 8 p. 1 q. 1. The Vatican numbers were not checked. Still open.]

The graded list of eight modes of identity (from the persons' properties up to the essence with its *summum esse*) is not in this form in Scotus's *Ordinatio*. Lists of modes of identity and distinction are characteristic of later Scotists, notably Francis of Meyronnes (*Conflatus* I d. 8). This source is a conjecture to be checked.

After *idem realiter essentialiter et formaliter*, the clause *differunt ex natura rei* seems contradictory, since Scotus's formal distinction is *ex natura rei*. Perhaps *non formaliter* or *modaliter* is meant, as in Scotus's doctrine of intrinsic modes (*Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 3 nn. 138–140). Kept as printed.  B has the same reading (*sed differunt ex natura rei*).
Aristotle, *APo.* I.4, 73b5–8: the third mode of *per se*, being by itself (*solitarium*), as substance, not said of a subject.
Anselm, *Monologion* c. 15: a *perfectio simpliciter* is *quod omnino melius est ipsum quam non ipsum*. Scotus discusses the definition at *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 3 and *Quodl.* q. 5.
Gorris uses three grades: *simplex* (irresolvable but composable), *simpliciter simplex* (the term of resolution, e.g. *ens*), and *summe simplex* (neither resolvable nor composable: God alone).
*perfectio simpliciter*: the standard rendering ‘pure perfection’.
The Latin (*sed in deo non vere est*) is compressed. The point is that wisdom in God is not a *per se* subsistent in the third mode, so the *auctoritas* does not apply.

anchor.lemma: sed est componibile alteri vt ens

notes.text: B omits everything from this clause to the second *vltimata resolutio* (*sed est componibile… stat vltimata resolutio*). It reads *Sed ipsum extat vltimata resolutio. nec est componibile alteri*, which is an eye-skip and runs the definitions of *simplex* and *summe simplex* together.
B: *sunt incomponibilia*. This is against the sense: creatures are not supremely simple because they are composable.
B: *creatura humana et diuina*.
B omits *vel tres persone… summa simplicitate* (eye-skip from *simplicitate* to *simplicitate*).
B: *ipsum est melius quam ipsum. i. non quolibet suo incompossibili*. *non* has been misplaced, and A's reading is the right one (Anselm's *melius ipsum quam non ipsum*).
= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 2, *utrum aliqua creatura sit simplex*.

Augustine, *De Trin.* VI 6.8: *creatura… nulla est simplex*. A gives no book number.  B also has no book number (*Aug. de tri. c. v. vbi dicit*). [Checked: Aug. *De Trin.* VI 6.8 (augustinus.it): ‘Nihil enim simplex mutabile est; omnis autem creatura mutabilis’. This is the dictum, so the paraphrase *nulla est simplex* gives its sense. Gorris’s *c. 5* is off by one chapter. Verified.]
Aquinas, *ST* I q. 3 a. 4 (in God alone are essence and *esse* the same) and q. 50 a. 2 ad 3 and ad 4 (angels are composed of *esse* and *quod est*, act and potency). Gorris's references are exact.

The composition of act and potency in intellectual creatures is *Summa contra Gentiles* II c. 52–53. Chapter 49 proves that intellectual substance is not a body. The chapter number is therefore doubtful. [Checked: *SCG* II c. 49 (Corpus Thomisticum) is ‘Quod substantia intellectualis non sit corpus’. c. 52 is ‘Quod in substantiis intellectualibus creatis differt esse et quod est’, and c. 53 is ‘… est actus et potentia’. Verified for cc. 52–53; Gorris’s c. 49 is wrong.]
Aristotle, *Metaph.* V.22, 1022b22–33 (*steresis*). The mole (*talpa*) as an example of privation relative to the genus is the medieval commonplace (cf. *Cat.* 10 and *De anima* III.1, 425a10).

Scotus rejects the thesis that every creature is composed of act and potency (essence and *esse*). His answer is that every creature is *composita vel componibilis*. [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 2 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA): ‘nulla creatura est perfecte simplex, quin aliquo modo sit composita vel componibilis’. Verified.]
*sanctus doctor*: Thomas Aquinas, canonized in 1323.
= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 3 (ed. Vat. IV), *utrum Deus vel aliquid formaliter dictum de Deo sit in genere*. Scotus's important discussion of univocity and the intrinsic modes falls here.

Avicenna, *Liber de philosophia prima* II c. 1: the division of being into *in subiecto* and *non in subiecto*, with substance as the latter. This is the standard citation in *Ord.* I d. 8. [Checked: Scotus himself cites ‘Avicenna 2. Metaph. C. 1. “Ens in subjecto et ens non in subjecto, non habent medium”’ in *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 3 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA). Verified as Scotus’s citation; the Avicenna Latin was not consulted.]

anchor.lemma: remouentur a deo illa predicata artis dyaletice

notes.text: The wording is Peter Lombard’s, not Augustine’s. *Sent.* I d. 8 c. 6 (‘Quod Dei simplicitas nulli praedicamentorum subicitur’) quotes Augustine, *De Trin.* V 1.2 (‘sine qualitate bonum, sine quantitate magnum … Quisquis Deum ita cogitat…’), and comments that ‘illa praedicamenta artis dialecticae Dei naturae minime convenire’. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 8 q. 3 (Wadding/Vivès), has ‘Contra est Magister in littera, et adducit Augustinum, et ostendit per eum, quod removentur a Deo illa Praedicamenta artis Dialecticae’. Boethius, *De Trin.* c. 4 (‘cuncta mutantur quae praedicari possunt’), expresses the same thought. [Checked: Lombard d. 8 c. 6 (PL 192 text, local); Augustine *De Trin.* V 1.2 (augustinus.it, local); Scotus *Ord.* I d. 8 q. 3 (Wadding/Vivès, local); Boethius *De Trin.* c. 4 (la.wikisource, Peiper). Verified as a reference to Augustine via the Master.]

Henry of Ghent, *Summa quaestionum ordinariarum* a. 21–22 (analogy of being: no concept common to God and creatures). Scotus attacks this opinion at *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 1 qq. 1–2 and d. 8 p. 1 q. 3. [Checked: Henry, *Summa* aa. 21–22 (Badius 1520 via SCTA); a. 22 qq. 2–3 on natural knowledge of God *inquantum … ens simpliciter*, already verified at n334. Verified.]

Henry, *Quodl.* X q. 7. Gorris's identification of the *responsio aliquorum* (on *ens ratum*) is to be checked against the Vatican apparatus. [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* X q. 7 (Badius 1518 via SCTA) is on whether the essence of a creature is really the same as its *esse*, with the *esse essentiae* / extrinsic participation distinction. This is related to an *ens ratum* reply, but no exact match was found. Still open.]

The ‘certain/doubtful concept’ argument for univocity: *Ord.* I d. 3 p. 1 qq. 1–2 n. 27 (*omnis intellectus certus de uno conceptu et dubius de diversis…*), repeated in d. 8 p. 1 q. 3. Gorris's cross-reference is correct.
John of Rodington again (cf. §s031-02), here *Roditori*, I d. 2 q. 6, credited with the ‘disjunctive certainty’ reply. To be checked. [Checked: Rodington is unedited (cf. n537). Still open.]

anchor.lemma: Alberti de Saxonia et fratris Roberti de Olcot. libro primo q. 5.

notes.text: Robert Holcot OP, *In quattuor libros Sententiarum quaestiones*, I q. 5, is plausible (Holcot's *Sentences* is arranged in questions). Albert of Saxony (d. 1390) wrote no known *Sentences* commentary. Either Gorris refers to a logical work of his, or *Alberti* stands for another author. To be checked.  B reads *fratris Roberti holcot*, which confirms Holcot. [Checked: no searchable Holcot *In Sent.* (Lyon 1497) or Albert of Saxony text was consulted. Still open.]
Aquinas, *ST* I q. 3 a. 5, *utrum Deus sit in aliquo genere*.

Boethius, *De Trinitate* c. 4–5: substance and relation are the two ways of predicating in God (*duo modi praedicandi*). *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 3 discusses the Boethian authority. [Checked: Boethius’s *De Trinitate* was not retrieved. Still open.] [Checked: Boethius, *De Trin.* (la.wikisource, Peiper). c. 4 distinguishes predication ‘secundum rem’ from predication ‘quasi circumstantias rei’; c. 6 ends ‘Ita igitur substantia continet unitatem, relatio multiplicat trinitatem’. Verified.]
Augustine, *De Trin.* VII 5.10: God is called *substantia* only *abusive*, since *substare* implies the bearing of accidents (*abusive substantiam vocari*).

Avicenna, *Liber de philosophia prima* VIII c. 4: the First has no genus. The chapter number *10* is to be checked.  B also reads *viij. metha. c. x.* [Checked: in *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 3 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA) Scotus has ‘Item arguit Avicenna 8. Metaph. c. 4. quod Deus non est in genere’. So the source Gorris follows reads c. 4, and his *c. 10* (with B) is wrong. Verified for VIII c. 4 as Scotus’s citation.]

Scotus's example of a whiteness with ten degrees: genus and difference taken from distinct *realitates* of one thing. Cf. *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 3 nn. 106–108 (*realitas a qua sumitur genus… realitas a qua sumitur differentia*). [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 3 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA): ‘si esset albedo sub decimo gradu intensionis … posset tamen concipi sub ratione albedinis tante … vel … precise sub ratione albedinis’, and also ‘in una re est aliqua prima realitas a qua sumitur genus, et alia realitas a qua sumitur differentia’. Verified.]
*gratia materiae* = ‘for the sake of the example’ (lit. ‘for the matter's sake’), a scholastic formula.
*ens ratum*: Henry of Ghent's *esse ratum*, the ‘ratified’ or certified being of an essence.
*doctor solennis*: Henry of Ghent's customary epithet.
Lat. *Roberti de Olcot*.
B: *formaliter est in genere* (om. *non*). This is against the conclusion, and A is right.
B: *sumuntur a distinctis rebus*.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 4, *utrum cum simplicitate divina possit stare distinctio perfectionum essentialium praecedens omnem actum intellectus*. This is the *locus classicus* of the formal distinction (*distinctio formalis a parte rei*). Gorris's *aliquo modo* differs from the Vatican wording (*omnem actum*?); to be checked. [Checked: the Wadding/Vivès text via SCTA has *Ord.* I d. 8 q. 4, ‘Utrum cum simplicitate divina possit stare distinctio perfectionum essentialium praecedens omnem actum intellectus’. Verified. The Vatican numbering is p. 1 q. 4 (Vat. IV).]

Ps.-Dionysius, *De divinis nominibus* (c. 5 or c. 13 in the Latin versions), on the unity of the divine perfections. The exact wording *multiplex formatio… est unita* has not been identified. [Checked: the Latin versions of *De divinis nominibus* were not consulted online. Still open.]

Aquinas, *Scriptum super Sent.* I d. 2 q. 1 a. 2–3: the attributes differ *ratione*, the *ratio* being in our intellect though founded in God. [Checked: Aquinas, *Scriptum super Sent.* I d. 2 q. 1 (SCTA text). Its a. 2 asks ‘utrum in illa unitate sit invenire diversitatem attributorum’. Its a. 3 asks ‘utrum pluralitas rationum, quibus attributa differunt, sit tantum in intellectu, vel etiam in Deo’. Verified.]

Hervaeus Natalis OP (d. 1323), whose *In I Sent.* d. 2 on the distinction of the divine attributes is meant. The form printed is *Eruey* (genitive?). This is a later author than Scotus, adduced by Gorris. [Checked: no searchable text of Hervaeus’s *In I Sent.* d. 2 was found online. Still open.]
*inquiunt* (plural: ‘they say’), referring to Thomas and Hervaeus together. As printed.

Godfrey of Fontaines, *Quodl.* VII q. 1 (on the distinction of the divine attributes). To be checked against the Vatican apparatus to *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 4. [Checked: Godfrey, *Quodl.* VII q. 1 (SCTA): ‘Utrum distinctio attributorum divinorum accipiatur per comparationem ad intrinseca vel … extrinseca’. Verified. The Vatican apparatus was not consulted.]

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* V q. 1 (the attributes distinguished by the act of the divine intellect), and *Quodl.* XIII q. 1 (?). The second reference is to be checked. [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: *Quodl.* V q. 1 asks ‘vtrum pluralitas & distinctio attributorum essentialium accipienda sit penes respectum … ad creaturas: an … ad aliquid intra’. Verified. *Quodl.* XIII q. 1 is on the vision of God by the blessed. It touches the attributes as distinct only ‘secundum rationem … secundum rationes attributales’, so it is a related passage, not a treatment of the question.]

Henry, *Summa* a. 37 (?) q. 7. Henry's treatment of the attributes falls in *Summa* aa. 32–75. The precise article is to be checked. [Checked in Badius 1520 via SCTA: *Summa* a. 37 is on divine knowledge as a habit, and only qq. 1–2 are given there. A q. 7 is not attested. Henry’s articles on the attributes (aa. 32ff.) were not searched individually. The reference looks wrong.]

Gorris's four grades of unity (aggregation, order, composition, indivision) are a compressed version of Scotus's scale of unity. Cf. *Ord.* I d. 2 p. 2 qq. 1–4 n. 403 and *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 4: *unitas aggregationis, ordinis, per accidens, per se compositi, simplicitatis*. [Checked: the Vatican paragraph numbers could not be consulted. The scale of unity in the Wadding text of d. 8 q. 4 was not matched term by term. Still open.]

The fifth conclusion is hard to construe as printed (*ad attributa non est ydemptitas et distinctio*). B reads *cum summa vnitate essentie cum attributis non est identitas et distinctio*, which is easier: there is no identity-with-distinction of the essence with the attributes that conflicts with supreme unity. The sense seems to be that the supreme unity of the essence excludes a real distinction of the attributes, but not their formal non-identity. B does not remove the difficulty of *non est*.

anchor.lemma: attributa habent non ydemptitatem preter intellectum

notes.text: Scotus's thesis: the attributes are formally non-identical *ex natura rei*, prior to any act of the intellect. Cf. *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 4 nn. 192–193 (*non-identitas formalis*). [Checked: Vatican nn. 192–193 could not be consulted (the edition is not openly online). Still open for the numbering.]
*bellum* … *ad ducem*: Aristotle's image of the army ordered to its general (*Metaph.* XII 10, 1075a13–15), here as *bellum*.
*rationes formales* is left half-untranslated: the formal ‘notions’ or ‘definitions’ of the attributes.
B: *quolib. iij. q. iij.* (B checked).
B: *vnitate essentie cum attributis*.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 2 q. un., *utrum solus Deus sit immutabilis*. Scotus's long treatment there of the philosophers' necessitarian emanation and of divine contingent causation is what Gorris summarises below (§§s037-04–07).
Gen. 6:6 (Vulg.): *et tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus*.
Mal. 3:6 (Vulg.): *ego enim Dominus et non mutor*. Gorris (or his source) has *deus* for *Dominus*.

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* VIII q. 9 (on whether a creature could be from eternity): the ten modes of having being. Gorris's list is to be checked against Henry's text. As printed, the sixth mode (*ex se possibile… et non est ab alio tamen necesse esse*) looks self-contradictory and may be corrupt. [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: *Quodl.* VIII q. 9 counts eleven modes, ending ‘Vndecimus modus est eius quod nec ex se nec ab alio est possibile esse’ (the *res a reor reris*, a being of imagination). Henry’s second mode (‘ex se formaliter ens: sed … ab alio’) is subdivided ‘tripliciter … principiatiue … causatiue … dependenter’. Gorris counts these three as his modes 2–4. Henry’s fifth mode is ‘ex se possibile esse: sed non possibile non esse, sed ab alio causatiue … necesse esse’, which Henry says implies contradiction. His sixth is ‘ex se possibile esse: sed ab alio causatiue necessario habet esse’ (Avicenna’s position). Gorris’s fifth corresponds to Henry’s sixth. His garbled sixth (*et non est ab alio tamen necesse esse*) is most likely a corrupt summary of Henry’s fifth (*non possibile non esse*). The English translates the text as printed. Verified.]

This sentence repeats the preceding one almost word for word; *Decē* is underlined in A by a later hand. It may be a printed doublet of a marginal heading.  B has the same doublet (*Decem modos ponit Hen. existendi res in qli. viij. q. ix.*), so it was in the common source. [Checked: purely textual, with no external source; it is confirmed against B as stated. Verified as a doublet.]

A prints *quodlibet⁹ ei⁹. 6⁹.*, with the *-us* sign on all three words. The grammar of *eiusdem quodlibetus eius* is defective; the sense is plainly ‘Henry's *Quodl.* VI, last question’. Reading kept as printed and flagged.  B reads *quolibet⁹ eiusdē. lxix. q. vl.* (B checked): it has the same *-us* form, and its numeral is corrupt. This confirms that the form goes back to the common source.

Henry, *Quodl.* VI (the last question, on the modes in which the heavens might be from the First). Gorris's remark that ‘in our Doctor’ the list sometimes has ten and sometimes four modes is notable. It points to variant textual states of Scotus's d. 8 p. 2 (*Ordinatio* vs *Reportatio*/*Lectura*?), which Gorris explains by Henry's two quodlibets. [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: the last question of *Quodl.* VI on SCTA is q. 33, ‘Utrum elementa sint distincta per corpora caelestia’. It discusses whether the heavens have *necesse esse* of themselves, with Averroes, *De substantia orbis*. That fits Gorris’s description, but the modes as listed there were not compared one by one.]

Henry, *Summa* a. 54 q. 3 (?). To be checked. [Checked in Badius 1520 via SCTA: *Summa* a. 54 q. 3 asks whether anything emanates from the unemanating person. How it bears on this passage was not established. Still open.]

A has *doctous* with a superscript, probably *doctoris*. The syntax of the sentence (*est doctoris contra Henricum quasi sibi contradiceret*) is loose.  B reads *est doctoris* in full, which confirms the reading.
Cross-reference to *Ord.* I d. 2 p. 1 qq. 1–2 (infinity of God proved from the intellect's knowing infinitely many things distinctly: the *via eminentiae/intellectus*). Cf. §§ on d. 2 above.

Cf. *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 2 q. un. nn. 275–299 (against necessary emanation). Gorris's list of six absurdities is his own ordering of Scotus's arguments, and the order is to be checked. [Checked: Gorris’s ordering was not compared against the Vatican paragraphs, which could not be consulted. Still open.]

*Ord.* II d. 7 q. un. (whether the bad angel necessarily wills ill), and *Ord.* IV d. 49 (beatitude: the impeccability of the blessed). [Checked: the SCTA listing of the Wadding text of book II did not yield a title for d. 7, so the question could not be confirmed. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: indisciplinati est querere omnium causas. 4°. metha.

notes.text: Aristotle, *Metaph.* IV 4, 1006a6–8: it is *apaideusia* (*indisciplinatio*) to seek a demonstration of everything. Scotus uses it in *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 2 n. 300 (*quare voluntas voluit hoc, nulla est causa nisi quia voluntas est voluntas*). A later hand repeats the phrase in A's margin.  B omits the reference *4°. metha.* and the following *vel* (*querere omnes causas. quia velle dei…*). [Checked: Bekker 1006a6–8 is the standard locus for *apaideusia*, but no edition was opened this pass. Still open.] [Checked: Aristotle, *Metaph.* IV 4, 1006a5–8 (Greek, Perseus/Ross), ‘ἀξιοῦσι δὴ καὶ τοῦτο ἀποδεικνύναι τινὲς διʼ ἀπαιδευσίαν· ἔστι γὰρ ἀπαιδευσία τὸ μὴ γιγνώσκειν τίνων δεῖ ζητεῖν ἀπόδειξιν’. Verified.]
Aristotle, *EN* VII 14, 1154b24–28: God always enjoys a single and simple pleasure (*Deus semper unam et simplicem gaudet delectationem*), because our nature is not simple.
A later hand in A's margin summarises: *deus non agit de necessario…*, with references (partly illegible).
*versio*: change as a ‘turning’ (cf. Jas. 1:17, *transmutatio… vicissitudinis obumbratio*). The sense of *immutatio que est versio* is somewhat obscure.
*voluntate antiqua*: Augustine's phrase (*Conf.* XII 15.18; *De civ. Dei* XII 17), a new effect from an eternal will.
B: *vbi causatus est*. A's *contentus* (‘is content with’) gives good sense, and the translation follows A.
B: *qlibetum viij. q. iij.* (B checked), against A's *q. 9* here and both texts' *q. ix* in §s037-02.
B: *ponerentur in non tempore*.

anchor.lemma: licet essentia sit prior in essendo

notes.text: B: *licet essentialiter sit prior in essentia*.
B: *gaudet voluntate*, a slip (Aristotle's *delectatio*).
= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 9 q. un., *utrum generatio Filii sit aeterna* (Vat. IV). [Checked: Wadding/Vivès text via SCTA, *Ord.* I d. 9 q. 1, ‘Utrum generatio Filii in divinis sit aeterna’. Verified.]
Ps. 109:3 (Vulg.): *ex utero ante luciferum genui te*.

anchor.lemma: ab initio et ante secula creata sum

notes.text: Ecclus. (Sir.) 24:14 (Vulg.): *ab initio et ante saecula creata sum*, quoted as *liber sapientie* in the broad sense of the sapiential books. Prov. 8:22–25 (*Dominus possedit me in initio…*).

Gregory the Great, *Moralia in Iob* XXIX (on Job 38). Gorris corrects Scotus's attribution. The passage is not on Job 38:21 (*sciebas tunc quod nasciturus esses*) but on Job 38:12, a little earlier in the same chapter and the same book of the *Moralia*. The verse is *numquid post ortum tuum praecepisti diluculo et ostendisti aurorae locum suum*. This is a notable piece of source-criticism by Gorris; the exact locus in *Moralia* XXIX is to be checked. [Checked: Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 9 q. 1 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA) has ‘Gregorius tamen Moralium 29. super illud Job. 38. Sciebas quando nasciturus’ and quotes ‘Non possumus dicere semper nascitur, ne imperfectum…’. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 9 c. 4 (Quaracchi via SCTA) gives the same Gregory passage as ‘Super Iob’. The *Moralia* text itself was not opened, so the verse (38:12 vs 38:21) is still open.] [Checked: Gregory, *Moralia* XXIX c. 1 n. 1 (PL 76, la.wikisource *Moralia/VI*): ‘Dominus Deus noster Jesus Christus in eo quod virtus et sapientia Dei est, de Patre ante tempora natus est; vel potius quia nec coepit nasci, nec desiit, dicamus verius semper natus. Non autem possumus dicere semper nascitur, ne imperfectus videatur’. The passage ends ‘Unde bene nunc ad beatum Job dicitur:’ and c. 2 opens ‘VERS. 12. Nunquid post ortum tuum praecepisti diluculo’. Gorris’s correction to Job 38:12 is verified.]
A has *Sciebas* in the first quotation and *Sciebat* in the second. B has the same, *Sciebas* first and *Sciebat* second (B checked). The Vulgate (Job 38:21) reads *sciebas*.
*amore*, A: read *aurore* with B (*aurorae*, Job 38:12 Vulg.). A's misreading (*m* for *ur*) produces nonsense (‘with love’).
*quem* A; *quam* B (agreeing with *auctoritas*). B's reading is grammatically preferable; this is a minor variant.

Motion as the act of the mobile passing from potency to act: Aristotle, *Phys.* III 1, 201a10–11 (definition of motion). Book VI deals with the divisibility of change. B also reads *vi.* [Checked: no Bekker text was opened this pass. Still open.] [Checked: *Phys.* III 1, 201a10–11 (Greek, Perseus/Ross), ‘ἡ τοῦ δυνάμει ὄντος ἐντελέχεια, ᾗ τοιοῦτον, κίνησίς ἐστιν’. The definition is verified at III 1. Gorris’s book number (*6.*, also B *vi.*) is not explained; probably a slip or a reference to the treatment of change in VI.]

Ambrose, *De fide* I. The Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 9 c. 2, cites it as ‘Ambrosius in I libro De Trinitate’: *si pater prius erat… generationis accessione mutatus est. Sed avertat Deus hanc amentiam*. The *in littera* is the Lombard's text, *Sent.* I d. 9. [Checked: Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 9 c. 2 (Quaracchi via SCTA): ‘Si enim ante Deus, postea Pater fuit, utique generationis accessione mutatus est. Sed avertat Deus hanc amentiam’. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 9 q. 1 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA): ‘Ambrosius 1. de Trin. cap. 6. et ponitur in littera’. Verified. The chapter is corrected from c. 4 to c. 2.]

Hilary, *De Trin.* XII (on ‘between begetting and being begotten there is no interval’), as cited in the Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 9. [Checked: Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 9 q. 1 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA): ‘auctoritas Hilarii in littera: Inter gignere et gigni nullum est medium’. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 9 c. 4 (Quaracchi via SCTA) cites Hilary, *De Trin.* XII, on eternal nativity (‘ab aeterno auctore aeterna nativitas est’), and VII. The exact words *inter gignere et gigni* were not found in the Lombard’s d. 9, and Hilary’s text was not opened.]

Cross-reference to *Ord.* I d. 5 p. 2 q. un. (whether the Son is generated from the substance of the Father), on generation not being *mutatio*; cf. section 030 above. [Checked: Wadding/Vivès via SCTA, *Ord.* I d. 5, the question whether the Son is generated from the substance of the Father. The cross-reference is internal and consistent with section 030. Verified.]

‘the Thomists’: Aquinas, *ST* I q. 42 a. 3 (*ordo naturae* without priority among the persons). Gorris names the school, not Thomas. [Checked: Aquinas, *ST* I q. 42 a. 3 co. (Corpus Thomisticum): ‘In divinis autem dicitur principium secundum originem, absque prioritate’, i.e. *ordo naturae* without priority. Verified.]

anchor.lemma: Aug. li. de fide ad Petrum

notes.text: *De fide ad Petrum* is by Fulgentius of Ruspe, transmitted under Augustine's name, as the medievals commonly took it. The quoted sentence on the persons (*nullus eorum… praecedit… excedit… superat*) is to be located. B reads *eternitate et excedit* for A's *aut*. [Checked: Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 19 c. 1 (Quaracchi via SCTA) quotes ‘Augustinus in libro De fide ad Petrum’: ‘Nullus horum alium aut praecedit aeternitate, aut excedit magnitudine, aut superat potestate’. This supports A’s *aut* against B’s *et*. Fulgentius’s own text was not opened. The sentence is located via the Lombard. Verified.]

The comment on John 16:13 (*audiet… audivit… audit*) is Augustine, *In Iohannis evangelium tractatus* 99.4–5, not tractate 18. Gorris's *omelia 18* is to be checked; possibly a corrupt numeral. [Checked on augustinus.it: *In Io. tract.* 99.5 has ‘et audivit, et audit, et audiet: quia … hoc est illi audire quod scire, et scire illi hoc est quod esse. Ab illo igitur audivit, audit, et audiet a quo est’. Verified for 99.5. Tract. 18 (§ 10) discusses hearing and seeing in the Word, not the Spirit’s hearing. Gorris’s ‘omelia 18’ is a parallel at best.]

Peter Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 8 c. 1: of God properly only *est* is said, not *fuit* or *erit*. The Master's discussion of tenses applied to God. [Checked: Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 8 c. 1 (Quaracchi via SCTA) quotes Augustine ‘Super Iohannem’: ‘Cum de sempiterna re proprie dicatur est, secundum nos bene dicitur fuit et erit’. Verified. In Quaracchi this is c. 1.]
A's abbreviation is ambiguous between *per* and *pro*; B's sign reads as *pro*. [Checked: purely palaeographical, with no external reference. Left open pending a re-reading of A.]
*lucifer*: the morning star (Ps. 109:3), rendered as in Douay.
Translating the correct reading *aurore* (B, Vulg.), not A's *amore*.
*esse existentie* (common to the persons) vs *esse subsistentie* (proper to each).
B: *moral. xxix. supra quam doctor subtilis*. In B the relative clause is attached by *supra*, not by A's *sumpta*. Both give acceptable sense, and the translation follows A.
B adds *non dico subsistentie* here as well as after the second *esse existentie*.
B: *siue significent personales* (om. *actus*).

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 10 q. un., *utrum Spiritus Sanctus producatur per modum voluntatis* (Vat. IV). Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 10 (the Holy Spirit as the love of Father and Son). [Checked: Wadding/Vivès via SCTA, *Ord.* I d. 10 q. 1, ‘Utrum Spiritus Sanctus producitur per actum et modum voluntatis’. Verified.]

Augustine, *De Trin.* XV (the Holy Spirit as love and gift, XV 17.27–19.37). The verbatim words *procedit necessario* are not located; they may be the scholastic gloss of the objection as Scotus states it.  B reads *Aug. xiij. de tri.* here, but *Aug. 15. de tri.* (*xv*) in §s039-08. [Checked: *procedit necessario* was not found in *De Trin.* XV (augustinus.it, local copy). Still open.] [Checked: Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 10 q. un. (Wadding/Vivès, local) opens with other arguments (the definition of *natura*; Averroes, *Phys.* VIII comm. 46) and cites no Augustine. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: doctoris solennis in summa articulo. 60. q. 1.

notes.text: Henry of Ghent (*doctor solemnis*), *Summa quaestionum ordinariarum* a. 60 q. 1, on the distinction of nature and will as principles of emanation. [Checked in Badius 1520 via SCTA: *Summa* a. 60 q. 1 is on whether the ratio of active spiration is the will or only nature. Verified.]

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* VI q. 1 (notional acts founded on essential acts). Scotus's reply is in *Ord.* I d. 10. [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* VI q. 1 (Badius 1518 via SCTA), already verified at n313, is on the notional acts and their essential foundations. Verified as the locus.]

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* V q. 1 (on the distinction of attributes in God, here of will and nature, *secundum rationem*). [Checked in Badius 1518 via SCTA: *Quodl.* V q. 1 is the general question on the distinction of the attributes. It is not specific to will and nature. Plausible but not confirmed for this point.]
A reads *sine actu*, which contradicts the argument. B reads *in actu intellectus et voluntatis* (B also writes *ethi.*). Read *in* with B.
Aristotle, *EN* X 7–8, 1177a12–1178b32 (happiness as the activity of the highest part). The ascription of beatitude to intellect *and* will is scholastic, not Aristotle's.

anchor.lemma: Sanctus doctor prima parte. q. 19. articulo. 1.

notes.text: Thomas Aquinas, *ST* I q. 19 a. 1 (*utrum in Deo sit voluntas*): *voluntas intellectum consequitur*; the parallel with sensitive appetite is in the corpus. Gorris calls Thomas *sanctus doctor* (canonised 1323).

Augustine, *De Trin.* V 14.15: *exiit enim non quomodo natus, sed quomodo datus*. Gorris's chapter number 17 follows a different capitulation. [Checked: Aug. *De Trin.* V 14.15 (augustinus.it): ‘Exit enim, non quomodo natus, sed quomodo datus, et ideo non dicitur Filius’. Verified.]

Scotus's argument from the reduction of productive principles to the two irreducible ones, nature and will (*Ord.* I d. 10 q. un.; cf. *Quaest. in Metaph.* IX q. 15 on the division of active powers into nature and will). [Checked: an internal Scotist cross-reference. *Quaest. in Metaph.* IX q. 15 was not opened. Still open.]

On essence and will as one total principle of spiration (essence concurring as object, will as power), cf. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 10 and the parallel for the intellect and the Word, *Ord.* I d. 2 p. 2 qq. 1–4. [Checked: an internal cross-reference, not compared with Vatican paragraphs. Still open.]

A school dispute on Scotus's intention: some held that Scotus posits no begotten act of understanding or willing in God (the acts are *innati*, not *eliciti*). Here Scotus is named in the text. The holders of this view are not identified.

*illicitos* A and B: = *elicitos* (i/e and ll spelling), not *illicitus* ‘unlawful’. B reads *illicitos .s. innatos* (‘elicited, that is, innate’?) for A's *illicitos sed innatos*. A gives the better sense.

Henry of Ghent's fourfold sense of *natura*: *Summa* a. 54 q. 3 / a. 60; cf. *Quodl.* VI q. 1. Exact locus to be checked. [Checked: *Summa* a. 54 q. 3 and a. 60 q. 1 (Badius 1520 via SCTA) exist and treat emanation by nature and will. The fourfold sense of *natura* was not located in them. Still open.]

Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 10 q. un.: the divine will is a principle of communicating the nature *ut infinita*; infinity as an intrinsic mode (cf. *Ord.* I d. 8 p. 1 q. 3). [Checked: an internal cross-reference, not compared with Vatican paragraphs. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: Doctor dicit quod ibi est libertas et necessitas

notes.text: Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 10 q. un. (the necessity of spiration stands with freedom; freedom has its own necessity, as nature has its own contingency). Cf. *Quodl.* q. 16. [Checked: an internal cross-reference. Scotus, *Quodl.* q. 16 (Vivès XXV) was not searched this pass. Still open.]

Unnamed. The distinction between necessity *quoad actum* and freedom *quoad electionem*, and the *libertas complacentiae*, are characteristic of later Scotist discussion, but the author is not identified.
Translating B's *in actu*, not A's *sine*.
*illicitos* = *elicitos*.
*libertas complacentiae*: the freedom of the will's delight or consent in a good that is necessarily loved.
B: *Tunc tercio respondet dubio*.
B: *pure noticiam genitam*, presumably a misreading of *ponere*.
B: *est sua perfectione*. A's *sine imperfectione* is the Scotist formula and is kept.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 11 q. 1, *utrum Spiritus Sanctus procedat a Patre et Filio* (Vat. V). Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 11. [Checked: Wadding/Vivès via SCTA, *Ord.* I d. 11 q. 1, ‘Utrum Spiritus Sanctus procedat a Patre et Filio’. Verified.]

John Damascene, *De fide orthodoxa* I c. 8 (Burgundio's Latin; ‘c. 7’ in the medieval capitulation): the Spirit *ex Patre procedens et in Filio quiescens*, as cited in Scotus's opening argument. The chapter number and the exact Latin wording are to be checked. [Checked: Burgundio’s Latin Damascene was not available online in searchable form. Still open.]
The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed in its Latin liturgical form, with the *Filioque*.
*Symbolum Quicumque* (‘Athanasian’ Creed): *Spiritus Sanctus a Patre et Filio, non factus nec creatus nec genitus, sed procedens*.

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* VI q. 1. The reference is as printed; Henry's discussion of the order of productions is also in *Summa* a. 54 and a. 60. [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* VI q. 1 (Badius 1518 via SCTA). See n313 and n658. Verified as the locus.]

*Passio sancti Andreae* (the ‘Letter of the presbyters and deacons of Achaia’), in Andrew's confession: *Spiritum Sanctum ex Patre procedentem et in Filio permanentem*. Cited in the *Filioque* controversy (e.g. Anselm, Aquinas, *Contra errores Graecorum*). [Checked: the *Passio Andreae* text was not opened. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: Si ascendero in celum mittam vobis paraclitum

notes.text: A paraphrase, not a verbatim Vulgate text: cf. John 16:7 *si autem abiero, mittam eum ad vos*; John 15:26 *cum autem venerit Paraclitus quem ego mittam vobis a Patre*.

anchor.lemma: Ille me clarificabit qui de meo accipiet

notes.text: John 16:14 (Vulg.): *ille me clarificabit quia de meo accipiet*. A has *qui* for *quia*.
John 20:22: *insufflavit et dicit eis: Accipite Spiritum Sanctum*.  B: *inflauit. Inflatio est processus*.

The Greek Fathers adduced for the *Filioque* (Athanasius, Dionysius, Chrysostom) form a standard Latin dossier (cf. Aquinas, *Contra errores Graecorum*; Council of Florence debates). Specific passages are not given. [Checked: no specific passages are given, so there is nothing to verify. Still open as a general note.]
*Liber Extra* X 1.1.1 *Firmiter* (Lateran IV, 1215): *Spiritus Sanctus ab utroque*.
