On *a Patre per Filium*: Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 2 (and d. 11 q. 1). The rejection of the Son as *principium quo*, as instrument, and as secondary cause is the standard scholastic analysis (cf. Aquinas, *ST* I q. 36 a. 3). [Checked: Wadding/Vivès via SCTA, *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 2, ‘Utrum Pater et Filius spirent uniformiter’. *ST* I q. 36 a. 3 co. (Corpus Thomisticum): ‘haec praepositio per designat in causali aliquam causam seu principium illius actus’. Verified.]

Augustine, *De Trin.* IX (mind, knowledge, love) and XV 21.41 (memory, understanding, will). The terminology *memoria fecunda / voluntas fecunda* is Scotist (*Ord.* I d. 2 p. 2 qq. 1–4; d. 10). [Checked: the general references to *De Trin.* IX and XV 21.41 were not matched to a specific wording here. Still open.]

Peter Auriol (d. 1322), *Scriptum super I Sent.* d. 11 (or d. 26–28 on the constitution of the persons). Gorris names Auriol here; the exact locus is to be checked. [Checked: Auriol’s *Scriptum* I is edited only in part online, and d. 11 was not found. Still open.]

Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 11 q. 2 / d. 28 q. 3: active spiration is not constitutive, since the persons are understood as constituted prior to the fruitful volition.  B: *Sed opi. doctoris est*. [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 11 q. 2 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA) asks whether, if the Spirit did not proceed from the Son, he would be really distinct from him. d. 28 q. 3 was not opened. Still open.]
*principium quo* (the formal principle) vs *principium quod* (the supposit that acts).
*permanere*; Damascene's *quiescere* (‘rest’) in 01.

anchor.lemma: pater posset esse filius et econtra

notes.text: B om. *econtra*.
B: *concurrit ad spirationem verbi*, an error anticipating *spiratio* (the parallel *ad constitutionem persone patris* follows in both).

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 11 q. 2, *utrum, si Spiritus Sanctus non procederet a Filio, distingueretur ab eo* (Vat. V). [Checked: the Wadding/Vivès text via SCTA has *Ord.* I d. 11 q. 2, ‘Utrum si Spiritus Sanctus non procederet a Filio, posset stare distinctio realis ipsius a Filio’. Verified.]

anchor.lemma: essentia continet vnitatem relatio multiplicat trinitatem

notes.text: Boethius, *De Trinitate* c. 6: *substantia continet unitatem, relatio multiplicat trinitatem*.

Augustine, *De Trin.* V 14.15 (*exiit… non quomodo natus sed quomodo datus*); cf. note at 039. In 02 the same place is cited as *capitulo 27*, apparently a numeral slip.  B also *c. 17* here. [Checked: Augustine, *De Trin.* V 14.15 (augustinus.it text): ‘exiit enim non quomodo natus, sed quomodo datus’. Verified, as at n663.]
As printed, and B agrees (*quia erit non quomodo natus*); the sense requires roughly ‘because he will go forth (*exibit*)’, so the reading is shared, not a slip of A alone.

Godfrey of Fontaines, *Quodl.* VII q. 4: whether the Holy Spirit could be said to proceed by way of will if he proceeded from the Father alone and not from the Son. The question number is as printed. [Checked: Godfrey, *Quodl.* VII q. 4 (SCTA): ‘Utrum Spiritus Sanctus possit dici procedere per modum voluntatis, si non procederet a Filio sed a solo Patre’. The question number is verified. The earlier paraphrase (‘whether he would be distinguished’) has been corrected to the printed title.]

Thomas Aquinas, *ST* I q. 36 a. 2 (*utrum Spiritus Sanctus procedat a Filio*): *si non esset ab eo, nullo modo posset ab eo personaliter distingui*. A's *q. 35* is apparently an error for *q. 36*.  B also *q. 35. arti. 2*. [Checked: *ST* I q. 36 a. 2 co. (Corpus Thomisticum): ‘Si enim non esset ab eo, nullo modo posset ab eo personaliter distingui’. Verified. *q. 35* is an error for q. 36. Question 35 is *de imagine*.]

anchor.lemma: Egidius de Roma quodlibeto primo questione sexta

notes.text: Giles of Rome, *Quodlibeta* I q. 6 (as printed). Giles follows Thomas on distinction by opposed relations of origin. [Checked: Giles, *Quodl.* I q. 6 (Venice 1504, SCTA transcription): ‘utrum spiritus sanctus distingueretur a filio si non procederet ab eo’. Verified.]
Aristotle, *Phys.* IV 6–9 (213a12–217b28): the inquiry into the void, which is shown to be impossible.
Contrast *capitulo 17* in 01 for the same Augustinian passage. One of the numerals is corrupt.  B apparently reads *c. 7* here (the numeral is blurred), against *c. 17* in 01 in both texts.

The topical *loci a toto in modo* and *a parte in modo* (Boethius, *De topicis differentiis* II; Peter of Spain, *Tractatus* V): from a universal or unrestricted proposition to a restricted one, and conversely. [Checked: Boethius, *De differentiis topicis* II (PL 64, cols. 1189–1190; archive.org scan of Migne): ‘Licet autem non solum in substantiis, verum etiam in modo, in temporibus, in quantitatibus, in loco, totum partesque respicere … si simpliciter aliquid proponamus, in modo totum est; si cum adiectione, aliqua pars fit modo’. Verified for Boethius. Peter of Spain was not consulted.]

Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 11 q. 2: the Spirit would be distinguished from the Son by his own absolute or proper ground, not by an opposed relation to him. [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 11 q. 2 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA) exists and treats the question. The *formaliter/fundamentaliter* wording was not found verbatim there. This remains an interpretive note. Still open.]
*a parte in modo*, a dialectical topic; rendered literally.
B: *hec questio secunda sit intelligenda*.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 1, *utrum Pater et Filius spirent Spiritum Sanctum inquantum sunt unum vel inquantum distincti* (Vat. V). Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 12. [Checked: Wadding/Vivès via SCTA, *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 1: ‘Utrum Pater et Filius spirent Spiritum Sanctum in quantum sunt omnino unum vel in quantum distincti’. Verified.]
Augustine, *De Trin.* V 14.15: *sicut Pater et Filius unus Deus… sic relative ad Spiritum Sanctum unum principium… ad creaturam Pater et Filius et Spiritus Sanctus unum principium*.

Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 54 (on the procession of the Holy Spirit; will as one or as concordant). [Checked: Henry, *Summa* a. 54 (Badius 1520, via SCTA) is on the procession of the Holy Spirit. Its q. 6 asks whether the Spirit emanates from the Son, and its q. 7 whether he emanates from the Father and the Son *aeque primo*. Verified for the article. The question within it is not specified in the text.]

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* V q. 9. Henry held that the Spirit would be distinguished from the Son even if he did not proceed from him (cf. d. 11 q. 2 above). [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* V q. 9 (Badius 1518, via SCTA): ‘arguitur quod spiritus sanctus non distingueretur a filio nisi procederet ab ipso’. Verified.]

*Liber Sextus* VI 1.1.1 *Fideli ac devota* (Second Council of Lyon, 1274): *fideli ac devota professione fatemur quod Spiritus Sanctus aeternaliter ex Patre et Filio, non tamquam ex duobus principiis sed tamquam ex uno principio, non duabus spirationibus sed unica spiratione procedit*. Gorris abridges the text.

Thomas Aquinas, *ST* I q. 36 a. 4 ad 1: *si consideretur virtus spirativa, Spiritus Sanctus procedit a Patre et Filio inquantum sunt unum… si considerentur supposita spirationis… procedit a Patre et Filio ut sunt plures*.
*ly* is the scholastic Old French article marking a word cited as a word (*ly inquantum*, ‘the [word] *inasmuch*’).

Avicenna, *Liber de philosophia prima* V c. 1: *equinitas est tantum equinitas*, of itself neither one nor many, neither universal nor particular. This is the locus classicus for the common nature; Scotus uses it in *Ord.* II d. 3 p. 1 q. 1.  B: *Auic. 2. metha. de equiuitate*; A's *5* is correct.

Aristotle on correlatives: *Cat.* 7, 6b28–7b15, and *Metaph.* V 15, 1020b26–1021b11 (father and son as correlatives). [Checked: *Cat.* 7 (First1KGreek text): ‘πάντα δὲ τὰ πρός τι πρὸς ἀντιστρέφοντα λέγεται, οἷον ὁ δοῦλος δεσπότου δοῦλος … ’ and ‘δοκεῖ δὲ τὰ πρός τι ἅμα τῇ φύσει εἶναι’. *Metaph.* V 15, 1021a23 (Perseus, Bekker milestones): ‘οὕτω γὰρ καὶ πατὴρ υἱοῦ λέγεται πατήρ’. Verified.]

anchor.lemma: relatio nec in diuinis nec in creaturis terminatur ad suum oppositum

notes.text: The thesis that a relation terminates at the foundation of its correlative, not at the opposite relation: cf. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 1 and d. 26 (and *Quodl.* q. 3 on the terms of relations). [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 1 and d. 26 exist in the Wadding/Vivès text. The thesis was not located verbatim, and *Quodl.* q. 3 was not searched for it. Still open.]

Scotus, *Quodl.* q. 1 (on *dicere* as a notional act, as distinct from essential *intelligere*). The exact article is to be checked. [Checked: Scotus, *Quodl.* q. 1 (Vivès XXV, c. p. 47) compares *memoria* and *dicere*. It says that ‘memoria est immediatior ipsi essentiae quam dicere’ and that ‘dicere est dicere’. Verified for the question. Gorris gives no article.]

Both A and B (*re|passi*) read *repassi*, which is not a recognisable word. The sense calls for ‘mutual/requited love’; perhaps *repensi* (*amor repensus*). This is a conjecture, and the word is left as printed.

anchor.lemma: potentia remota sed non potentia propinqua

notes.text: Remote vs proximate power: the Father alone has the fruitful will, but its proximate actuation is the mutual love of Father and Son (cf. Richard of St Victor, *De Trin.* III on the *condilectus*). [Checked: Richard of St Victor, *De Trin.* III c. 11 (PL 196; archive.org scan of Migne): ‘summe … dilectorum … uterque oportet ut pari voto condilectum requirat’. This confirms the comparison. The remote/proximate distinction itself is not attributed in the text.]
*principium quod*; see note at 040.
*equinitas*, Avicenna's stock example of a nature considered in itself.
Translating conjecturally; see the note on *repassi* in the Latin.

anchor.lemma: In hac questione vbi mouetur dubium

notes.text: B: *In hac questione vnum mouetur dubium*, which is smoother; A's *vbi* may be a misreading of *vnū*.
B: *concurrunt vt vnum principium concurrunt* and ends there (om. *vt vnum essentialiter*).

The question whether Father and Son are *duo spirantes* or *duo spiratores* is not a separate question in Scotus's *Ordinatio* I d. 12 as edited (Vat. V has qq. 1–2). Gorris may take it from the *Reportatio* or from Scotus's discussion in d. 12. B also has a separate question here. The Scotist source is to be identified. [Checked: the SCTA Wadding/Vivès text of *Ord.* I d. 12 has only qq. 1–2. The point stands. Gorris’s Scotist source for the separate question was not identified. Still open.]

Aquinas, *ST* I q. 36 a. 4 ad 7 (the last article of q. 36): *duo spirantes… non tamen duo spiratores, propter unam spirationem*. A's *q. 35* is apparently an error for *q. 36*. The same slip occurs at 046 (*q. 35 a. 2*); compare *q. 41* for q. 42 at 045.  B also *q. 35. ar. vl.*. [Checked: *ST* I q. 36 a. 4 ad 7: ‘duo spirantes, propter pluralitatem suppositorum; non autem duo spiratores, propter unam spirationem. Nam adiectiva nomina habent numerum secundum supposita, substantiva vero a seipsis’. Verified.]

The grammatical doctrine of the *nomen verbale* (agent noun) signifying *per modum habitus et quietis*, as against the participle signifying *per modum fluxus*, from modistic grammar. Scotus applies it to *spirator/spirans*. [Checked: the grammatical basis is given in Aquinas, *ST* I q. 36 a. 4 ad 7: ‘adiectiva nomina habent numerum secundum supposita, substantiva vero a seipsis’. The modistic *per modum habitus* doctrine was not checked in a grammatical source. Still open.]
‘A certain new doctor’. The person is not identified. The phrase marks a recent author, distinct from *doctor* (Scotus) used in the same paragraph.
*duo spirantes* (participle) is rendered ‘two spirating’ throughout, to keep the grammatical point against *duo spiratores* (agent noun).
B: *quare materialis terminus*, and again *terminus materialis appositus* in 03, a misreading of *numeralis* that destroys the argument.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 2, *utrum Pater et Filius spirent Spiritum Sanctum uniformiter* (Vat. V). This is Gorris's third question because of the preceding question on *spiratores*. [Checked: Wadding/Vivès via SCTA, *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 2: ‘Utrum Pater et Filius spirent uniformiter Spiritum Sanctum’. Verified.]

Augustine, *De Trin.* XV 17.29 and 26.47: *de quo [Patre] procedit principaliter*. B reads only *Aug. 15. de tri.* without a chapter, so A's ‘c. 7’ has no support from B; perhaps for c. 17. [Checked: *De Trin.* XV 17.29, ‘de quo procedit principaliter Spiritus Sanctus nisi Deus Pater … Ideo autem addidi, Principaliter’, and XV 26.47, ‘de Patre principaliter … communiter de utroque procedit’. Verified. A’s *c. 7* is probably for c. 17.]
Thus also in B (*Dum dicit soluendo argumenta principalia*). The clause is elliptical and probably refers to Scotus's own reply to the principal arguments.

Alexander of Alessandria OFM (d. 1314), Franciscan minister general and commentator on the *Sentences*, I d. 12 q. 2. [Checked: no searchable text of Alexander of Alessandria’s *In I Sent.* was found online. Still open.]

Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* d. 12 a. un. q. 2 (end) and *dubium* 3 *circa litteram*. On the Father as spirating *principalius*. [Checked: Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* d. 12 a. un. q. 2 (Quaracchi via SCTA): ‘Utrum Spiritus sanctus a Patre plenius et principalius quam a Filio procedat’. Verified.]

The initial is ambiguous in A (it resembles a G or S). B reads *Guilhel. var|ronis*, and A itself has *Guillermi varronis* at 046-02. This is William of Ware OFM (Guillelmus de Ware, ‘Varro/Guaro’; fl. c. 1290–1305), *In I Sent.* d. 12, Scotus's reputed teacher.  B confirms: *frater Guilhel. var|ronis in presenti dist.*

Scotus's ‘signs (*signa*) of origin’: *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 2. In the first sign the Father has both fecundities from himself; in the second he generates and the Son has the second fecundity; in the third the Father and the Son spirate together. [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 2 (Wadding/Vivès via SCTA) exists. The three signs were not verified there clause by clause. Still open.]

Scotus, *Ord.* II d. 1 q. 1 (the *instantia/signa naturae* in the divine productions and in creation). [Checked: Wadding/Vivès via SCTA, *Ord.* II d. 1 q. 1: ‘Utrum primaria causalitas respectu causabilium de necessitate sit in tribus personis’. The question exists. Its treatment of the *signa* was not checked in detail. Probable.]
See the Latin note: William of Ware.

No fourth question on d. 12 in Scotus's *Ordinatio* as edited. The articles on order and priority of origin draw on *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 2, d. 9 and d. 20 (*utrum in divinis sit ordo*). The Scotist source of this compilation is to be identified. [Checked: there is no d. 12 q. 3 in the SCTA Wadding/Vivès text. *Ord.* I d. 20 q. 1 is ‘Utrum tres personae sint aequales in potentia’, which is the closest *Ordinatio* locus on priority and order. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: sanctus doctor prima parte. q. 41. articulo. 3.

notes.text: Aquinas, *ST* I q. 42 a. 3 (*utrum in divinis personis sit ordo naturae*): *ordo naturae… non quo alius sit prior alio*. A's *q. 41* is apparently an error for *q. 42*. In the Munich copy a contemporary hand has written ‘tho.’ in the margin here.  B also *q. xli.* (om. *sanctus*). [Checked: *ST* I q. 42 a. 3 (Corpus Thomisticum), as at n647. Verified. *q. 41* is an error for q. 42.]

The comparison of prior/posterior to order with even/odd to number has not been located in *De civ. Dei* X. The citation is as printed.  B: *aug. x. de tri. dei*, a conflation that does not help locate the passage.

Comparison: *prior* (comparative) and *primus* (superlative) presuppose a positive. Grammarians gave the adverb *pridem* (or the preposition *prae*) as the positive. [Checked: no grammatical source was consulted for the *pridem prior primum* paradigm. Still open.]
Ps.-Dionysius, *De caelesti hierarchia* (cc. 6–10, the three triads ascending to the seraphim).

Ps.-Augustine, *De triplici habitaculo* (PL 40, 991–998), on the vision in the heavenly homeland. Gorris's polemic (*salua gracia*) suggests that the attribution of the passage was disputed. [Checked: the archive.org OCR of PL 40 was searched, but the text of *De triplici habitaculo* was not found in it (OCR or scan incomplete). The passage on the Father’s priority remains unlocated. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: nulla res est que se ipsam gignat

notes.text: Augustine, *De Trin.* I 1.1: *nulla omnino res est quae se ipsam gignat ut sit*.

Anselm, *Monologion* c. 6 (nothing can be the cause of its own being, since it would be prior to itself). ‘primo’ is perhaps ‘in the first [book]’. To be checked. [Checked: Anselm, *Monologion* (PL 158, Gerberon text; archive.org scan of Migne, poor OCR), in the chapter headed *Caput VI [al. V]*: ‘aut per se, aut per aliud est ex nihilo. Nam per se, alioquin ipsa esset seipsa prior’. Verified for c. 6 (Schmitt numbering).]

*Prius in quo* vs *prius a quo*: Scotus's distinction of ‘signs’ of nature (*in quo*) and priority of origin (*a quo*). Cf. *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 2 and II d. 1 q. 1. [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 12 q. 2 and II d. 1 q. 1 exist (SCTA). The *in quo/a quo* wording was not checked verbatim. Still open.]

As printed. The argument seems to need ‘none of them is from another (*ab alia*)’, since an order of origin requires one thing to be from another. B not checked.  B agrees (*nulla illarum est a se*), so the difficulty is shared by both printings.

anchor.lemma: But is there an order of nature in God?

notes.text: The Latin has no mark of interrogation. It is taken as an indirect question introducing the two school positions.
*De triplici habitaculo* (pseudo-Augustine).
B: *vsque ad vltimum ierarcham*.

anchor.lemma: nam sicut pater prius est quam filius. et prius spirat quam filius

notes.text: B: *Nam si pater prius est quam filius etc.*, om. *et prius spirat quam filius*.
B: *iure absoluto*, a corruption of A's reading.

= Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 13 q. un., *utrum productio Spiritus Sancti sit generatio* (Vat. V). Scotus also reviews and rejects several ways of distinguishing the productions. [Checked: Wadding/Vivès via SCTA, *Ord.* I d. 13 q. 1: ‘Utrum Spiritus Sanctus sit genitus, sive utrum productio Spiritus Sancti sit generatio vel distinguatur ab ea’. Verified.]

Thus A. The argument (*ergo vnus motus*) and Aristotle, *Phys.* V 1 (224b7–10, motions are distinguished by their *termini ad quem*), require *motus*. The translation reads ‘motion’.  B also has *modus* (*Generatio et modus distinguuntur preter modos*), so the error is common to both printings.
Augustine, *De Trin.* V 14.15: *exiit enim, non quomodo natus, sed quomodo datus; et ideo non dicitur filius*. Gorris's ‘c. 17’ again (compare 039, 041).  B also *v. de tri. ca. xvij.*
Giles of Rome, *In I Sent.* d. 13 (article 2 as cited): the processions are distinguished by their terms. [Checked: no searchable text of Giles’s *In I Sent.* was found online. Still open.]
William of Ware OFM, *In I Sent.* d. 13. Here A spells the name clearly (compare 044-02).

Probably Aquinas, *ST* I q. 36 a. 2 ad 7 (the Son is from one, the Spirit from two). For *q. 35* compare 043.  B also *q. xxxv. arti. ij.* [Checked: *ST* I q. 36 a. 2 ad 7: ‘filius est solum a patre, spiritus sanctus vero a patre et filio. Non enim aliter processiones distinguerentur’. Verified.]

Godfrey of Fontaines, *Quodl.* III q. 3, as printed. This is wrong: III q. 3 asks whether angelic nature is composed of matter and form. The intended locus is perhaps *Quodl.* VII q. 4, on procession by way of will (see 041). [Checked: Godfrey, *Quodl.* III q. 3 (SCTA): ‘Utrum natura angelica sit composita ex vera materia et vera forma’. This does not fit the passage. *Quodl.* VII q. 4 is a candidate but has not been confirmed. Uncertain.]
Aquinas, *ST* I q. 27 a. 4 ad 1 (*utrum processio amoris sit generatio*). [Checked: *ST* I q. 27 a. 4 ad 1 (Corpus Thomisticum): ‘utrum processio amoris in divinis sit generatio’. Verified.]
Henry of Ghent, *Summa*, as printed (a. 27 q. 7). Henry's doctrine of distinction by the elicitive principles (intellect and will) is mainly in *Summa* a. 54 and a. 60. The numeral may be corrupt.

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* V q. 1 (nature and will as the principles of the productions); cf. 039. [Checked: Henry, *Quodl.* V q. 1 (Badius 1518) is on the distinction of the attributes. It touches nature and will as principles, as at n659. Probable.]
‘Brother Adam’, *I Sent.* d. 6 q. 1 a. 2. This is probably Adam Wodeham OFM (d. 1358), or possibly another Adam. A post-Scotistic authority added by Gorris; not in Scotus.

Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 13 q. un.: the productions are distinguished by themselves formally (*se ipsis formaliter*), and by their principles (nature and will) as by their elicitive *rationes*. [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 13 q. 1 exists (SCTA). The phrase *se ipsis formaliter* was not checked verbatim. Still open.]

Augustine, *De Trin.* XV 27.50: *quantum distet nativitas verbi a processione doni*… *ut voluntatem de cognitione procedere… non tamen eius esse imaginem*. Gorris reads *dati* for *doni*. [Checked: *De Trin.* XV 27.50: ‘quid distet nativitas Verbi Dei a processione Doni Dei’. Verified.]

anchor.lemma: Cur spiritus sanctus non sit filius

notes.text: Augustine, *De Trin.* V 14.15.

anchor.lemma: aliqua res est infinita in se et a se

notes.text: Threefold classification: infinite *in se et a se* (Father), infinite *in se* but not *a se* (Son, Spirit), finite (creature). Cf. Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 13 (on the *infinitas* of the produced persons). [Checked: no verbatim source for the threefold classification was found in *Ord.* I d. 13 (SCTA). Still open.]
‘Hypostatically’, i.e. as a person (*hypostasis*), as against *substantialiter* (the common essence).
A prints *modus*; translated as *motus*. See Latin note.
*argutive*: in the order of argument or knowledge (*innotescunt*), as against *quidditative* and *elicitive*.
B: *secundum Augustinum v. de trini. capitulo iij.*
B: *intelligi distantiam*.
B: *Item. v. de trini. ca. xxiij.* A's *c. 17* agrees with its other citations of the passage.

anchor.lemma: et tamen sunt seipsis primo formaliter distincte

notes.text: B: *et non sunt seipsis…*, which contradicts the argument; A is right.

Lombard, *Sent.* I dd. 14–15 (on the temporal procession, mission and giving of the Son and the Holy Spirit). Scotus treats these distinctions together with d. 16 (*Ord.* I dd. 14–16); the exact correspondence of Gorris's three questions to Scotus's text has not been checked. [Checked: the SCTA Wadding/Vivès *Ordinatio* lacks I dd. 14–16, and Bonaventure’s d. 14–15 question titles were compared only in outline. Still open.]

Augustine, *Ep.* 187 (*ad Dardanum*). The formula *quelibet persona dat et datur* has not been found there verbatim. Compare Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 15 c. 1, where the Holy Spirit *et dat et datur*, citing *De Trin.* XV. [Checked: *Ep.* 187 (augustinus.it) has no *dat et datur*. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 15 c. 1 (Quaracchi via SCTA) reads ‘et ideo et dat et datur. Dat quidem in quantum Deus, et datur in quantum donum’. The *ad Dardanum* attribution is unconfirmed. Uncertain.]

Augustine, *De Trin.* IV 20.28: *Sed pater cum ex tempore a quoquam cognoscitur, non dicitur missus; non enim habet de quo sit aut ex quo procedat*. The chapter is cited as ‘c. 17’ here and as ‘c. 7’ in 047-02. Neither matches the modern division (c. 20).  B: *augu. [?] de trini. capitulo xvij.* (the book numeral is lost at the cropped line start); in 02 B has *iiij. de trini. c. vij.*, as A.

anchor.lemma: In his distinctionibus non sunt opiniones

notes.text: An unusual statement in this work: Gorris finds no rival opinions to report and goes straight to the solution.

anchor.lemma: non enim habet a quo sit aut a quo procedit

notes.text: Augustine reads *de quo sit aut ex quo procedat* (*De Trin.* IV 20.28); Gorris quotes freely.

Thus A, in two words both times (047-03). The sense is ‘sub-authoritatively’, i.e. as working under the authority of the person from whom the power to act is received.  B has *quasi sub|auctoritatiue* (hyphenated at line end) and then *quasi subauctoritatiue* as one word, which supports the reading ‘sub-authoritatively’.

Isa 61:1 (*Spiritus Domini super me*, cf. Luke 4:18), not Isa 6; a numeral has probably dropped out. Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 15 c. 3, also cites Isa 48:16, *Nunc misit me Dominus et Spiritus eius*.  B also *esa. vi.* [Checked: Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 15 c. 3 (Quaracchi via SCTA) quotes Ambrose, *De Spiritu sancto* III: ‘Dicit enim Filius Dei: Spiritus Domini super me, propter quod unxit me: evangelizare pauperibus misit me’, with *Nunc misit me Dominus et Spiritus eius* (Isa 48:16). This matches Gorris’s ‘magister dicit … Spiritus domini super me. Et Ambrosius. Spiritus domini misit me’. Verified. *Isaie 6* is for Isa 61:1.]

anchor.lemma: Spiritus domini misit me ad predicandum

notes.text: Ambrose, *De Spiritu Sancto* (book II according to Lombard), as quoted by Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 15 c. 3: *Bene autem dixit super me, quia quasi filius hominis et unctus est et missus ad praedicandum*. Lombard's own conclusion is that the Son is sent by the Spirit. Gorris's reply (*de christo homine*) takes up Ambrose's own qualification.

*vt non videamur habere penuriam nominum*: the appeal to ‘poverty of names’ is a commonplace of Trinitarian terminology (compare Augustine, *De Trin.* V 9.10 on *tres personae*). The precise source here is not identified.
*sub auctoritatiue*: see the Latin note.

Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 15, citing Augustine, *De Trin.* IV 20.28 (see n766): only a person that is from another is sent. [Checked: *De Trin.* IV 20.28: ‘Mittit qui genuit; mittitur quod genitum est’. Verified.]
A prints *bonor*. In A's type at this resolution *h* and *b* are hard to tell apart, and B reads *honor*.

*Sapientia genita*: the stock example of a ‘mixed’ term, essential (*sapientia*) qualified by a notional determinant (*genita*). Compare Augustine, *De Trin.* VII 1.2–2.3, on *sapientia de sapientia*. [Checked: *De Trin.* VII is local, but *sapientia genita* as a school example was not found verbatim. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: opera trinitatis sunt indiuisa ad extra

notes.text: The scholastic axiom *opera Trinitatis ad extra sunt indivisa*, regularly ascribed to Augustine; compare *De Trin.* I 4.7 (*inseparabiliter operentur*) and *Enchir.* 38. [Checked: *De Trin.* I 4.7: ‘sicut inseparabiles sunt, ita inseparabiliter operentur’. Verified. *Enchiridion* 38 was not fetched.]
A prints Q with a superscript abbreviation (*Qꝫ*/*Qꝛ*). B reads *ꝙ aūt sic competit* (*quod autem*), which confirms *Quod*.
Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 15 c. 4 (*Quod Filius sit missus a se*), with Augustine, *De Trin.* II (as cited by Lombard), on the inseparable operation.

Ambrose, quoted by Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 15 c. 4: *Cum non definitum fuerit per Prophetam a quo datus sit Filius, ostenditur datus gratia Trinitatis, ut etiam ipse Filius se dederit*. Gorris takes the book number from Lombard's preceding citation (*in II libro De Spiritu Sancto*). A later gloss on Lombard (LombardPress text cv8jk9) remarks that Lombard departs from Ambrose's meaning.

anchor.lemma: vt et iam filius ipse dederit se

notes.text: *et iam* (= *etiam*) is printed as two words in A.

The objection identifies temporal mission with origin. Compare Aquinas, *ST* I q. 43 a. 4, and Scotus, *Ord.* I dd. 14–16, on whether a person sends itself. The holder of this opinion is not named. [Checked: *ST* I q. 43 a. 4 co.: ‘missio … importat processionem ab alio … cum pater non sit ab alio, nullo modo convenit sibi mitti’. Verified as a comparison. The opinion’s holder is unnamed. Still open.]
The whole Trinity *incarnates* (effects the incarnation) but only the Son is *incarnate*: a standard example that active and passive terms in God do not correspond one to one.
Following B's *honor*; A prints *bonor*.

anchor.lemma: vtrum relatio quecunque possit fundare respectum

notes.text: A question whether a relation can be the foundation of a further relation (relation of relation). Its place in Scotus's dd. 14–16 has not been identified; it may come from a later Scotist (compare the *Reportatio* or Francis of Meyronnes).

Attributed to Hilary of Poitiers. Not located; compare *De Trin.* (Hilary) III–VII on the Son's birth by nature, not will. [Checked: Hilary, *De Trin.* (PL 10, archive.org OCR of Migne). Searches for *necessitas* near *Filius/nativitas/natura* found nothing usable, because the OCR of this volume is very poor. Scotus *Ord.* I d. 15 is not in the local Wadding text. Still open.] [Checked: Hilary, *De Trin.* IX (PL 10, la.wikisource text of Migne). There is no *necessitas … constituit*. IX 56 has *Nativitas Filii patrem constituit majorem*. Gorris's *necessitas* may be a misreading of an abbreviated *nativitas*. This is a conjecture; the English is unchanged.]

anchor.lemma: si relatio potest immediate fundare substantiam

notes.text: Thus A (*Primum si relatio …*). B reads *Primum relatio potest immediate fundare substantiam* (without *si*). Both are elliptical for *Primum vtrum*.
*Sanctus doctor*: Thomas Aquinas (canonized 1323), set against *doctor* without epithet, i.e. Scotus, the *Doctor subtilis*.

As printed. *ST* I q. 39 a. 2 concerns the plurality of persons and essence, so the reference may be corrupt. Aquinas's teaching that the relation does not found the substance is better sought in *ST* I q. 28 aa. 1–2.  B also *q. 39. arti. 2.*
Thus A and B. The argument requires *causalitas* (compare *ista causalitas* immediately after); the translation reads ‘causality’.

Aristotle, *Physics* I (cf. 9, 192a13–14, matter with form as *concausa*). The wording looks like an *auctoritas* rather than a quotation: compare the *Auctoritates Aristotelis*, which has a similar maxim that matter and form are causes of the accidents. [Checked: *Phys.* I 9, 192a13–14 (First1KGreek text): ἡ μὲν γὰρ ὑπομένουσα συναιτία τῇ μορφῇ τῶν γιγνομένων ἐστίν (the matter that persists is a co-cause, with the form, of what comes to be). This is the nearest Aristotelian text. The maxim about the causes of *accidents* is not in Aristotle in this form. The *Auctoritates Aristotelis* were not consulted. Probable.]

anchor.lemma: fundat respectum primum. quia respectum quem fundat

notes.text: A is corrupt here. B reads *fundat respectum quadruplicem. Primus respectus quem fundat est relatio distinctionis*, which the enumeration that follows (*Secundus … Tertius … Quartus*) requires. The translation follows B.
B reads *fundari* for A's *fundare* (passive spiration ‘be founded’ vs ‘found’). Not substantive for the solution, which concerns relations founded *by* a divine relation.

Pseudo-Dionysius on order among the divine properties; perhaps *De div. nom.* II. Not located. [Checked: no Latin Dionysius (Eriugena, Sarracenus, or the *Corpus Dionysiacum*) was available on the box or opened in this batch. Still open.]
A prints a single letter between points, *b* or *h*. B reads *minor* here (*pater est relatio minor*?). Neither yields a clear sense; the word is left untranslated.
A is barely legible in the reproduction and could be read *dissimilis*. B clearly has *diffinibilis*, which the answer (*diffinitionem minime*) requires.
A and B *causaliter*; read *causalitas*.
Supplied from B (*quadruplicem*); A has *primum. quia*.

*fundare substantiam*: literally ‘found a substance’, but the argument shows that the sense is ‘be founded immediately on a substance’ (*fundatur super materiam et formam*). The same applies in 049-03.

anchor.lemma: vtrum in missione visibili spiritus sancti spiritus sanctus referatur ad creaturam

notes.text: Scotus treats the visible mission in *Ord.* I dd. 14–16. The question whether God is related to the creature by a real relation is Scotus's *Ord.* I d. 30 qq. 1–2. Which text Gorris abridges here has not been checked. [Checked: Wadding/Vivès *Ord.* I d. 30 qq. 1–2, ‘Utrum de Deo dicatur aliqua relatio ex tempore; Utrum Dei ad creaturam possit esse aliqua relatio realis’, matches the substance of s050-02/03. Gorris's preliminary conclusions on the visible mission run parallel to Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* d. 16 a. 1 q. 2 (‘Ad quid sit utilis missio visibilis Spiritus sancti’) and q. 3 (‘Quibus modis facta sit missio visibilis’), Quaracchi. *Ord.* I dd. 14–16 are not in the local Wadding text. Probable.]

The four visible species: the dove at the Baptism (Mt 3:16), the bright cloud at the Transfiguration (Mt 17:5), the breath (Jn 20:22, *insufflavit*), and the tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). Thomas, *ST* I q. 43 a. 7 ad 6, has the same list of four, but gives different purposes: the dove for the authority to give grace through regeneration, the cloud for the abundance of doctrine, the breath for the power of the ministry of the sacraments, and the tongues for the office of teaching. Gorris's purposes (humility, illumination of truth, fraternal charity, and preaching) are not Thomas's. [Checked: *ST* I q. 43 a. 7 ad 6 (Corpus Thomisticum): ‘in Baptismo quidem sub specie columbae … ad ostendendum in Christo auctoritatem donandi gratiam … sub specie nubis lucidae, ad ostendendam exuberantiam doctrinae … sub specie flatus, ad ostendendam potestatem ministerii … sub linguis igneis, ad ostendendum officium doctrinae’. The earlier claim of ‘similar purposes’ has been corrected.]

*Relatio fundamentalis*: God is ‘related’ only in that his being is the foundation of the creature's real relation to him. It is neither a real relation nor a relation of reason. The term has not been traced to a particular Scotist author. [Checked: a search of the local Wadding/Vivès text of *Ord.* I d. 30 qq. 1–2 for *fundamental-* found no hit. The term has not been traced. Still open.]

anchor.lemma: nec per actum rationis diuine vt dicit Henricus

notes.text: Henry of Ghent held that God's relations to creatures are relations of reason caused by the divine intellect. Scotus reports and rejects this in *Ord.* I d. 30 qq. 1–2. Henry's own locus (*Summa* or *Quodlibet*) has not been verified. [Checked: the Wadding note to *Ord.* I d. 30 q. 2 cites ‘Henric. quodl. 7. quaest. 1. et quodl. 9. quaest. 4 [sic]. et quodl. 3. quaest. 4’, and the Scholium says ‘Ponit responsionem Henrici ad utramque quaestionem’. Henry, *Quodl.* IX q. 1 (Badius 1518) is ‘de relatione dei ad creaturas … Vtrum scilicet omnis relatio inter deum & creaturam sit quia ipsa creatura refertur ad deum: & non econuerso’. It says that God's relation to creatures arises through the essences known ‘ab intellectu diuino’ and ‘est in deo relatio secundum rationem ex parte voluntatis’. *Quodl.* IX q. 1 is the probable locus.]

anchor.lemma: Spiritus sanctus visus est in specie columbe

anchor.lemma: Johan. 14. ego in patre et pater in me est

notes.text: Jn 14:10 (*Ego in Patre et Pater in me est*).

Henry of Ghent, *Summa quaestionum ordinariarum*, art. 53 q. 10: ‘quod in diuinis non sit vna persona in alia mutuo & eodem modo’ (the objection). Henry asks whether one person is in another by substance or by relation, and quotes Hilary, *De Trin.* III 1. Gorris gives no article number. [Checked: Henry, *Summa* art. 53 q. 10 (Badius 1520, via SCTA). The Wadding note to *Ord.* I d. 19 q. 2 cites ‘Henr. sum. art. 1. et quodlib. 6. quaest. 5’. Hilary, *De Trin.* III 1–4 (on Jn 14:10). [Checked: Hilary, *De Trin.* III 1 (PL 10, la.wikisource): ‘Affert plerisque obscuritatem sermo Domini, cum dicit: Ego in Patre, et Pater in me’. This is quoted by Lombard, *Sent.* I d. 19, and by Henry, *Summa* art. 53 q. 10. Verified.]

anchor.lemma: sicut auis est in laqueo per pedem

anchor.lemma: vtrum tres persone sint equales in potentia

notes.text: Corresponds to Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 20 q. un. (on the equality of the persons in power, and whether the *potentia generandi* falls under omnipotence). [Checked: Wadding/Vivès heading, ‘Liber 1 > Distinctio 20 > Quaestio 1: Utrum tres personae sint aequales in potentia’. Verified.]

notes.text: Ps.-Augustine (Fulgentius), *De fide ad Petrum*. Compare 1.4–5. notes.text: Aristotle, *Phys.* III 1, 200b26–28.

anchor.lemma: potentia generandi non cadit sub omnipotentia

notes.text: Scotus's thesis (*Ord.* I d. 20): omnipotence regards only what is possible *ad extra*. The notional power of generation is therefore not an object of omnipotence. This is consistent with ¶4. [Checked: *Ord.* I d. 20 q. 1 (Wadding/Vivès). Scotus refutes the view that generating belongs to the Father's omnipotence but not the Son's: ‘ergo carens tali potentia ut Filius, non habet omnipotentiam absolute’. notes.text: Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* d. 4, *dubia circa litteram*, dub. 3. [Checked: Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* d. 4 dub. 3 (Quaracchi I, OCR). Verified.]

anchor.lemma: vtrum deus sit nominabilis ab homine viatore aliquo nomine proprio

notes.text: Corresponds to Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 22 q. un. (on whether God is nameable by a wayfarer with a proper name). [Checked: Wadding/Vivès heading, ‘Liber 1 > Distinctio 22 > Quaestio 1: Utrum Deus sit nominabilis a nobis aliquo nomine significante essentiam divinam in se, ut est “haec”’. Verified.]
*Doctor solemnis* is Henry of Ghent; the work is his *Summa quaestionum ordinariarum*.

B has *ar. 22. q. 12. et. 3.*, with the *et* written out, which confirms the reading of A's third *z* as the *et* sign. ‘q. 12’ may still be an error for ‘q. 1, 2’ in the common source; Henry, *Summa* a. 22 (on the knowledge of God), and also a. 24, have not been checked.

Henry of Ghent, *Quodl.* V q. 1 and XIII q. 1. In V q. 1, on the plurality of attributes, the intellect ‘primo & simplici intelligentia concipit ipsam essentiam sub ratione essentiae, & deinde negotiando’ forms the rational distinctions. In XIII q. 1, on whether God can be seen *sub ratione veri* without *sub ratione boni*, the divine nature ‘obiectiue se offert & representat vt vnum simpliciter sub vna ratione simplicissima tantum, videlicet sub ratione esse’. anchor.lemma: vix potest reperiri ista questio completa nisi compleatur aut ex reportatoriis parisiensibus aut aliunde

notes.text: This is an important philological remark. anchor.lemma: vtrum persona secundum quod dicit aliquid commune patri filio et spiritui sancto dicat precipue aliquid secunde intentionis

notes.text: Corresponds to Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 23 q. un. (whether ‘person’, as common to the three, signifies a second intention). [Checked: Wadding/Vivès heading, ‘Liber 1 > Distinctio 23 > Quaestio 1: Utrum persona secundum quod dicit aliquid commune Patri et Filio et Spiritui Sancto, dicat praecise aliquid secundae intentionis’. B omits *eius*. B checked.

anchor.lemma: respectus intrinsecus adueniens. quia ponitur positis extremis

notes.text: Scotist terminology: a relation *intrinsecus adveniens* arises necessarily once its extremes are posited (likeness, equality, number), unlike a relation *extrinsecus adveniens*. B garbles this: *respectus intransitus adueniens quia predicatur presentis extremis*. A is correct. B checked.
Cross-reference to Book II (Lombard, *Sent.* II d. 9, on the orders of angels).

B: *cum numerus sit forma positiua et positiuum non constituitur pro parua tantum et ideo numerus non constituitur ex vnitatibus .ix. metha.* B omits *et vnitas priuatiua*, corrupts *per priuatiuum* into *pro parua tantum*, and has *non constituitur ex vnitatibus* where A has *constituitur vno*. B checked.
Aristotle, *Metaph.* X 1 (unity as the measure and principle of number), here numbered *9*. The medieval Latin numbering of the books varied. The numbering has not been checked.
Aristotle, *Metaph.* V 14, 1020b7–8: six is not twice three but once six. B: *Nam sex vel semel sexies*. B checked.

Cf. Euclid, *Elem.* VII def. 2, and Boethius, *Inst. arith.* I 3 (*numerus est unitatum collectio*); Aristotle, *Metaph.* X 1, 1053a30 (number as a plurality of units). B: *aggrauata*, an error. B checked.
Aristotle, *De caelo* I 1, 268a10–20: the triad is the number of the whole.

anchor.lemma: Item tres sunt qui testimonium dant in celo

notes.text: 1 Jn 5:7 (the *Comma Johanneum* of the Vulgate).
B: *similitudinem*, an error for *solitudinem*. B checked.
Signature at the foot of p. 99 printed *g.z* (= g.2). Headline *Di.xxv. Q.i*, although d. 24 runs on until halfway down the page.

anchor.lemma: a relation that comes from within

notes.text: *respectus intrinsecus adueniens*; see the Latin note.

anchor.lemma: persona ita est ad se sicut deus

notes.text: Augustine, *De Trin.* VII 6.11: *non enim aliud est Deo esse, aliud personam esse* (checked locally).

anchor.lemma: trinitas diuina est personarum inuicem relatiuarum

notes.text: A paraphrase of Augustine, *De Trin.* V–VII (the persons are said relatively to one another); the exact wording has not been located.
Augustine, *De Trin.* VII (see n1145).

anchor.lemma: et aliqua persona sit absoluta vt potentia

notes.text: B: *cum ens diuidatur … et aliqua sint absoluta vt potentia*. B gives better sense: *being* is divided into absolute and relative, and the absolute example (power) is not a person. A’s *persona* is probably a compositor’s anticipation, and A also lacks *ens*. The translation follows B. B checked.
An English Thomas, presumably a Dominican (Thomas Sutton?) or Thomas Wylton; possibly Thomas Jorz (*Thomas Anglicus*). Not identified. B: *Tho. anglicus* (= A). B checked.

This second series follows Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 25 q. un. closely (Wadding text checked locally): ‘person’ is not a proper relation (it is common); it is not a common relation (the *duplum/multiplex* argument); it is not the substance (which is not numbered); and the two views, that ‘person’ is a double negation connoting the persons, the relations and the essence, or that it is something positive and abstracting.

anchor.lemma: Si sunt inquit tres persone: commune est eis hoc quod est persona

notes.text: Augustine, *De Trin.* VII 4.7: *Si enim tres Personae, commune est eis id quod persona est* (checked locally). Gorris’s *c. 7* is his chapter division.
A *dimidium*; B *duplum dimidij*, which the sense requires (cf. *multiplex dimidii* following). The translation follows B. B checked.
Cf. *Ord.* I d. 25 q. un.: Scotus sets out both views without condemning the first.

anchor.lemma: some things are absolute, as power

notes.text: The translation follows B (*cum ens diuidatur … et aliqua sint absoluta*). A reads ‘and some person is absolute, as power’.
The translation follows B *dimidij*; A has *dimidium*.

anchor.lemma: vtrum persone diuine constituantur in esse personali per relationes originis

notes.text: Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 26 q. un. (*Utrum personae divinae constituantur in esse personali per relationes originis*; Wadding text checked locally).

*substantia* belongs to Boethius’ definition (*rationalis naturae individua substantia*); Richard of St Victor (*De Trin.* IV 21–22) rejects it in favour of *existentia*. The attribution to Richard reflects the conflation already seen in n945.
Boethius, *De Trin.* 6: *substantia continet unitatem, relatio multiplicat trinitatem*; cited in *Ord.* I d. 26.

anchor.lemma: quidquid est ad se est omnibus commune

notes.text: Augustine, *De Trin.* V 8.9 (*quidquid ad se dicitur*), as cited in *Ord.* I d. 26.
Praepositinus of Cremona († c. 1210). Cf. *Ord.* I d. 26: *opinio … Praepositivi, quod personae seipsis distinguuntur* (Wadding, checked locally).
B: *se totum distingui*. B checked.
‘Henry the Preacher’, i.e. a Dominican Henry. Not identified; perhaps a confusion with Henry of Ghent, whose arguments against Praepositinus Scotus reports.

A (reading not quite clear) and B (*q. xxxix. ar. ii*) both cite q. 39 a. 2. The locus is Aquinas, *ST* I q. 40 a. 2 (*utrum relationes distinguant et constituant personas*), which is also the locus Wadding gives. A and B share the error. B checked.
John of Ripa OFM (fl. 1350s), *Lectura in I Sent.* and *Quodlibet*. The numbers *26* and *25* (B *xxvi. et xxv.*) have not been checked.

Bonaventure was canonised by Sixtus IV on 14 April 1482, four years before this edition; hence *sanctus*. Locus: Bonaventure, *In I Sent.* d. 25 a. 1 q. 1? (not checked). B omits *Johannis*. B checked.

*inuetur* gives no sense; read *iuuetur* (‘so that John [of Ripa] may be helped by John [Bonaventure]’), a pun. B: *vt iohannes inuere videatur in principio suo dist. xxv. q. i.*, also corrupt. B checked.
Whether Lombard himself (cf. *Sent.* I d. 26 c. 2–3) or the *magister* Praepositinus is meant has not been determined.
B: *persone in diuinis*. B checked.
In *Ord.* I d. 26 Scotus treats the view that the persons are constituted by something absolute as probable and does not condemn it; Gorris’s ‘the opinion of the Doctor, and the true one’ simplifies.

Ps.-Dionysius, *De div. nom.* I 1 (Latin translations: *non audendum … dicere aut cogitare praeter ea quae nobis divinitus ex sacris eloquiis sunt expressa*). B: *Non est credendum*, an error. B checked.

anchor.lemma: scilicet pater verbum et spiritus sanctus

notes.text: 1 Jn 5:7. B: *pater et filius et spiritus sanctus*. B checked.
Anselm, *De processione Spiritus sancti* 1: *ubi non obviat aliqua relationis oppositio*.
B: *Sed alias quereret*. B checked.
*insistens*/*assistens*: the terminology goes back to Gilbert of Poitiers (relations as *assistentes*, not inhering), discussed by Bonaventure and Scotus. Exact source not checked.

anchor.lemma: so that John may be helped by John

notes.text: Reading *iuuetur* for A’s *inuetur*; see the Latin note.

anchor.lemma: vtrum relatio in creatura differat realiter a fundamento

notes.text: The doctrine follows Scotus, *Ord.* II d. 1 qq. 4–5 (Wadding) against Henry of Ghent: relation is really distinct from its foundation. Scotus has no *Ord.* I d. 26 q. 2.

anchor.lemma: omne quod est ad aliud est aliquid ab eo

notes.text: Augustine, *De Trin.* VII 1.2 (*omnis essentia quae relative dicitur est etiam aliquid excepto relativo*). B: *ad aliquid est aliud ab eo*. A’s *aliquid* matches Augustine. B checked.
Peter Auriol OFM († 1322). His view that relation is a being of reason is in his *Scriptum* I d. 30 (locus not checked).

Henry of Ghent (cf. *Quodl.* V q. 2; IX q. 3): a relation is not a thing distinct from its foundation, since a new relation comes to a thing without change in it. Scotus reports and refutes this in *Ord.* II d. 1 q. 4 (Wadding, checked locally).
B: *fundamentum esset sine relatione*. B checked.

anchor.lemma: Hec etiam patet. quia distinguntur essentialiter

notes.text: B: *distinguuntur realiter*. B checked.
B: *formaliter dicitur saluis*, corrupt. B checked.

anchor.lemma: Sed suppleret vicem terminationis per primam sequeretur quod haberet nouum esse

notes.text: Sense obscure. Perhaps read *Si suppleret* and take *per primam … per secundam* to refer to the two ways (the term vs the formal *ratio* of filiation). B: *haberet nouum quod est impossibile per secundam*, omitting *esse* and *vero non*. B checked.
The thesis that relation is caused by what produces the opposite foundation has not been located in Scotus or a named Scotist.

Aristotle, *Phys.* V 2, 225b11–13 denies that there is motion in the category of relation; the commentators (Averroes) teach that relation follows motion *per accidens*. B: *ii. phi.*, wrong. B checked.
*abstractionem* is probably for *subtractionem* (the counterpart of *susceptionem*); the translation renders the sense.
The sentence is obscure in A and B; see the Latin note. The translation is tentative.

anchor.lemma: the existence of the same [foundation remaining]

notes.text: *cum existentia eiusdem*: the foundation still exists.

anchor.lemma: vtrum verbum mentis create sit intellectio actualis

notes.text: Scotus, *Ord.* I d. 27 qq. 1–3 (Wadding text checked locally), where Henry’s view of the *verbum* as *intellectio declarativa* is reported.
Probably a paraphrase of Augustine, *De Trin.* XV 11.20: *verbum quod foris sonat signum est verbi quod intus lucet*.
Cf. Augustine, *De Trin.* IX 10.15 (*verbum … est … cum amore notitia*). Not checked.
Henry of Ghent. His doctrine of the *verbum* is in *Summa* aa. 58–59 and *Quodl.* V q. 25; *Quodl.* VI q. 1 has not been checked.

anchor.lemma: voces sunt signa earum que sunt in anima passionum

notes.text: Aristotle, *De int.* 1, 16a3–4 (Boethius’ translation: *sunt ergo ea quae sunt in voce earum quae sunt in anima passionum notae*).
Augustine, *Enchiridion* 7.22: words were instituted *ut eis … cogitationes suas perferat* (quoted from memory, not checked against the text). B also reads *compositiones animorum*. B checked.
